  • End: Brown cries "Faith! Faith! look up to heaven, and resist the wicked one!" Instantly he is alone in the calm, silent forest, the rock cold and a twig dripping cold dew on his cheek. The next morning he walks into Salem Village. The minister blesses him, Deacon Gookin is praying, and Goody Cloyse is teaching a little girl her catechism, which Brown snatches the child away from. Faith runs out joyfully to meet him, pink ribbons and all, but he looks at her sternly and passes without a word. Hawthorne asks whether Brown only fell asleep and "dreamed a wild dream of a witch-meeting", and answers "Be it so if you will". Either way, Brown becomes "a stern, a sad, a darkly meditative, a distrustful, if not a desperate man". He can't stand to hear hymns or sermons, shrinks from Faith at night, and sees hypocrisy everywhere. When he dies an old man, followed to the grave by Faith, children, grandchildren and neighbors, they carve no hopeful verse on his tombstone, "for his dying hour was gloom".
  • Character: Goodman Brown: Protagonist. Young, naive, curious about evil, then bitter. Dynamic: he returns changed forever. Importance: every man who loses his faith in others.
  • Character: Faith: Brown's wife, with her pink ribbons. Importance: both a person and a symbol of his religious faith; "My Faith is gone!" works both ways.
  • Character: the traveler / the devil: Older man resembling Brown, with a serpent staff. Importance: the tempter; his claims make Brown doubt his family and church.
  • Characters: Goody Cloyse, the minister, Deacon Gookin: Respected Puritan leaders seen serving the devil. Importance: they expose the town's hypocrisy (Goody Cloyse and Martha Carrier are real Salem-trial names).
  • Point of view: Third person, limited mostly to Brown, so the reader shares his uncertainty about what is real.
  • Themes: Loss of innocence and faith; hypocrisy of the Puritans; the idea that evil lives in everyone; doubt that poisons a whole life.
  • Other important factors: Allegory and symbols (Faith; the pink ribbons for innocence; the forest for the moral wilderness; the serpent staff for evil); Biblical allusion (Eden, baptism and communion parodies); foreshadowing; deliberate ambiguity. The Introduction says Hawthorne added moral "specific gravity" and describes the story as a journey from light into darkness and back.

"The Custom House" (Hawthorne, 1850)

Hawthorne's long autobiographical essay that introduces The Scarlet Letter. It is nonfiction blended with one big literary trick: Hawthorne claims the novel that follows is a true story he found, not one he invented.
  • Intro: Hawthorne describes his job as Surveyor of the Custom House in Salem, Massachusetts, where he inspects incoming ships' cargo and collects duties for the federal government. He is openly unimpressed with his co-workers: a crew of old, half-asleep political appointees who got their jobs through favoritism and do almost no real work. The most dignified is the elderly "Collector," a Revolutionary War veteran (based on General James Miller) who naps through most of the day but still commands respect.
  • Middle: Poking around in the building's dusty upper story, Hawthorne says he discovers a small bundle left by a former Surveyor named Jonathan Pue: old documents and a faded, moth-eaten scrap of scarlet cloth shaped like a capital letter "A," with gold embroidery. Pue's papers tell the story of a woman named Hester Prynne, who lived generations earlier. When Hawthorne holds the letter to his chest, he claims to feel it burn, "as if the letter were not of red cloth, but red-hot iron." He frames The Scarlet Letter as simply his retelling of Pue's manuscript, not his own invention. He also reflects at length on his Puritan ancestors, especially a stern early judge who persecuted Quakers and a witch-trial judge, and says he feels a kind of inherited guilt that his writing might be paying off.
  • End: Hawthorne loses his customs job when a change in presidential administration brings in a new political appointee to replace him — he jokes that he has been "guillotined," though, unlike a real beheaded victim, he survives it and can write about it afterward. Being pushed out of the practical, unimaginative world of the Custom House is what frees him to finally become a writer and finish the novel.
  • Character: Hawthorne (the narrator): The essay's first-person voice, blending the real Nathaniel Hawthorne with a partly invented persona. Importance: he sets up why the reader should trust the story that follows, and explains his own conflicted identity as both a Custom House officer and a writer.
  • Character: the Collector (based on General James Miller): An elderly, dignified Revolutionary War veteran who nominally runs the Custom House but naps through most of his duties. Importance: represents a fading, honorable past next to Hawthorne's more cynical, satirical view of the other officers.
  • Character: Jonathan Pue: A former Surveyor of the Custom House, long dead, whose old manuscript and the scarlet letter "A" Hawthorne claims to discover. Importance: the whole "found manuscript" conceit depends on him; he is Hawthorne's fictional source for Hester Prynne's story.
  • Character: Hawthorne's Puritan ancestors: Unnamed but based on real ancestors, including a judge who persecuted Quakers and a judge from the Salem witch trials. Importance: Hawthorne says he feels their harshness as a kind of family curse, and sees his writing as a way of answering for it.
  • Point of view: First person. Hawthorne writes as himself, an autobiographical essayist, though he mixes in the invented discovery of Pue's manuscript as if it were also true.
  • Themes: The tension between practical, commercial life (the Custom House) and the imaginative life of an artist; the weight of inherited guilt from Puritan ancestors; using a "found document" to make fiction feel authentic; gentle satire of government patronage jobs.
  • Other important factors: Genre: nonfiction essay, but built around an invented frame device (the discovered manuscript), a technique used to make an invented story feel like a rediscovered true one. Extended metaphor: losing his job as a political "guillotining." The scarlet letter "A" is introduced here as already strange and almost magical (it burns him) before the novel proper even begins. Hawthorne also describes his parlor at night, moonlight mixed with firelight, as the ideal condition for his imagination -- the mindset he needed to finally write the novel.
  • Important lines — Key passages from the essay, in order, for close-reading and presentation prep.
  • Lines 5-25 "It is a little… or his own.": Opening paragraph -- Hawthorne explains why he's writing another autobiographical sketch (he did one before, in "The Old Manse") and sets the ground rules for how personal an author may get without "violating either the reader's rights or his own."
  • Lines 26-55 "It will be…barbed arrows": Explains this sketch's real purpose (to explain how he got the manuscript and prove it's authentic), then describes the actual Custom-House building in Salem, including the American eagle over the door -- federal symbol, warns everyone off, "has no great tenderness."
  • Lines 56-86 "The pavement… Custom-House officers": Describes the mostly-empty, grass-grown Custom-House, the occasional busy morning when ships arrive, and introduces the row of old, half-asleep officers sitting around -- "Custom-House officers."
  • Lines 87-123 "Furthermore…to know": Describes his own office and desk, notes he's since been swept out of the job by political "reform," and begins reflecting on his strange, deep attachment to plain, unglamorous Salem.
  • Lines 124-153 "But the sentiment… with mine": Introduces his Puritan ancestor (persecuted Quakers) and that ancestor's son (a Salem witch-trial judge) -- his sense of inherited family guilt, and his ancestors' imagined scorn at him being "a writer of story-books."
  • Lines 154-181 "Planted… earth": Traces his family's generations in Salem (mostly sea captains) and how deeply the family became rooted -- literally buried -- in the town's soil.
  • Lines 182-214 "On emerging… to Paradise": Explains how he actually got the Surveyor job (a political appointment, "the President's commission"), meets his new staff of very old officers, and jokes that neither door of the Custom-House "opens on the road to Paradise."
  • Lines 215-248 "The greater part…any remedy": Most of his officers are Whigs, but he -- not a political operator -- doesn't fire them; describes their comic incompetence (missing real smuggling, over-fussing small things) with dry irony.
  • Lines 249-302 "Unless people… of the two": He grows genuinely fond of the old officers despite everything, then introduces the ancient, cheerful permanent Inspector -- pure appetite, "no soul, no heart, no mind" beyond his stomach.
  • Lines 303-333 "I used to… axe and handsaw": Continues the Inspector's portrait: he remembers old dinners in vivid detail but nothing else; the "chief tragic event" of his life was a famously tough goose he once tried to carve.
  • Lines 334-364 "But it is… alien weeds": Moves on to the Collector (General Miller) -- a once-great, now-frail soldier, described as hard to read as the ruined fortress of Ticonderoga, "overgrown... with grass and alien weeds."
  • Lines 365-413 "Nevertheless… desk": Gives the Collector real dignity -- a quiet, massive inner strength ("a deep, red glow, as of iron in a furnace") -- and pictures him as an old sword out of place among the office's inkstands and paper-folders.
  • Lines 414-458 "There was one… the change": Gives the Collector's famous battle motto, "I'll try, sir!," then introduces a totally different figure: the sharp, efficient "man of business" clerk who actually keeps the whole Custom-House running.
  • Lines 459-500 "Literature.. now writing": Hawthorne says he stopped caring about literature entirely while working there, valued only as "a tolerably good Surveyor of the Customs," and realizes how little his writing means to the people around him.
  • Lines 501-550 "In the second… skull itself": The key discovery scene: his own name is now famous only as a customs stamp on cargo; poking through attic barrels he finds an old parchment package -- Surveyor Jonathan Pue's actual royal commission and papers (Pue's exhumed remains, he notes, were basically just a skeleton and a well-preserved wig).
  • Lines 551-586 "They were documents… upon the floor": Describes Pue's private antiquarian notes, then the discovery of the scarlet cloth letter "A" itself -- and the famous moment Hawthorne holds it to his chest, feels it burn "as if the letter were not of red cloth, but red-hot iron," and drops it in shock.
  • Lines 587-609 "In the absorbing… the outline": He opens the roll of paper wrapped around the letter and finds Pue's manuscript telling Hester Prynne's story -- the passage where Hawthorne explicitly claims the novel is "authenticated" by a real document, while admitting he invented plenty of the details himself.
  • Lines 610-625 "This incident… I will": The whimsical ghost-of-Surveyor-Pue scene -- Hawthorne imagines Pue's ghost formally commissioning him to write up Hester Prynne's story. "Do this," says the ghost, "and the profit shall be all your own!" Hawthorne answers: "I will!"
  • Lines 626-654 "On Hester… many-hued description": Hawthorne obsessively paces the Custom-House halls thinking about Hester Prynne's story, annoying the old Inspector -- but his imagination stays dead. Says if he'd stayed in the job "through ten Presidencies," the novel never would have been written.
  • Lines 655-685 "If the imaginative… from me": The famous moonlight passage -- moonlight in a familiar room is the ideal condition for a writer's imagination, turning ordinary objects into "things of intellect." None of it worked on him: "An entire class of susceptibilities... was gone from me."
  • Lines 686-716 "It is my belief… of mankind": He reflects he might have written something better by capturing the old sea-captain Inspector's storytelling gift instead. Ends with his verdict on Custom-House work: it doesn't let a man "share in the united effort of mankind."
  • Lines 717-740 "An effect… manly character": The passage on leaning on "the mighty arm of the Republic" -- his theory that public office slowly destroys a man's self-reliance, comparing a government salary to "the Devil's wages."
  • Lines 741-777 "Here was… struck off": His fear of becoming like the old Inspector, then the political guillotine section -- Taylor's election, the Whigs sweeping Democrats from office. "My head was the first that fell!"
  • Lines 778-804 "In short… that fell / The moment… friendly one": Losing his job actually suits him -- he compares it to a man who wanted to commit suicide and got the "good hap to be murdered" instead.
  • Lines 806-828 "Meanwhile… literary man / Now it was… of quiet": Newspapers mock him as Irving's Headless Horseman; freed from the job, he becomes a writer again. Pue's old papers "came into play" -- this is where he actually starts writing the novel. Ends: "For I am in the realm of quiet!"
  • Lines 829-849 "The life of… without me / It may be… town pump": Final farewell to the Custom-House and Salem, naming the real merchants he worked among and saying the town won't miss him. Closes on the ironic Town Pump joke as his one hoped-for legacy.

Background and reference

Everything around the six stories: devices and terms, the anthology intro, Romanticism, Emerson, the American Dream, how to answer analysis questions, the authors cheat sheet, handouts and the periods timeline. Each block starts with its own bold heading.
  • Words and tools (devices, terms and settings) — Every literary device and term for the unit in one place, followed by each story's setting.
  • Anthropomorphism: giving animals or living things human traits (the bluejays).
  • Personification: giving nonliving objects human traits (the House of Usher's "eye-like" windows).
  • Imagery: language that appeals to the senses.
  • Mood / Tone: mood is the feeling created for the reader; tone is the author's attitude toward the subject.
  • Setting: time and place.
  • Characterization: how the author reveals a character. Direct: the narrator tells you. Indirect (STEAL): Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks.
  • Round / flat, static / dynamic: round characters are complex, flat have one or two traits; static characters don't change, dynamic ones do (Goodman Brown).
  • Point of view: who narrates: first person, third limited, omniscient. A frame narrative is a story that holds another story.
  • Allusion: an indirect reference to a well-known person, place, text or event (the serpent staff and Eden).
  • Foreshadowing: hints about what comes next (the Mad Trist sounds).
  • Symbolism / Allegory: a symbol stands for a bigger idea; an allegory is a whole story whose characters and events stand for moral or political meanings.
  • Irony: verbal (saying the opposite of what you mean), situational (the opposite of what is expected), dramatic (the reader knows more than the character).
  • Juxtaposition: putting things side by side for effect (Baker's serious tone vs. an absurd story).
  • Metaphor / Simile / Hyperbole: direct comparison; comparison with like or as; exaggeration ("two tons" of acorns).
  • Diction / Syntax: word choice; sentence structure.
  • Dialect: speech showing a region or class (Jim Baker).
  • Ambiguity: an ending or event left open to more than one reading (Brown's dream).
  • Tall tale / Yarn / Fable: exaggerated story told as true; a beast fable uses animals to teach a point.
  • Gothic: horror plus romance in gloomy old buildings (Poe).
  • Spenserian stanza: nine lines, ABABBCBCC, last line longer (Keats).
  • Rhetorical appeals: ethos (credibility), logos (logic), pathos (emotion).
  • SOAPSTone: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.
  • Setting: "Rip Van Winkle": a Dutch village and the Kaatskill (Catskill) Mountains on the Hudson, before and after the American Revolution (about 1770s to 1790s).
  • Setting: "The Eve of St. Agnes": a medieval castle on a freezing St. Agnes' Eve, January 20, during a loud feast; the lovers escape into a storm.
  • Setting: "The Fall of the House of Usher": the decaying Usher mansion beside a black tarn on a dull, soundless autumn day, ending on a stormy night.
  • Setting: "Baker's Bluejay Yarn": a lonely, empty log cabin in the woods of California (near Yosemite), told by a miner.
  • Setting: "Young Goodman Brown": Puritan Salem Village, Massachusetts, in the late 1600s; the dark forest at night, then the village next morning.
  • Introduction to Great American Short Stories — has its own section at the top of this unit (the first concept), with the editors' main claims in plain words.
  • Romanticism and Washington Irving — Romanticism is the frame for the whole unit. Irving's packet content is on the exam, so know the movement's vocabulary as well as the man.
  • Romanticism (late 18th to mid 19th century, per the Britannica handout) rejects the order, calm, harmony, balance and rationality of Classicism and late-18th-century Neoclassicism, and reacts against the Enlightenment, rationalism and physical materialism.
  • Romanticism emphasizes the individual, the subjective, the irrational, the imaginative, the emotional and the transcendental; it loves nature, exalts emotion over reason and the senses over intellect, and has a predilection for the exotic, mysterious, occult, monstrous and even satanic.
  • Classicism and Neoclassicism prized order, reason and restraint; Rationalism trusted reason above feeling. Romantic writers push back with intuition, mystery and the sublime.
  • Washington Irving (1783-1859) is often called the first American author to win international fame. "Rip Van Winkle" appeared in The Sketch Book (1819-20) under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon.
  • Irving frames the tale as papers left by the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker, a playful fake-history frame (historiography: how history gets written).
  • Romantic markers to spot in the stories: dreamlike or supernatural events, wild nature, nostalgia for the past, a lone individual against society, and strong emotion.
  • Packet vocabulary to know: Classicism, Neoclassicism, Enlightenment, Rationalism, Transcendental, exaltation, predilection, occult, satanic, historiography.
  • English Romanticism began in the 1790s with Wordsworth and Coleridge's Lyrical Ballads; Wordsworth's 1800 Preface called poetry "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings". Blake was a third early poet; Keats, Byron and Shelley are the later high point; Scott is credited with the historical novel.
  • Gothic fiction combines horror and romance. Its origin is credited to Horace Walpole's The Castle of Otranto (1764, subtitled "A Gothic Story"); later examples include Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Poe, and Stoker's Dracula. "Gothic" refers to the pseudo-medieval buildings where many of the stories take place.
  • Emerson and Transcendentalism — The Emerson handout (Lesson #5) is an excerpt from "The Transcendentalist". Bullet-point summary of the argument is on your notes.
  • Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803-1882) was the leading voice of American Transcendentalism, a Romantic movement that trusts intuition, individual conscience and nature over institutions and tradition.
  • From the excerpt: the materialist "takes his departure from the external world" and esteems a man as one product of it, respecting society, government, social art, luxury and "every mass". The idealist "takes his departure from his consciousness, and reckons the world an appearance".
  • The idealist's measure is metaphysical: the rank things take in his consciousness, not their size or appearance. "Mind is the only reality, of which men and all other natures are better or worse reflectors." Nature, literature and history are "subjective phenomena".
  • The idealist does not respect government, church, charities, property or the arts for themselves, only as symbols of the laws of being, and sees facts flowing outward "from an invisible, unsounded centre in himself". His thought "is the Universe".
  • Use the handout: quote how Emerson defines each side, then say what he means and how you know from his diction.
  • Connect to the unit: Rip resists social duties (individual vs. society); Goodman Brown loses faith in his community; Poe's Roderick lives inside his own mind; Keats prizes imagination.
  • Emerson is nonfiction (an essay/lecture), so you can also discuss purpose, audience, tone and ethos, logos and pathos in it.
  • The American Dream (James Truslow Adams) — How can we critically interpret the American Dream? Start with James Truslow Adams' definition.
  • James Truslow Adams popularized the phrase in The Epic of America (1931): a dream of a land where life is better, richer and fuller for everyone, with opportunity for each person according to ability or achievement.
  • Adams stresses that it is not just cars and high wages but a social order where each person can reach their fullest stature. Notice how diction like "better and richer and fuller" makes it about more than money.
  • Handout details: Adams wrote it in The Epic of America (1931, pp. 214-215); the dream is "for the European upper classes" hard to interpret, many Americans had "grown weary and mistrustful of it", and each person should be "recognized by others for what they are, regardless of the fortuitous circumstances of birth or position".
  • The handout also quotes the Declaration of Independence (life, Liberty and the Pursuit of Happiness), asks whether homesteaders, immigrants and World War II veterans pursued the same dream, and notes critics who say it became material prosperity or is out of reach for the working poor. Thomas Wolfe is quoted on "his shining, golden opportunity".
  • Ask of each story: whose version of the dream is shown, and who is left out or disillusioned?
  • Rip Van Winkle: freedom from duty and the birth of a new nation. Goodman Brown: the Puritan ideal of a godly community, undone by hypocrisy. Baker's yarn: folksy Western tall tale that pokes fun at human effort.
  • Definition is a moving target: consider how the dream has evolved and what it is not.
  • How to write and answer analysis questions — Most analysis questions ask how an author uses a device to convey a message.
  • Use direct text evidence and cite it (author, title, page or line). Explain how the exact words create the effect.
  • For multi-part questions, write ONE cohesive response that covers every part, using transitions to link them to your claim.
  • Effective paragraph basic structure: claim, evidence, commentary, and a link back to the claim. Use the template on the Effective Paragraph handout for multiple quotes.
  • Mood-of-the-text (MOT) routine: underline evidence, circle the key word that creates the feeling, label the mood, then explain how the words work together.
  • Pivotal questions are open-ended and text-based, not hunt-and-fetch: To what extent... In what ways... For what reasons... How is/does... and why is it significant?
  • SOAPSTone (Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone) works on fiction and nonfiction; state purpose as a verb phrase (to warn, to satirize, to mourn).
  • Authors, dates and forms cheat sheet — A fast-recall table for the recognition questions. Dates are the standard publication years; check any date on your packet.
  • Irving (1783-1859): "Rip Van Winkle" (The Sketch Book, 1819-20). Romantic, satirical, folk-legend tone.
  • Keats (1795-1821): "The Eve of St. Agnes" (written 1819, published 1820). Narrative poem, Spenserian stanza.
  • Poe (1809-1849): "The Fall of the House of Usher" (1839). Gothic; contains "The Haunted Palace" and the "Mad Trist" of Ethelred.
  • Twain (1835-1910): "Baker's Bluejay Yarn" (1880). Humorous frame plus tall tale; anthropomorphism and dialect.
  • Hawthorne (1804-1864): "Young Goodman Brown" (1835). Dark Romanticism / Puritan allegory.
  • Emerson (1803-1882): "The Transcendentalist" (essay/lecture). Nonfiction; idealism vs. materialism.
  • Hawthorne (1804-1864): "The Custom House" (1850), the introductory essay to The Scarlet Letter. Nonfiction with an invented "found manuscript" frame.
  • Irving's life and impact (Lesson #1 handout) — The Irving handout is a Wikipedia biography with discussion questions. Expect accuracy-of-information and historical-context questions from it.
  • Washington Irving (April 3, 1783 - November 28, 1859) was born in Manhattan the same week New Yorkers learned of the British ceasefire that ended the Revolution. His mother named him for George Washington, whom he met at age six.
  • Boyhood trips up the Hudson, including the Catskill region (the setting of "Rip Van Winkle"), shaped him: he wrote that the Kaatskill Mountains had "the most witching effect on my boyish imagination". Tarrytown gave him Sleepy Hollow's Dutch customs and ghost stories.
  • Early writing: letters to the Morning Chronicle (1802) as Jonathan Oldstyle; the magazine Salmagundi (1807), which nicknamed New York "Gotham"; then A History of New-York by Diedrich Knickerbocker (1809), promoted with a hoax about the missing historian.
  • "Rip Van Winkle" is in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. Irving wrote it overnight in Birmingham, England, staying with his sister Sarah and her husband Henry van Wart. He lived abroad for 17 years (1815-1832).
  • He served as U.S. Minister to Spain (1842-1846), lived at Sunnyside, and is buried in Sleepy Hollow cemetery (Dec 1, 1859). He encouraged writers such as Hawthorne, Melville, Longfellow and Poe, though Poe called him "much over-rated".
  • Legacy: called the first American man of letters and the first to earn a living by his pen; he advocated copyright protection, popularized "Gotham", is credited with the phrase "the almighty dollar", and helped shape the American image of St. Nicholas and Christmas. His Columbus biography also spread the flat-Earth myth.
  • Literary periods timeline (Literary Devices packet) — The last page of your Literary Terms packet gives a timeline and movement definitions. Historical-context questions can ask you to place a work in its period.
  • Puritanism 1620-1770s (plain style; obedience to God; journals, sermons, poems). Neoclassic 1770s to early 1800s (rationalism, the Age of Reason).
  • Romanticism early 1800s-1870s: a revolt against Rationalism. Realism 1850s-early 1900s. Regionalism 1884-early 1900s. Naturalism late 1800s-mid 1900s. Modernism 1920s-1945. Post-Modernism 1945 on.
  • Transcendentalism: a 19th-century movement in the Romantic tradition holding that every individual can reach ultimate truths through spiritual intuition, which transcends reason and sensory experience.
  • Rationalism: truth reached by reason instead of the authority of the past, the Church or an institution (also called Neoclassicism or the Age of Reason).
  • Plain style: writing that stresses simplicity and clarity, the main form of the Puritan writers. Regionalism / local color: emphasis on a specific setting's speech, customs and landscape, as in Twain's dialect.
  • Place the texts: Hawthorne's Puritan Salem is set in the 1600s but written in the 1830s Romantic period; Irving, Keats, Poe, Hawthorne and Emerson are Romantic-era writers; Twain (1880) bridges toward Realism and Regionalism.
  • A. A. Rubin's Poe-style poems (Lesson #2 handout) — Rubin, a former teacher turned professional poet, wrote these poems to imitate Edgar Allan Poe.
  • "Night Walkers" won first place in a Poe-style contest: a speaker whistling through a graveyard walks all night with a ghost until daybreak, when "all ghosts must go away".
  • "The Widow's Walk" (first published July 29, 2021 in Love Letters to Poe) uses the refrain "round and round she goes" and repeated end lines to create a haunting, hypnotic sound; children invent stories about the widow, and the dead husband follows her without knowing he is dead.
  • "The Widow's Walk (1849)" is set at Cold Spring Harbor: a widow paces the roof waiting for a husband whose ship sank; his ghost returns at night and leaves at dawn. The year 1849 is the year Poe died.
  • Recurring Poe-like elements: ghosts, graveyards, the pale moon, night's "dark inky gloom", refrain and repetition, and a supernatural companion. These echo Poe's Gothic style and mood.
  • Use for practice: identify allusion, refrain, imagery and mood in short poems, then connect them to Poe's Gothic style in "The Fall of the House of Usher".
Mixing up anthropomorphism (animals or living things given human traits) with personification (nonliving objects given human traits). The bluejays are anthropomorphism; the House of Usher's "eyes" are personification.
Retelling the plot instead of analyzing how the author's language creates the effect. Always tie a specific word or device to a purpose.
Treating "Young Goodman Brown" as clearly a dream or clearly real; the story's power comes from the ambiguity.
Reading the pronoun or the speaker too quickly: check who is talking and who is being addressed (Roderick to the narrator; Rip to the villagers; Angela to Porphyro).
Using dictionary meanings instead of the meaning that fits the line. For vocabulary in context, test each choice back in the sentence.
Putting events in the wrong order. For chronology questions, run a quick timeline in your head for each story before choosing.
Choosing an interpretation that is true in general but not supported by the quote. Pick the answer the quote itself supports.
Seven texts: Rip Van Winkle (Irving), Eve of St. Agnes (Keats), Fall of the House of Usher (Poe), Baker's Bluejay Yarn (Twain), Young Goodman Brown (Hawthorne), The Custom House (Hawthorne), Emerson handout.
Anthropomorphism = animals/living things with human traits; personification = objects.
Answer = claim + text evidence + how the words create the effect + purpose.
STEAL: Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks (indirect characterization).
Practice Question Bank — 446 questions
Unit 1: The Rhetorical Situation (28)

  1. A politician gives a eulogy at a colleague's funeral. What is the OCCASION?

    • The politician’s long career and the party he represented in office
    • The colleague's death and the funeral service
    • The audience’s shared grief and the comfort they seek from the speaker
    • The political climate surrounding the colleague’s final months in office

    Occasion is the event that prompts the writing — here, the death and funeral.

  2. A textbook chapter and a passionate op-ed can share the same subject but differ in what?

    • Subject and topic
    • Grammar and syntax
    • Purpose and tone
    • Subject matter

    Two texts can share a subject but differ completely in purpose and tone.

  3. Identifying a speech's specific intended audience (rather than 'everyone') is important because:

    • Writers aim for the broadest readership so the text reaches as many people as possible
    • Audience shapes spoken speeches, where listeners respond at once, but not written essays
    • The audience decides a speech's topic, so a writer must name one first
    • Rhetorical choices are tailored to a specific audience's values and knowledge

    Writers tailor their rhetorical choices to a specific audience, not a generic one.

  4. A company's product recall letter is an example of what shaping the occasion?

    • A broad essay assignment that gives the writer wide freedom over the subject
    • A news story about an unrelated industry that has caught the writer’s attention
    • The writer’s personal preference to explain a policy before anyone has asked about it
    • A specific real-world event requiring a response

    The recall itself is the event/occasion prompting the letter.

  5. A CEO's shareholder letter written just after a scandal is shaped mostly by what exigence?

    • The company’s annual calendar, which sets the date by which the letter must reach investors
    • The need to respond to and address the scandal
    • A general trend in the industry that has little to do with the scandal itself
    • The CEO’s wish to reflect on the history of the company and the lessons of its founders

    The scandal creates the urgent need (exigence) prompting this specific letter.

  6. Which SOAPSTone element asks 'who is writing or speaking?'

    • Speaker
    • Subject
    • Purpose
    • Tone

    Speaker identifies who is behind the text and what we know about them.

  7. A formal court filing versus a casual text message about the same event differ mainly in what?

    • Subject matter, since a court filing must cover the facts in far more detail than a casual text
    • Register and constraints appropriate to the occasion
    • The event itself, which is described differently in a legal context than in a private one
    • The language used, since formal filings are written in a different language than private messages

    The occasion and its constraints shape register/formality even when the underlying subject is the same.

  8. Why is 'the audience is everyone' usually a weak rhetorical analysis claim?

    • Effective rhetoric is normally shaped for a specific, identifiable audience
    • Texts are normally written for a broad readership, so a specific audience limits their reach
    • A writer cannot reliably know who will read a text, so audience is best left out of the analysis
    • Naming an audience adds length to the analysis without improving the evidence for any claim

    Strong analysis identifies a specific intended audience the rhetorical choices are shaped for.

  9. A letter to the editor responding to a specific recent news event best illustrates:

    • Exigence driving the occasion for writing
    • A timeless, abstract meditation that could have been written in any year about anything
    • A text addressed to no one in particular and shaped by no specific reader’s concerns
    • A text written under no constraints, since the editor imposes no limit on a letter’s length or topic

    The recent news event is the exigence prompting the letter.

  10. Which best distinguishes SPEAKER from the actual author in some rhetorical texts (e.g., a persona)?

    • The speaker is the biographical author, and a persona is merely a label for the author's style
    • The speaker is the narrator in fiction, while in nonfiction the speaker and author are the same
    • The speaker is the audience that the text addresses, while the author is the person who wrote it
    • The speaker is the voice/persona presented in the text, which may differ from the biographical author

    In some texts a constructed persona speaks, distinct from the historical author.

  11. Which SOAPSTone element would you use to analyze WHY a writer chose formal academic language?

    • Speaker and subject
    • Subject and structure
    • Tone and subject area
    • Audience and occasion

    Register often reflects choices shaped by both intended audience and occasion.

  12. A graduation speech given right after a school tragedy would have its content most shaped by:

    • The conventional traditions of graduation speeches, which seldom change from year to year
    • The specific exigence of the tragedy
    • The weather and setting of the ceremony, which would dominate how the speaker chose to begin
    • The preferences of the school’s administration, who customarily approve each speech in advance

    The tragedy is the driving exigence shaping the speech's content and tone.

  13. Which correctly identifies constraints in an opinion column limited to 800 words for a general newspaper audience?

    • The writer’s personal beliefs and the strength with which she holds them, which limit what she can argue
    • Word count and audience expectations for the publication
    • The topic itself, which the editor has chosen and which sets the boundaries of the argument
    • The date of publication, which determines how much recent evidence the writer is able to use

    Word limits and audience/publication norms are classic constraints.

  14. In the SOAPSTone framework, the 'S' that refers to the argument's central idea or message is:

    • Subject
    • Speaker
    • Syntax
    • Setting

    SOAPSTone: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.

  15. A speech delivered the day after a natural disaster, urging immediate aid, is a strong example of using:

    • kairos
    • hyperbole
    • anaphora
    • litotes

    Kairos is choosing the opportune moment and fitting the message to it.

  16. 'Constraints' in a rhetorical situation refers to:

    • the limit on the length of the essay that the writer is given and the time allowed to write it
    • factors that limit how the writer can respond (beliefs, conventions, prior events)
    • the rules of grammar and punctuation that the writer must follow in the formal parts of the text
    • the word choices a writer makes that restrict the range of tones available to the audience

    Constraints shape and restrict the available means of persuasion.

  17. A well-reasoned op-ed published years after the relevant debate has ended most clearly fails at:

    • kairos
    • logos
    • organization
    • citation

    It may be logically sound but misses the opportune moment and audience.

  18. Which question best begins an audience analysis?

    • How long is the passage, and how many paragraphs does it contain about the writer’s main topic?
    • What does this audience already believe, and what would it take to move them?
    • What devices does the writer use, and in which paragraphs do they appear most often?
    • When was the text published, and how did readers at that time respond to the writer’s ideas?

    Effective analysis starts from the audience's assumptions, values, and needs.

  19. A principal writes to parents: "I know many of you worry that a later bell means later practices and later dinners. Consider instead what the sleep research says about your teenager's grades and safety on the road." Which choice best describes how the writer responds to the rhetorical situation?

    • He establishes authority by citing his credentials as a sleep researcher before offering any advice
    • He appeals to the audience’s fear of change by describing the dangers of early school start times
    • He anticipates the audience's likely objection and redirects it toward a concern the audience already shares
    • He shifts from a personal tone to an impersonal one in order to give his claim greater objectivity

    The first sentence names the objection; the second recasts the issue around grades and safety, which parents care about. The excerpt cites no credentials and never frames change itself as the threat.

  20. A writer composing a newsletter article for retired teachers about a new pension rule chooses to explain the rule through two short anecdotes about retirees instead of quoting the statute. The writer's choice is best explained by:

    • The need to demonstrate expertise in pension law, since the readers expect the writer to cite the statute
    • The exigence of a rule most readers cannot easily interpret, combined with an audience who values personal stories
    • The constraint of a strict word limit that rules out any long explanation of how the new rule works
    • A purpose of entertaining readers rather than informing them, since the audience prefers a lighter tone

    Choosing anecdotes over statute language responds to audience (retirees, not lawyers) and the need to make a complex rule understandable. A word limit is not mentioned, and the purpose is to inform.

  21. Which pairing correctly distinguishes a writer's subject from the text's exigence?

    • Subject: to persuade the council to keep the branch open; Exigence: a city’s budget for libraries
    • Subject: the council; Exigence: a persuasive essay that the author has written to influence its members
    • Subject: library budgets; Exigence: the author’s own opinion that libraries should receive more funding
    • Subject: a city's plan to close a library branch; Exigence: the vote scheduled for next week that could end the plan

    Exigence is the particular pressing occasion that makes writing necessary (an imminent vote), while the subject is what the text is about. Persuading the council describes purpose, not subject.

  22. A speech by a mayor after a flood begins, "Tonight I am not speaking to you as a politician; I am speaking as someone who also lost a basement." What is the primary rhetorical effect of this opening?

    • It undermines the speaker’s authority by admitting that he has suffered the same losses as the audience
    • It aligns the speaker with the audience's experience to create common ground before making requests
    • It signals that the speech will be primarily a technical report on the causes and costs of the flood
    • It shifts blame for the flood away from the speaker’s office and toward the weather and the residents

    Identification with the audience builds trust. The admission does not cost authority; it adds credibility through shared experience.

  23. A student's argument essay about school cafeteria policy is intended for the school board. Which revision best reflects awareness of the actual audience?

    • Replacing slang and complaints with specific budget figures and a proposal the board could vote on
    • Adding more emotional stories about hungry children so that board members feel the cost of the current policy
    • Addressing the essay to “all students” so that the writer’s argument reaches the largest possible readership
    • Using a humorous tone throughout to keep the board’s attention and to make the proposal seem less threatening

    A decision-making audience needs evidence and a feasible proposal. Emotion alone, an altered addressee, or humor would not meet the board's needs as a deliberative audience.

  24. A writer notes that a magazine's readers are suspicious of corporate claims. Which strategy would best account for this audience in an article defending a company's new safety program?

    • Opening with the company’s mission statement and a list of the awards its safety record has received
    • Conceding a past failure candidly before presenting independent audits of the new program
    • Quoting the company’s CEO at length about her personal commitment to protecting the people who work there
    • Avoiding any mention of past problems so that readers’ attention stays on the program’s present results

    For a skeptical audience, concession and independent evidence build credibility. Corporate statements and silence about problems reinforce suspicion.

  25. In an editorial, the sentence "We have debated this for years; the next meeting is the last chance" most directly establishes which element of the rhetorical situation?

    • Audience
    • Subject
    • Genre
    • Exigence

    The urgency of a final meeting is the occasion that demands a response. It signals timing and necessity, not who the readers are or what the topic is.

  26. Which description best identifies the difference between a text's purpose and its message?

    • Purpose is the idea the text conveys to the reader; the message is what the writer wants the text to accomplish
    • Purpose is the writer’s emotion at the moment of writing; message is the audience’s reaction to the text
    • Purpose is what the writer wants the text to accomplish with the audience; the message is the idea the text conveys
    • Purpose concerns the text’s style and word choice; message concerns the structure of its paragraphs

    Purpose concerns the writer's intended effect (inform, persuade, inspire); message is the content of the claim or idea.

  27. A nonprofit's fundraising letter and its annual report cover the same project but differ greatly in diction and structure. This difference is best attributed to:

    • A change of subject between the documents
    • Differences in genre, audience and purpose
    • Stylistic choices of the individual writers
    • Differences in tone and sentence length

    Genres carry conventions shaped by their audience and purpose, so the same subject is presented differently.

  28. A writer says, "I will not pretend that this policy is perfect." Which statement most accurately describes the likely rhetorical function?

    • It abandons the writer’s position by admitting that the policy has flaws that cannot be defended
    • It weakens the writer’s logos by suggesting that the evidence for the policy is incomplete or unreliable
    • It builds ethos through honesty and prepares the audience to accept qualified support
    • It is an appeal to pity that asks the audience to sympathize with the difficulties of the policy’s authors

    Admitting imperfection can increase credibility and make a measured argument appear more reasonable.

Unit 2: Rhetorical Appeals & Logical Fallacies (34)

  1. A charity ad showing images of hungry children to evoke sympathy relies primarily on:

    • Pathos
    • Logos
    • Ethos
    • A straw man fallacy

    Vivid, emotional imagery designed to evoke sympathy is a pathos appeal.

  2. A doctor citing peer-reviewed studies to support a health claim uses primarily:

    • Pathos, supported by an appeal to the audience’s fear of illness and the stakes of ignoring medical advice
    • A slippery slope fallacy, which connects a minor choice to a catastrophic outcome without evidence
    • An appeal to tradition, since the doctor relies on accepted medical custom rather than new research
    • Logos, supported by ethos from expertise

    Data/studies are logos; the doctor's expertise also lends ethos.

  3. 'If we allow students one retake, soon no test will ever count' is an example of:

    • Slippery slope fallacy
    • Valid logical reasoning
    • Ethos appeal
    • Antithesis

    This claims an extreme, unjustified chain reaction from one small step — a slippery slope.

  4. 'My opponent wants to cut this program, so he clearly hates poor families' misrepresents the opponent's actual position. This is:

    • A straw man fallacy
    • A valid rebuttal
    • An example of logos
    • Antithesis

    This exaggerates/distorts the opponent's real position to attack a weaker version — a straw man.

  5. 'Either we ban the product entirely, or we do nothing at all' ignores middle-ground options. This is:

    • A false dilemma
    • A hasty generalization
    • Ethos
    • Pathos

    Presenting only two extreme options when others exist is a false dilemma.

  6. Attacking a scientist's argument by mocking their appearance instead of their data is:

    • Ad hominem
    • Logos
    • A valid ethos critique
    • Antithesis

    Attacking the person rather than the argument is ad hominem.

  7. 'I met three rude tourists from that city, so everyone from there must be rude' is a:

    • Hasty generalization
    • Slippery slope
    • False dilemma
    • Appeal to logos

    Drawing a broad conclusion from too small a sample is a hasty generalization.

  8. A speaker who fairly acknowledges the opposing view before responding builds:

    • Ethos, by appearing reasonable and fair
    • Pathos, by arousing sympathy for the opposing side and so softening the audience’s feelings
    • A logical fallacy, since conceding any point weakens the speaker’s own position in the debate
    • Authority by command, since the speaker shows that the opposing view has already been defeated

    Fair acknowledgment of opposing views builds credibility/ethos.

  9. Which is the best full analysis, not just labeling?

    • This sentence is an example of logos, because it uses a number to support the writer’s claim
    • Logos is used in this sentence, and it appears in the middle of the paragraph where the claim is made
    • The writer used numbers in this sentence, and the numbers are specific and easy for readers to follow
    • The statistic builds logos, making the argument feel objective and hard to dispute

    Strong analysis explains the effect of the device, not just names it.

  10. A veteran discussing the human cost of war through a personal story primarily appeals to:

    • Logos, and secondarily ethos from the order of events
    • Pathos, and secondarily ethos from firsthand experience
    • Ethos, and secondarily logos from statistics he cites
    • Pathos, and secondarily logos from a chain of reasoning

    Personal storytelling evokes emotion (pathos) while firsthand experience also builds ethos.

  11. Using vivid, charged language ('this catastrophe will devastate families') primarily builds:

    • Kairos
    • Pathos
    • Bathos
    • Syntax

    Emotionally charged language is designed to evoke feeling — pathos.

  12. 'You can't trust her tax plan, she's not even an economist' dismisses her plan based only on her credentials rather than its content. This mixes:

    • A valid logos critique of the plan’s economics, since the speaker lacks the training to judge it
    • Antithesis, since the sentence sets her credentials against the contents of her tax plan
    • Parallelism, since the sentence repeats a grammatical form to emphasize the speaker’s authority
    • Ad hominem-style dismissal disguised as an ethos critique

    Dismissing an argument based only on the person's background, without engaging the actual plan, echoes ad hominem reasoning.

  13. Which best explains why using pathos is NOT automatically a logical fallacy?

    • Emotional appeals can be a legitimate, valid rhetorical strategy alongside logic
    • Pathos is a fallacy once it is used in a formal argument, since emotion cannot be tested
    • Pathos is valid in speeches but not in written arguments, which are judged by their logic
    • Appeals to emotion are fallacies if they appear in a conclusion, where evidence is due

    Pathos is a legitimate classical appeal; it becomes a fallacy only when it replaces valid reasoning deceptively.

  14. 'Studies from three major universities all found the same result' primarily supports:

    • Logos, through convergent evidence
    • Pathos alone
    • A straw man
    • A false dilemma

    Multiple corroborating studies is evidence-based reasoning — logos.

  15. Identify the fallacy: 'We must ban video games entirely, or violence will completely destroy society.'

    • A valid appeal to logos, since the speaker states a cause and its likely effect in order
    • An ethos appeal that relies on the speaker’s authority to justify a total ban
    • Antithesis, since the sentence sets two outcomes against each other for rhetorical effect
    • False dilemma combined with slippery slope

    This presents only two extremes (false dilemma) and an unjustified extreme chain (slippery slope).

  16. On the exam, why is simply writing 'this is pathos' insufficient?

    • It doesn't explain HOW the appeal functions or its effect on the audience
    • Pathos is not an AP term, so the writer should name the specific device instead
    • It names the appeal correctly, but the grader also wants the writer's opinion
    • It omits a quotation, and a quotation by itself would complete the analysis

    Analysis must connect the device to its specific effect, not just name it.

  17. A speaker who cites their own years of firsthand field experience is primarily building:

    • Ethos
    • Pathos
    • A slippery slope fallacy
    • Antithesis

    Firsthand experience/credentials build credibility — ethos.

  18. An appeal based on the speaker's character, expertise, and trustworthiness is:

    • ethos
    • pathos
    • logos
    • kairos

    Ethos is the appeal to credibility.

  19. 'You can't trust her argument about the budget; she failed a math class in college' is an example of:

    • ad hominem
    • straw man
    • false dilemma
    • slippery slope

    Ad hominem attacks the person rather than the argument.

  20. Misrepresenting an opponent's position to make it easier to attack is:

    • a straw man
    • begging the question
    • an appeal to authority
    • post hoc

    The straw man refutes a distorted version of the argument.

  21. Reasoning that moves from specific observations to a general conclusion is:

    • inductive
    • deductive
    • circular
    • analogical

    Induction builds a general claim from particular cases and is always provisional.

  22. Which best completes strong rhetorical analysis of an emotional appeal?

    • state that the author uses pathos, and then quote the sentence in which the appeal is most evident
    • quote a particularly sad sentence from the passage and note that it is emotional
    • name the words used, then explain the feeling they create and its effect on the audience
    • list three emotions that the passage seems to arouse, and then move to the next paragraph

    Always connect the specific language to the effect on the reader and the writer's purpose.

  23. 'This policy must work; the senator who wrote it is very experienced' relies on:

    • an appeal to authority (which is weak if the authority is not relevant or is the only support)
    • logos, since the senator’s experience is a reason that the policy’s success is likely
    • a concession to the opposition, since the speaker grants that the policy might fail
    • an analogy between the senator’s experience and the policy’s likelihood of succeeding in practice

    Authority can support a claim, but it is a fallacy when the authority is irrelevant or offered as sole proof.

  24. A writer who admits a personal mistake early in an essay is most likely trying to:

    • strengthen ethos by appearing honest
    • weaken the argument by drawing attention to the writer’s own failings before the thesis is stated
    • introduce a fallacy by shifting the reader’s attention from the argument to the writer’s character
    • establish kairos by linking the admission to the moment in which the essay appears

    Acknowledging limits can build trust with the audience.

  25. "If we allow students to retake one exam, soon they will demand to retake every assignment, and the school will lose all standards." Which fallacy does this sentence most clearly commit?

    • Slippery slope
    • Ad hominem
    • Straw man
    • Circular reasoning

    The sentence claims a small step will inevitably cause an extreme chain of consequences without showing the links.

  26. A candidate says, "My opponent wants to cut the parks budget, so clearly he hates children." The most precise label for the flaw is:

    • An appeal to authority that relies on the opponent’s office in order to prove the claim about children
    • A bandwagon appeal that suggests everyone agrees with the speaker and so the opponent must be wrong
    • Circular reasoning that assumes the conclusion is true and then offers it again as the evidence
    • A straw man that exaggerates a position and then attacks the exaggeration

    The claim misrepresents a budget position as hatred of children and attacks that distorted version.

  27. "Everyone in my neighborhood supports the new stadium, so it must be a good idea." The reasoning depends on which flaw?

    • Post hoc reasoning, assuming earlier events caused the support
    • False dilemma, presenting the stadium as the sole option
    • Red herring, raising a related subject to distract from cost
    • Bandwagon appeal, assuming popularity proves correctness

    The claim substitutes popularity for evidence that the stadium is a good idea.

  28. A writer argues, "Ever since the new highway opened, crime has risen, so the highway caused the increase." Which statement best evaluates the reasoning?

    • It correctly uses deductive logic by moving from a general rule about highways to a specific conclusion
    • It uses an emotional appeal by describing the effect of crime on families in the writer’s neighborhood
    • It commits a post hoc fallacy by treating sequence as proof of cause
    • It is an ad hominem attack on the officials who approved the highway before it opened to traffic

    Two events occurring in sequence does not establish that one caused the other; other factors might explain the rise.

  29. A speaker begins a speech to nurses with a story of a night shift, then cites staffing data, and ends with an appeal to professional pride. Which sequence of appeals does this reflect?

    • Pathos, logos, ethos
    • Logos, ethos, pathos
    • Ethos, pathos, logos
    • Pathos, ethos, logos

    The story is an emotional appeal, the data is logical, and the appeal to professional pride speaks to shared identity and values (ethos-based).

  30. Which of the following is the best example of a writer using logos?

    • Describing a student’s tears on the first day of the program so readers share her fear
    • Citing the writer’s twenty years of experience in the district to establish authority
    • Using a metaphor of a sinking ship to suggest the danger to the school’s budget
    • Presenting a comparison of test scores before and after a program, with the sample sizes

    Logos appeals to reason through evidence and logical structure; the others use pathos, ethos or figurative language.

  31. "You can either support this tax or you can watch the city fall apart." What is the primary flaw?

    • A hasty generalization that draws a broad conclusion from a few examples of cities that raised taxes
    • An appeal to tradition that assumes the tax is justified because earlier councils had approved similar ones
    • False dilemma that presents only two extreme options
    • Circular reasoning that assumes the tax is necessary and then offers its necessity as the evidence

    The sentence ignores alternatives between the extremes.

  32. A pharmaceutical advertisement features a famous athlete praising a medicine. Which fallacy might the ad rely on?

    • Hasty generalization
    • Appeal to inappropriate authority
    • Slippery slope
    • Equivocation

    The athlete's fame does not make them an expert on medicine.

  33. "The senator is wrong about education policy because she dropped out of college." Which statement best identifies the error?

    • A slippery slope that predicts a series of consequences from the senator’s decision to leave college
    • An equivocation that shifts the meaning of “education” between the senator’s experience and her policy
    • Ad hominem, because it attacks personal history rather than the argument
    • An appeal to emotion that asks the audience to feel contempt for the senator’s failure to graduate

    The claim attacks the person instead of addressing the policy's merits.

  34. "It's a good law because it is the law." This argument is best described as:

    • Red herring
    • False dilemma
    • Post hoc
    • Circular reasoning

    The conclusion simply restates the premise.

Unit 3: Rhetorical Devices & Figurative Language (26)

  1. 'I have a dream... I have a dream... I have a dream' at the start of successive sentences is:

    • Anaphora
    • Epistrophe
    • Antithesis
    • Simile

    Repetition at the BEGINNING of successive clauses is anaphora.

  2. '...government of the people, by the people, for the people' repeats a phrase at the END of clauses. This is:

    • Epistrophe
    • Anaphora
    • Chiasmus
    • Hyperbole

    Repetition at the END of successive clauses/phrases is epistrophe.

  3. 'Ask not what your country can do for you—ask what you can do for your country' reverses grammatical structure. This is:

    • Chiasmus
    • Simile
    • Personification
    • Hyperbole

    A reversal of grammatical structure across clauses is chiasmus.

  4. 'The wind whispered through the trees' gives human qualities to wind. This is:

    • Personification
    • Simile
    • Antithesis
    • Epistrophe

    Giving human qualities to something nonhuman is personification.

  5. 'Do you really think that plan will work?' asked with no expectation of a literal answer is a:

    • Rhetorical question
    • Simile
    • Antithesis
    • Epistrophe

    A question asked for effect, not a literal answer, is rhetorical.

  6. Saying 'Great job' sarcastically after someone makes a mistake is an example of:

    • Verbal irony
    • Personification
    • Anaphora
    • A simile

    Saying the opposite of what is meant, often to criticize, is verbal irony.

  7. 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times' places two contrasting ideas in parallel structure. This is:

    • Antithesis
    • Chiasmus
    • Personification
    • Understatement

    Placing contrasting ideas in parallel grammatical structure is antithesis.

  8. Placing a description of extreme wealth directly next to a description of extreme poverty to highlight the contrast is:

    • Juxtaposition
    • Anaphora
    • Hyperbole
    • Simile

    Placing two things side by side to highlight contrast is juxtaposition.

  9. Repeating the last word of one clause at the start of the next ('Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hate.') is:

    • Anadiplosis
    • Chiasmus
    • Antithesis
    • Personification

    Repeating the final word of one clause at the start of the next is anadiplosis.

  10. A list of parallel infinitive phrases ('to run, to jump, to swim') used for rhythm and balance is:

    • Parallelism
    • Antithesis
    • Personification
    • Hyperbole

    Repeating a grammatical structure across a series is parallelism.

  11. Which distinguishes simile from metaphor?

    • Metaphor uses 'like' or 'as'; simile makes a direct comparison without them
    • A simile compares two things of the same kind; a metaphor compares two unlike things
    • A simile extends a comparison across a passage, while a metaphor stays in a phrase
    • Simile uses 'like' or 'as'; metaphor makes a direct comparison without them

    The comparison word 'like'/'as' is present in a simile but absent in a metaphor.

  12. Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses is:

    • anaphora
    • epistrophe
    • chiasmus
    • asyndeton

    Anaphora repeats at the START of clauses; epistrophe repeats at the end.

  13. Deliberately omitting conjunctions from a list ('I came, I saw, I conquered') is:

    • asyndeton
    • polysyndeton
    • parallelism
    • anaphora

    Asyndeton speeds a list and can create urgency or breathlessness.

  14. An extended metaphor is best described as:

    • a metaphor used once in a sentence, with each of its terms stated in a single phrase
    • a comparison using “like” or “as,” developed through more than one sentence in the passage
    • two metaphors placed in the same sentence so that the second reinforces the meaning of the first
    • a single comparison developed across several sentences or a whole passage

    It structures a stretch of text around one governing comparison.

  15. Verbal irony occurs when a writer:

    • describes a sensory image so vividly that the reader can feel what the writer is describing
    • repeats a phrase at the beginning of successive clauses to emphasize the writer’s central claim
    • says the opposite of what is meant, expecting the audience to catch the gap
    • uses a formal citation in order to give the argument the authority of a recognized source

    Sarcasm is a common, pointed form of verbal irony.

  16. After identifying anaphora in a passage, the next step in analysis is to:

    • name two more devices in the passage and move to the next paragraph in order to cover the whole text
    • explain the emphasis or momentum it builds and how that serves the purpose
    • quote the whole paragraph that contains the anaphora so that the grader can see its context
    • identify the audience of the passage and then summarize how it would have responded to the writer

    Analysis must move from naming the device to explaining its effect.

  17. "Our schools do not need more money; our schools do not need more slogans; our schools need more teachers." Which pair of devices is most clearly at work?

    • Anaphora and parallelism building to a climactic claim
    • Antithesis and hyperbole that set opposing needs against each other and exaggerate the schools’ plight
    • Oxymoron and paradox that join contradictory terms to make a statement that seems true on reflection
    • Allusion and irony that refer to a well-known work and say the opposite of what the speaker means

    The repeated 'our schools do not need' is anaphora in parallel clauses that culminate in the claim.

  18. The sentence "The report was long on promises and short on proof" depends primarily on which device?

    • Personification that treats the report as a person who makes promises and then fails to keep them
    • Synecdoche that uses a part of the report to represent the whole of the document and its findings
    • Onomatopoeia that imitates the sound of a long document being read aloud to a restless audience
    • Antithesis within a parallel structure

    It balances contrasting terms (long/short, promises/proof) in parallel construction.

  19. A writer describes a city council as "a committee of the willing, appointed by the unprepared." The phrase most strongly employs:

    • Simile
    • Irony and parallel structure
    • Apostrophe
    • Understatement

    The reversal of expected terms is ironic and delivered in a balanced form.

  20. In "The White House issued a statement," the use of 'White House' for the president's staff is an example of:

    • Metonymy
    • Synecdoche
    • Hyperbole
    • Euphemism

    A related object stands in for the thing it represents; synecdoche would use a part of the whole.

  21. "All hands on deck" used to request help from workers is an example of:

    • Metonymy
    • Simile
    • Oxymoron
    • Synecdoche

    'Hands' is a part representing the whole person.

  22. Which sentence best exemplifies understatement for rhetorical effect?

    • “The flood destroyed everything in the world,” in an essay that describes a single ruined house
    • "The flood caused some inconvenience for the town's residents," in an essay describing destroyed homes
    • “The river wept as it rose,” in a passage that gives human feelings to the water
    • “The flood was like a monster,” in a paragraph that compares the water to a destructive beast

    Understatement deliberately minimizes a serious matter to produce irony or emphasis.

  23. A writer says a rival's plan is "a masterpiece of confusion." The phrase is best characterized as:

    • Ironic and an oxymoron-like reversal of praise
    • Literal praise of a plan that the writer regards as admirably complicated and sophisticated
    • An allusion to a famous work of art that the writer expects the audience to recognize
    • An understatement that minimizes the plan’s faults in order to make the criticism sound milder

    Praising the plan for confusion turns the praise sarcastic.

  24. "We shall not be moved by fear, nor shaken by threats, nor turned by flattery" is notable for:

    • Alliteration, as repeated initial sounds make the line memorable
    • An extended metaphor comparing fear and threats to physical forces
    • Parallel structure that accumulates force through repetition
    • Dialect, which lends the words a regional, conversational tone

    The repeated grammatical pattern builds momentum and emphasizes resolve.

  25. Which statement best explains why a writer might choose a euphemism?

    • To increase the harshness of a statement so that the reader cannot avoid its meaning
    • To soften or avoid a harsh reality, which can also obscure the truth
    • To imitate spoken dialect, which gives the passage the sound of an actual conversation
    • To create a rhyme that makes the sentence easier to remember and more pleasant to hear

    Euphemisms mask unpleasant realities, sometimes for tact and sometimes for evasion.

  26. "I've told you a million times to knock" most clearly contains:

    • Understatement
    • Metonymy
    • Hyperbole
    • Antithesis

    The exaggeration is not meant literally.

Unit 4: Style: Diction, Syntax & Tone (22)

  1. Choosing elevated, precise vocabulary over casual everyday words reflects:

    • Formal diction
    • Slang diction
    • Informal diction
    • Formal syntax

    Elevated, precise word choice is formal diction.

  2. A single long sentence with many clauses piling on top of each other can create a sense of:

    • Accumulation or breathless momentum
    • Abrupt, clipped finality of tone
    • Stark simplicity and quiet restraint
    • Detached, clinical distance from events

    Long, complex sentences can build accumulation or momentum.

  3. Mixing short and long sentences throughout a passage primarily controls:

    • Grammar and spelling accuracy
    • Diction and level of formality
    • Thesis clarity and claim scope
    • Pacing and reader engagement

    Sentence variety controls pacing and keeps the reader engaged.

  4. A transition word like 'however' appearing mid-passage most likely signals:

    • A tone or idea shift
    • The end of the essay
    • A grammar error
    • A repeated claim

    Contrast transitions often mark a shift in tone or idea.

  5. The combination of a writer's characteristic diction, syntax, and tone is called their:

    • Style
    • Subject
    • Occasion
    • Constraint

    Style is the recognizable combination of diction, syntax, and tone across a writer's work.

  6. Concrete, sensory diction ('the acrid smell of smoke') mainly creates:

    • Abstract, general analysis
    • Formal, detached register
    • Logical, data-driven proof
    • Vivid, specific imagery

    Concrete, sensory words create vivid images for the reader.

  7. Abstract diction ('justice,' 'freedom,' 'progress') tends to create a more:

    • Analytical or conceptual feel
    • Vivid sensory feel
    • Casual feel
    • Humorous feel

    Abstract, conceptual words create a more analytical, less sensory tone.

  8. How formal or informal language is, relative to the occasion, is called:

    • Register
    • Denotation
    • Anaphora
    • Exigence

    Register describes the formality level of language relative to context.

  9. Assuming short sentences always signal 'simple ideas' is a mistake because:

    • Short sentences signal haste, so they seldom stress weighty ideas
    • Long sentences signal complex ideas, so short ones must signal simple ideas
    • Sentence length is a minor matter that readers rarely notice in prose
    • Short sentences are often used to emphasize complex or weighty ideas

    Short sentences frequently emphasize complex or weighty points, not just simple ones.

  10. 'The committee shall convene' vs. 'let's get together' differ mainly in:

    • Diction and register
    • Grammar and mechanics
    • Subject and setting
    • Purpose and message

    These phrases describe the same action with very different formal vs. casual diction/register.

  11. 'The negotiations collapsed. Talks failed. Trust was gone.' uses short syntax primarily to create:

    • A blunt, emphatic sense of finality
    • A relaxed, meandering tone
    • Confusion about the sequence of events
    • No rhetorical effect

    The clipped, short sentences create emphasis and a sense of blunt finality.

  12. A sudden shift from long, complex sentences to a short, blunt one usually functions to:

    • create emphasis by contrast
    • confuse the reader
    • signal a citation
    • establish the audience

    The abrupt change in rhythm draws attention to the short sentence's content.

  13. A writer follows several long, flowing sentences with the sentence "Then nothing." The most likely effect of this contrast in syntax is to:

    • Make the passage easier to read by relieving the reader after a sequence of complex clauses
    • Create abrupt emphasis and a sense of sudden finality
    • Introduce a new subject that the writer will take up in the following paragraph
    • Express the writer’s uncertainty about whether anything remains to be said on the matter

    A short sentence after long ones produces emphasis through contrast.

  14. Which description best captures the connotative difference between "thrifty" and "stingy"?

    • They have different denotations, since “thrifty” refers to saving and “stingy” to refusing to spend
    • “Stingy” is the more formal word, while “thrifty” belongs to everyday speech and so sounds casual
    • "Thrifty" carries a positive judgment while "stingy" carries a negative one, though both denote spending little
    • They are interchangeable, since both words describe a person who spends very little money

    The words refer to similar behavior but suggest opposite attitudes.

  15. A passage uses long periodic sentences that withhold the main clause until the end. The most likely effect is:

    • Creating a casual, conversational tone in which the writer seems to speak directly to the reader
    • Making the argument seem hasty, since the reader waits for the point and may lose the thread
    • Reducing complexity, since the main idea is placed in the sentence’s last clause for clarity
    • Building suspense or emphasis for the final idea

    Delaying the main idea creates anticipation.

  16. A writer opens an essay with technical jargon and then shifts to plain language. The most likely purpose is to:

    • Confuse the audience so that readers accept the writer’s claims without examining them
    • Show disrespect for the audience by suggesting that its members are unable to follow the argument
    • Create a humorous tone by contrasting the difficult opening with the simple language that follows
    • Demonstrate expertise before making the ideas accessible

    The shift establishes credibility and then clarifies for readers.

  17. Which phrase most strongly suggests a sarcastic tone?

    • "Oh, what a wonderfully efficient system, requiring only three hours of waiting"
    • “The system requires three hours of waiting before an applicant can be seen by a clerk”
    • “The wait is three hours, though it is sometimes shorter when the office is not crowded”
    • “Waiting takes time, and the system’s users should plan their visits with that in mind”

    The praise contrasts with the described inefficiency, signaling sarcasm.

  18. A writer repeatedly uses first-person plural pronouns like 'we' and 'our' in an argument. This choice most likely:

    • Creates a sense of shared responsibility and solidarity
    • Distances the writer from the audience by presenting the argument as a formal and impersonal report
    • Shows scientific objectivity by removing the writer’s own voice from the account of the evidence
    • Indicates uncertainty, since the writer shares the responsibility for the claim with other people

    Inclusive pronouns unite the speaker and audience.

  19. A passage shifts from formal diction ("proceeded to commence") to blunt monosyllables ("it broke"). The shift most likely functions to:

    • Make the passage more formal by moving from simple words to those that are more elevated
    • Create ironic contrast between pomp and reality
    • Express the writer’s confusion about how the event is to be described in a single sentence
    • Provide historical context by showing how the vocabulary of the period differed from ours

    The deflation from elevated to blunt language undercuts the pretension.

  20. Which sentence most clearly uses a conversational tone?

    • “The aforementioned procedures shall be implemented in accordance with the guidelines issued earlier.”
    • "Look, nobody likes paying more, but here's the thing: the old way wasn't working."
    • “It is incumbent upon the committee to deliberate with care before it renders any decision.”
    • “Pursuant to the statute, the fee has been adjusted to reflect the cost of administration.”

    Contractions, direct address and informal phrasing mark conversational tone.

  21. A writer lists seven examples in rapid succession with commas and no conjunction (asyndeton). The most likely effect is:

    • Slow, formal pacing in which each example receives the same weight and the reader is invited to dwell on it
    • Ambiguity about how the items are related, since no conjunction tells the reader how to connect them
    • A reduction in emphasis, since a long list makes each of its items seem less important
    • Rapid pacing and a sense of accumulation or urgency

    Omitting conjunctions speeds the list and can suggest overwhelming quantity.

  22. Which of the following best explains the effect of an imperative sentence such as "Imagine a town without a school"?

    • It directly engages the reader and invites participation in a hypothetical
    • It states a fact the audience is expected to accept without checking evidence
    • It reports an event the writer witnessed in the order it occurred
    • It qualifies an earlier claim, suggesting it does not hold in some cases

    Commands pull the audience into the writer's scenario.

Unit 5: Claims, Evidence & Commentary (24)

  1. An argument claiming something is TRUE or FALSE and can be verified is a claim of:

    • Fact
    • Value
    • Policy
    • Style

    A claim of fact asserts something verifiable as true or false.

  2. Citing a peer-reviewed study's data supports an argument primarily through:

    • Statistical evidence
    • Anecdotal evidence
    • Personification
    • Antithesis

    Numerical/data-based evidence is statistical evidence.

  3. Quoting a leading scientist's opinion on climate change borrows credibility through:

    • Anecdotal evidence
    • Expert testimony
    • Statistical data
    • Historical example

    Citing an authority's opinion is expert testimony, which lends ethos.

  4. A recommended ratio of evidence to commentary in a strong paragraph is roughly:

    • Four sentences of evidence to one of commentary
    • One sentence of evidence to two or more of commentary
    • Two sentences of evidence to one of commentary
    • Equal evidence and commentary, sentence for sentence

    Strong paragraphs favor more commentary/analysis than raw evidence.

  5. The logical thread connecting a thesis through evidence to a coherent argument is called the:

    • Line of reasoning
    • Rhetorical situation
    • Exigence
    • Register

    This is the definition of a line of reasoning.

  6. Evidence presented without ever connecting back to the thesis is a weakness because:

    • The reader shouldn't have to guess why the evidence was included
    • Readers can supply the link, but the paragraph then runs too long
    • Quoted evidence explains itself, so added commentary would repeat it
    • The topic sentence already links it, so evidence needs no tie-back

    Every piece of evidence needs explicit commentary connecting it to the thesis.

  7. A strong thesis usually combines which claim types?

    • Claims of fact alone, since a thesis must be provable by checkable evidence
    • Elements of fact, value, and/or policy as needed for a specific position
    • Claims of policy alone, since a thesis must recommend a course of action
    • Claims of value alone, since a thesis must state a judgment about the topic

    Strong theses often blend claim types into one specific, arguable position.

  8. Which is the best example of commentary, not summary?
