    • The study found a 40% increase in reported cases over the decade in the three cities examined
    • The article discusses pollution and its effects on the health of residents in the region
    • The data presented in the second source were collected by a team of three researchers
    • This statistic reveals how widespread the problem truly is, undermining the claim that it's rare

    This explains the significance of the evidence rather than just restating it.

  9. A paragraph that only restates evidence in different words, without analysis, is best described as:

    • Mostly summary
    • Strong commentary
    • A rebuttal
    • A synthesis

    Restating evidence without analysis is summary, not commentary.

  10. Why is repeating the same underlying point across multiple paragraphs a weakness?

    • It sharpens the essay's focus, since each paragraph reinforces one central point
    • It fails to build a genuine line of reasoning that advances the argument
    • Graders expect it, looking for the thesis to be restated in each paragraph
    • It clarifies organization, since each paragraph has the same clear purpose

    Genuine line of reasoning requires each paragraph to add something new.

  11. Which type of evidence draws a parallel to a past event to support a claim?

    • Anecdotal evidence
    • Statistical evidence
    • Historical evidence
    • Literary evidence

    Referencing a past event or precedent is historical evidence.

  12. A claim asserting 'social media usage has tripled since 2015' is a claim of:

    • Fact
    • Value
    • Policy
    • Tone

    This is a verifiable factual claim.

  13. Which best shows a logical LINE OF REASONING across paragraphs?

    • Paragraph 1 states the claim; paragraph 2 restates it with a new statistic; paragraph 3 restates it again
    • Paragraph 1 establishes the problem's scope; paragraph 2 explains its cause; paragraph 3 proposes a solution
    • Paragraph 1 offers a solution; paragraph 2 describes the problem; paragraph 3 introduces an unrelated topic
    • Paragraph 1 states the thesis; paragraph 2 summarizes the topic; paragraph 3 lists examples without connection

    Each paragraph builds a distinct, connected part of the overall argument.

  14. Which sentence is commentary rather than summary?

    • The author states that 40 percent of families in the study could not afford basic medical care.
    • The passage includes several statistics, which are drawn from the survey of families in the region.
    • The author cites a government report in the second paragraph in order to support the main claim.
    • This statistic matters because it shows the policy affects the very group it claims to help.

    Commentary interprets the evidence's significance for the argument.

  15. Which thesis is most defensible and specific enough for a rhetorical analysis?

    • “Lopez persuades skeptical readers by combining personal experience with data, which makes her argument effective and convincing.”
    • “Through a personal anecdote and comparative statistics, Lopez uses ethos and logos to argue that other cities should adopt the policy.”
    • "By pairing a personal anecdote with comparative statistics, Lopez persuades skeptical readers that the policy has worked in other cities."
    • “Lopez opens with an anecdote and closes with statistics, a structure that shows her argument is organized from the personal to the general.”

    A strong thesis identifies specific choices and their effect on a particular audience for a purpose.

  16. In an argument essay a student writes: "Social media harms teenagers. A survey found that students who spend more than four hours a day online report lower sleep." What is the best revision to strengthen the commentary?

    • Add another survey statistic about teenagers’ sleep without comment, so that the evidence appears more complete
    • Replace the claim with a question so that the reader is invited to consider whether social media is harmful
    • Remove the survey and rely on the writer’s own experience of social media to support the claim
    • Explain how lower sleep connects to the claim of harm and acknowledge the survey shows correlation rather than cause

    Commentary connects evidence to the claim and handles limits of the evidence.

  17. Which sentence best qualifies a claim for accuracy?

    • “Later start times have been proven to raise attendance wherever a district has tried them.”
    • "In most large districts, later start times have been associated with modest gains in attendance."
    • “Few people can deny that later start times work well in the districts that adopted them.”
    • “Start times have little effect on attendance, as the studies of the topic have repeatedly shown.”

    Qualifiers like 'most' and 'associated with modest' acknowledge limits.

  18. A student's body paragraph states a claim, quotes a source, and moves on. Which element is missing?

    • Commentary explaining how the evidence supports the claim
    • A topic sentence that tells the reader what the paragraph will argue before the quotation appears
    • A transition linking the paragraph to the one before it so that the argument moves in a clear line
    • A concluding sentence for the entire essay that restates the thesis and its significance

    Evidence must be followed by explanation tying it to the argument.

  19. Which source would be most credible for a claim about the economic effects of minimum-wage increases?

    • An anonymous blog post that summarizes the debate and cites several news articles in its footnotes
    • A politician’s campaign speech that cites recent figures from her state’s department of labor
    • A viral social media post that reports an economist’s opinion in a short and confident message
    • A peer-reviewed study by labor economists with a clear method

    Credibility depends on expertise, method and transparency.

  20. A writer cites a statistic: "Seventy percent of surveyed students support the policy." Which question would best test the evidence's reliability?

    • How long is the sentence, and does it follow the conventions for presenting a statistic in a formal essay?
    • Who was surveyed and how were they selected?
    • What color is the chart, and is it easy to read for someone who is color-blind?
    • When was the paper printed, and did the publisher have a good reputation at the time?

    Sampling method determines whether results can be generalized.

  21. Which of the following is an example of commentary rather than evidence?

    • “Test scores rose 8 percent over the three years in which the program was in operation.”
    • “The study followed 1,200 students in six districts from the fall of 2019 until the spring of 2022.”
    • “The mayor said that the plan would help families in the neighborhoods most affected by the closure.”
    • "This pattern suggests the program's benefits are strongest where funding is steady."

    Commentary interprets and links evidence to the argument.

  22. A writer concedes that a policy has costs and then argues the benefits outweigh them. This strategy primarily:

    • Weakens the claim by drawing attention to costs that the writer cannot refute
    • Changes the subject from the policy's costs to the policy's benefits
    • Shows a lack of conviction, since admitting a cost suggests the writer is unsure
    • Strengthens credibility by acknowledging a counterpoint before refuting it

    Concession and rebuttal show fairness and strengthen the argument.

  23. Which claim would be most appropriate for an argument essay that needs a defensible position?

    • “Year-round calendars exist in several states, and some of them are used by large school districts.”
    • “Many schools have calendars that divide the year into terms of various lengths and breaks of different sizes.”
    • “Summer is a season in which many students are away from school, and some of them travel with their families.”
    • "Schools should adopt year-round calendars because they reduce learning loss over the summer."

    A defensible claim takes a position that reasonable people could dispute and signals reasons.

  24. A writer uses a hypothetical example to illustrate an abstract idea. Which assessment is most accurate?

    • A hypothetical is the strongest form of evidence, since it can be designed to fit the claim exactly
    • A hypothetical is irrelevant to an argument, since graders credit only examples that have really occurred
    • A hypothetical is a kind of statistic, since it represents what would happen in a typical case
    • A hypothetical can clarify an idea but cannot serve as proof of how the world actually is

    Illustrations aid understanding; they do not substitute for empirical evidence.

Unit 6: Organization, Structure & Counterargument (23)

  1. 'In this essay, I will discuss climate change' is a weak thesis because it:

    • Takes a position, but it is too broad for a single essay
    • Makes an arguable claim but gives no evidence for it
    • Announces intent instead of taking an arguable position
    • Takes an arguable position that few readers would dispute

    This merely announces the topic rather than making a claim.

  2. Acknowledging a valid point on the opposing side before returning to your own argument is called:

    • A concession
    • A rebuttal
    • A thesis
    • Anaphora

    Acknowledging a fair opposing point is a concession.

  3. 'Also' and 'another thing' are often weak transitions because they show:

    • Strong causal relationships, since each of these words marks the effect of the preceding sentence
    • A clear contrast between ideas, so that the reader expects a change of direction in the argument
    • Addition, but not the actual logical relationship between ideas
    • A concession to the opposing view, so that the reader knows the writer is about to qualify a claim

    These words only signal addition, not deeper logical connections.

  4. Introducing a completely new, unsupported argument in the conclusion is considered:

    • A strong closing move
    • A sign of sophistication
    • A structural weakness
    • A stylistic preference

    New unsupported arguments in a conclusion weaken structural coherence.

  5. A body paragraph missing commentary that ties evidence back to the thesis is:

    • Structurally complete
    • Structurally incomplete
    • Stylistically incomplete
    • Adequately developed

    Every body paragraph needs commentary linking evidence explicitly to the thesis.

  6. Why should an introduction establish context briefly before the thesis?

    • It orients the reader without delaying the argument unnecessarily
    • It lets the writer survey the full history of the topic so that readers need no further background later
    • It delays the thesis long enough for the reader to feel the importance of the issue before the claim
    • It gives the thesis a stronger position by placing it at the end of a long and detailed opening paragraph

    Brief context orients the reader efficiently before the thesis arrives.

  7. A thesis that simply restates a factual prompt statement is weak because it:

    • Is too controversial, since it takes a stand many readers would reject
    • Is too narrow, since it covers a single detail of the prompt
    • Lacks evidence, since a thesis must include its supporting quotations
    • Isn't arguable — no one could reasonably disagree with a plain fact

    A thesis must be arguable; a bare fact restatement isn't.

  8. Which paragraph structure element ties the evidence back to the paragraph's claim?

    • The topic sentence alone, since it announces the claim that the paragraph is meant to support
    • The transition at the paragraph’s opening, since it links the evidence to the previous paragraph’s claim
    • The quotation itself, since a well-chosen piece of evidence makes its own connection to the claim
    • Commentary at the paragraph's close

    Closing commentary should tie the evidence explicitly back to the thesis/claim.

  9. Which best represents a genuine counterargument being engaged, not dismissed?

    • Acknowledging the opposing view in one sentence and then moving straight to the writer's own evidence
    • Quoting the opposing view at length and then restating the thesis without explaining why it falls short
    • Agreeing with the opposing view in the conclusion so that the essay seems balanced and fair to readers
    • Explaining the opposing view's strongest form, then explaining specifically why it falls short

    Genuine engagement requires presenting the opposing view fairly before rebutting it.

  10. Which best distinguishes a concession from a rebuttal?

    • A concession refutes a flawed opposing point, while a rebuttal grants one that is valid
    • A concession acknowledges a valid opposing point; a rebuttal explains why a point is flawed
    • A concession restates the thesis in new words; a rebuttal introduces a fresh piece of evidence
    • A rebuttal belongs in the conclusion, while a concession belongs in the introduction

    Concession = acknowledge; rebuttal = refute — they are distinct, often paired, moves.

  11. A conclusion that only repeats the thesis word-for-word is considered:

    • The strongest possible conclusion, since a repeated thesis reminds the reader of the central claim
    • A requirement for a passing score, since the rubric asks the writer to restate the thesis at the end
    • A missed opportunity to extend the argument's significance
    • A conclusion that cannot be improved, since the thesis has already been stated in its best possible form

    Strong conclusions go beyond simple restatement to broaden significance.

  12. 'Concede-then-counter' means:

    • ignoring opposing points so that the argument seems unanswerable in the reader’s eyes
    • granting an opposing point, then explaining why it does not defeat the thesis
    • agreeing with the opposition and changing the thesis to match the opposing position
    • restating the opposing view sympathetically and leaving the reader to judge which side is stronger

    It shows fairness, then limits the concession's force.

  13. Repeating a key term across paragraphs, rather than always finding synonyms, helps:

    • pad the word count so that the essay reaches the length that graders seem to expect
    • keep the argument's thread visible to the reader
    • avoid plagiarism by ensuring that each term in the essay is used exactly as it appears in the sources
    • establish a formal tone by repeating the words that are used most often in academic prose

    Consistent key terms aid coherence more than 'elegant variation'.

  14. An essay on school uniforms opens with a vivid scene of a student turned away at the door, then states a claim, then concedes the strongest opposing point before refuting it. Which sequence correctly identifies the structure?

    • Anecdotal introduction, claim, concession, refutation
    • Claim, anecdote, refutation, conclusion
    • Concession, anecdote, claim, call to action
    • Narration, definition, comparison, summary

    The anecdote opens, the thesis follows, and the writer then concedes and refutes in the standard concession-and-rebuttal pattern.

  15. A writer ends a paragraph with, "Critics are right that the program is costly; they are wrong that it is wasteful." This sentence primarily:

    • Changes the topic from the cost of the program to its waste, so that the reader considers a new issue
    • Provides a statistic about the program’s cost that the reader can compare with the claim in the next paragraph
    • Concedes a point and then distinguishes it from the claim the writer rejects
    • Introduces a new thesis that the writer will defend in the second half of the essay

    It accepts the criticism of cost while separating it from waste, which the writer denies.

  16. Which transition best signals that the next paragraph will complicate the previous argument?

    • “For example, consider the following case, which shows how the principle works in practice.”
    • “In addition, the evidence shows that the policy has also been effective in other communities.”
    • “Similarly, the same is true of the other cases that the writer has considered in the essay.”
    • "Yet this account overlooks an important complication."

    'Yet' and 'overlooks' announce a complication; the others extend or illustrate.

  17. A writer organizes an essay by identifying a problem, explaining its causes, proposing a solution, and anticipating objections. This pattern is best described as:

    • Compare-contrast
    • Classification
    • Problem-solution
    • Cause-and-effect

    The organization moves from problem to a proposed remedy and addresses objections.

  18. Which of the following would most effectively place a counterargument in an essay?

    • After the main claim, where the writer acknowledges and then answers a serious objection
    • In the opening paragraph, where the writer names an objection and does not answer it
    • At the very end of the essay, where the writer concedes it and leaves it unanswered
    • Throughout the essay, repeated in each paragraph to show the opposing view's strength

    A good counterargument is acknowledged and answered, strengthening the thesis.

  19. A paragraph moves from a general principle to a specific example and then to a conclusion about the claim. Which reasoning pattern does it follow?

    • Inductive reasoning from many examples
    • Analogy
    • Causal chain
    • Deductive reasoning

    Beginning with a general principle and applying it to a case is deductive.

  20. A writer examines five cases of town councils that reduced speed limits and concludes that lower limits reduce accidents. The most important limitation of this reasoning is that:

    • Inductive reasoning is invalid, since general claims cannot rest on cases
    • Town councils lack authority, since speed limits are set by state agencies
    • Five cases may not be representative enough to support a general claim
    • Speed limits rarely change behavior, since carelessness causes most crashes

    Inductive conclusions are only as strong as the sample's size and representativeness.

  21. A conclusion that merely repeats the introduction word for word is least effective because it:

    • Is too long for a final paragraph, since a conclusion should be brief and should not resemble the introduction
    • Fails to show how the argument developed or why it matters
    • Uses a quotation from the sources, which turns the writer’s last words into another writer’s argument
    • Introduces a new claim that the essay has not defended, so that the reader finishes with a loose end

    A strong conclusion synthesizes and extends the argument.

  22. A writer uses an extended analogy between a school and a ship to explain leadership. Which weakness is most associated with arguing by analogy?

    • The analogy may not hold in all relevant respects
    • Analogies are fallacies, since compared things differ
    • Analogies appeal to emotion rather than to reason
    • The analogy supplies no evidence unless it cites numbers

    Analogies are persuasive only to the extent the compared cases are alike in relevant ways.

  23. Which revision most improves coherence between two body paragraphs?

    • Adding an unrelated quotation that gives the reader a break between the two paragraphs and renews interest
    • Deleting the second paragraph’s topic sentence so that its idea seems to flow directly from the first
    • Repeating the introduction at the start of the second paragraph so that the thesis stays in view
    • Adding a sentence that links the previous paragraph's idea to the next paragraph's claim

    Transitions that connect ideas maintain the line of reasoning.

Unit 7: The Synthesis Essay (33)

  1. The synthesis essay primarily requires the writer to:

    • Develop their own argument, supported by at least three provided sources
    • Summarize the provided sources in order with a brief comment on each
    • Compare the reliability of the provided sources and rank them for the reader
    • Develop an argument using outside knowledge, with sources as optional support

    The synthesis essay is the writer's own argument, using sources as support.

  2. What is the minimum number of sources that must be cited in the synthesis essay?

    • Three
    • One
    • All provided sources
    • Zero

    At least three of the provided sources must be cited.

  3. Organizing a synthesis essay strictly source-by-source ('Source A says... Source B says...') is:

    • A strong strategy, since it shows each source was read carefully
    • Expected by the prompt, which asks for each source in turn
    • Acceptable with few sources, since the essay can then track each one
    • A common weakness — it becomes a summary rather than an argument

    Source-by-source organization tends to become summary instead of a genuine argument.

  4. A 'qualified' thesis on the synthesis prompt (agreeing with conditions/nuance) is:

    • Not acceptable on the synthesis prompt, which asks for one firm position
    • Acceptable on the argument essay, but the synthesis task requires a firm stance
    • Completely acceptable and often stronger than an all-or-nothing stance
    • A weakness, since conditions and exceptions suggest the writer is undecided

    A specific, qualified position is a legitimate and often strong approach.

  5. A vague thesis that doesn't commit to any real position on the synthesis prompt is:

    • A strength, since a broad claim is hard to refute
    • Expected, since the rubric rewards neutrality
    • Acceptable if the sources themselves disagree
    • A weakness — it isn't defensible or specific

    Vague, noncommittal theses fail to take a defensible position.

  6. Citing a source and then explaining how it supports your specific claim demonstrates:

    • Overreliance on quotation over the writer's claim
    • Proper integration of evidence with commentary
    • Summary of the source in place of an argument
    • Needless repetition of the source in commentary

    Sources need commentary connecting them to the writer's own argument.

  7. Citing sources by their letter (e.g., 'Source B') or clear paraphrase, rather than quoting at length, is generally:

    • Discouraged in favor of long quotes
    • Acceptable for one source per essay
    • Penalized as inexact summarizing
    • Preferred, when paired with analysis

    Concise citation paired with analysis is generally more effective than long unanalyzed quotes.

  8. A synthesis essay that could be outlined using ONLY the writer's own claims (sources filling in support) is:

    • A sign of too little reliance on the sources
    • A sign of strong, argument-driven organization
    • A sign the writer ignored the provided sources
    • A sign of strong summary-based organization

    This shows the essay is organized by argument, not merely summarizing sources.

  9. Anticipating the strongest counterargument to your synthesis position and addressing it with a source is:

    • A strong strategic move
    • A risky strategic choice
    • A common structural flaw
    • A weak organizational move

    Addressing the strongest counterargument, supported by a source, strengthens the essay.

  10. Which best distinguishes synthesis from summary?

    • Synthesis restates what the sources say, while summary builds the writer's own argument
    • Synthesis analyzes a single source in depth, while summary compares several sources
    • Synthesis develops the writer's OWN argument; summary just restates sources' content
    • Summary requires a thesis and commentary, while synthesis relies on quotation alone

    Synthesis is argument-driven; summary is restatement without a governing claim.

  11. Why is using FEWER than three sources a problem on the synthesis essay?

    • It makes the thesis harder to defend in a short, timed essay
    • It lowers the score, because graders want at least five sources
    • It breaks the rule that the sources must appear in order
    • It fails to meet the minimum sourcing requirement of the task

    At least three sources must be cited to meet the task's requirements.

  12. A synthesis essay thesis that says 'Some believe X, others believe Y' without taking a position is:

    • Too noncommittal to be defensible
    • An ideal thesis
    • Required by the rubric
    • The safest possible choice

    A thesis must commit to a specific, defensible position, not just describe both sides.

  13. Which best represents strategic sourcing to acknowledge a counterargument?

    • “Source C says cost is a concern, and Source A says the plan has long-term benefits for the town.”
    • 'While Source C raises a valid concern about cost, the long-term benefits described in Source A outweigh it.'
    • Leaving out Source C altogether so that the essay’s argument appears to face no serious objection
    • Quoting Source C at full length with no commentary, so that the reader can judge its force directly

    This acknowledges the counterpoint, then explains why the writer's position still holds — using sources purposefully.

  14. Why might a writer use a source they don't fully agree with in a synthesis essay?

    • To avoid taking a position by presenting both sides equally
    • To prove the source wrong without engaging its claims
    • To acknowledge and then rebut it as part of the argument
    • To show agreement with the source's main conclusions

    Sources can be used to represent and then rebut opposing views.

  15. A synthesis essay entirely organized as 'Source A, then Source B, then Source C' with no unifying claim across paragraphs is:

    • An ideal structure, since it ensures that each source receives careful attention in turn
    • Required by the College Board, whose scoring guide asks writers to treat the sources in order
    • The best way to cite sources, because it prevents the writer from confusing them with one another
    • A structural weakness resembling a summary, not an argument

    This organization pattern fails to build a genuine, unified argument.

  16. Which best reflects a synthesis essay's core goal?

    • Summarizing the sources in order to show how well the writer has read them
    • Using sources as evidence to support the writer's own defensible claim
    • Rebutting the weakest sources to show the writer's independent judgment
    • Presenting a balanced view of the sources without committing to a position

    The synthesis essay's core goal is the writer's argument, supported by sources.

  17. Which best shows a synthesis essay citation properly paired with commentary?

    • “Source A discusses wait times in the emergency department and the effect they have on care.”
    • “According to Source A, patients wait longer than they used to, and the delay is a problem.”
    • “Source A’s full paragraph on wait times is reproduced here, and readers can judge it for themselves.”
    • 'Source A's data on wait times shows the current system is failing patients most in need.'

    This pairs the citation with commentary explaining its significance to the argument.

  18. The AP synthesis essay requires the writer to:

    • summarize each of the provided sources in turn, noting its main point and evidence
    • develop an argument that uses at least three of the provided sources as support
    • compare the reliability of the provided sources and rank them from strongest to weakest
    • choose one source to analyze in depth, using the others for brief contrast

    Sources are evidence for the writer's own position, cited (at least three).

  19. The 'summary trap' in a synthesis essay is:

    • using too many quotations, so that the writer’s own claims are crowded out of each paragraph
    • citing fewer than three sources, so that the essay fails to meet the task’s minimum requirement
    • writing an essay that is too short to develop the writer’s own argument beyond a brief statement
    • walking through the sources one by one instead of organizing by your own claims

    Body paragraphs should be built around sub-claims, drawing in sources as needed.

  20. A 'defensible' thesis for a synthesis prompt is one that:

    • takes a clear, arguable position that the sources can be used to support
    • restates the prompt in new words to show the grader it was understood
    • agrees with each source provided so that the essay shows the writer read them
    • avoids taking a side so that the essay can be defended against objections

    It should be specific and possible to argue against.

  21. In a synthesis essay, a quotation should generally be:

    • dropped in without framing, so the source's own words make the point
    • introduced and then explained, used only when the exact wording matters
    • used for most of each paragraph, since graders reward close reading
    • avoided, since paraphrase shows better understanding than quotation

    Frame quotations and keep them short; paraphrase when wording is not the point.

  22. Organizing a synthesis essay 'by your claims' means:

    • each body paragraph advances one of your sub-points, supported by whatever sources fit
    • each paragraph covers one source in the order given, with the writer’s view added at the end
    • paragraphs alternate between sources that support the claim and sources that oppose it
    • the essay follows the order in which the sources are printed in the packet that is provided

    Your argument, not the source list, provides the structure.

  23. A qualified synthesis thesis (e.g. 'Public financing helps in local races but less in national ones') is preferable because it:

    • is longer, which gives the grader more evidence of control
    • cites more sources than a plain thesis would cite
    • avoids a position, so it can be defended against objections
    • is more precise and defensible than a sweeping claim

    Nuance that the sources can support tends to score higher.

  24. A student writes: "Source A says later start times help sleep. Source B says they cost money. Source C says they improve grades." What is the main weakness?

    • It uses too many sources for a short essay, so no source gets depth
    • It cites the sources incorrectly, since each needs the author's full name
    • It states a position too early, before the evidence has been presented
    • It summarizes sources in sequence without using them to develop an argument

    Synthesis requires the writer's argument to organize the sources, not the other way around.

  25. Which sentence best integrates evidence from a source into a synthesis argument?

    • “As Rivera's study of three districts shows, later bells improve attendance, while Chen's study of adjustment periods found different results.”
    • “Rivera's study of three districts found that benefits of later bells appear within a year, while Chen worries about long adjustment periods.”
    • "As Rivera's study of three districts shows, the benefits of later bells appear within a year, which counters Chen's worry about long adjustment periods."
    • “According to Rivera, who studied three districts, benefits of later bells appear within a year, which proves that Chen is wrong about adjustment.”

    It uses the source for a purpose in the argument and links it to a second source, creating dialogue between them.

  26. A synthesis prompt provides six sources. Which approach best meets the expectation to synthesize?

    • Quoting each of the six sources at length so that the grader can see that each was read with care
    • Using at least three sources in service of the writer's own position and showing how they relate to each other
    • Using a single source for the whole essay, since one strong source can support a defensible position
    • Summarizing each source in a separate paragraph, with a brief remark on how it supports the thesis

    Synthesis integrates multiple sources into the writer's own argument.

  27. A student cites a source by writing, "According to the source, the policy works." What is the best revision for credible attribution?

    • "According to economist Maria Lopez in a 2021 report, the policy raised participation by 12 percent."
    • “Some people say the policy works, and the evidence of their experience is persuasive to many readers.”
    • “Experts agree that the policy works, and their view is shared by most of the people who study it.”
    • “The source says it works, and the source’s evidence is strong enough to support the writer’s claim.”

    Strong attribution identifies the source and gives a specific claim.

  28. Two sources reach opposite conclusions about a policy. Which response best reflects sophisticated synthesis?

    • Explaining why the sources differ, such as differences in sample or context, and taking a position
    • Ignoring the source that disagrees with the writer so that the essay appears to rest on a consensus
    • Choosing the shorter source, since a concise source is easier to integrate into a brief essay
    • Summarizing each source without comment and leaving the reader to decide which of them is right

    Evaluating the reasons for disagreement shows analysis.

  29. A writer uses a source's statistic to support a claim but the source's data come from a very different context. What is the most significant concern?

    • The statistic is too specific, since a precise figure suggests a certainty that the data cannot support
    • The source is too short, since a brief document cannot give the context that a statistic requires
    • The evidence may not apply to the writer's claim
    • The statistic is cited, which shows the writer has not done any independent reasoning about the claim

    Evidence must be relevant to the claim being supported.

  30. Which thesis for a synthesis essay on public libraries is best?

    • “Although digital resources have reduced demand for books, libraries remain valuable because they offer a wide range of services that communities rely on.”
    • "Although digital resources reduce some demand for books, libraries remain essential community spaces because they provide access, programming and a refuge that online alternatives do not."
    • “Libraries remain essential community spaces because they provide access, programming and a refuge, as the sources by Rivera and Chen both show.”
    • “Digital resources are replacing libraries, but communities should still fund them because many residents continue to visit them each year.”

    A strong thesis takes a position, acknowledges complexity and previews reasoning.

  31. A student's synthesis essay includes quotations that are longer than the student's own commentary. What is the most likely consequence?

    • The essay may read as a patchwork of sources rather than the student's argument
    • The essay will receive higher credit, since the quotations show the writer’s command of the sources
    • The essay will sound more objective, since the writer’s own voice is limited by the quotations
    • The essay will have a clearer thesis, since the quotations state the central claims directly

    The writer's analysis should dominate.

  32. In synthesis, what is the best use of a source that opposes your position?

    • Avoid it, since mentioning an opposing source gives the reader grounds to doubt the writer’s claim
    • Acknowledge it and respond with evidence or reasoning
    • Quote it without comment, so that the reader can see that the writer has represented it fairly
    • Use it as your own claim, since the opposing source states a position that the essay can adopt

    Engaging opposing evidence strengthens credibility.

  33. A student cites Source D to show that the problem is urgent and Source B to show that the proposed solution is feasible. This best demonstrates:

    • Over-reliance on sources, since the essay appears to be built from other writers’ ideas
    • Using different sources for distinct purposes in an argument
    • Plagiarism, since the writer has used the sources’ ideas without developing independent reasoning
    • A weak thesis, since the writer’s claim depends on the sources more than on the writer’s own thinking

    Each source supports a different part of the reasoning.

Unit 8: The Rhetorical Analysis Essay (27)

  1. The rhetorical analysis essay primarily asks the writer to:

    • Explain HOW a writer builds their argument and its effect on the audience
    • Argue for or against the passage's claim using the writer's own evidence
    • Summarize the passage's content in order and comment on its tone
    • Identify the devices in the passage and define each with an example

    Rhetorical analysis focuses on HOW the argument is built, not whether the reader agrees with it.

  2. The single most common error in rhetorical analysis essays is:

    • Using too many quotations, so that the writer’s own analysis is crowded out of each paragraph
    • Citing too few devices, so that the essay does not cover the passage’s rhetorical strategies
    • Being too concise, so that each paragraph’s claim is stated without enough support from the passage
    • Arguing for or against the passage's topic instead of analyzing the writer's choices

    Students often mistakenly argue the topic itself instead of analyzing HOW the writer argues.

  3. A strong rhetorical analysis thesis should:

    • Restate the passage's topic and summarize its main argument briefly
    • Name the writer's purpose and then list the devices in the order they appear
    • Identify the writer's purpose and preview the strategies to be analyzed
    • State the writer's opinion of the passage's argument and its fairness

    An effective thesis names purpose and previews the specific strategies discussed.

  4. How many rhetorical strategies should a strong essay typically focus on?

    • 4–5, each in modest depth
    • 2–3, discussed in real depth
    • 6–8, each briefly mentioned
    • As many as time allows, briefly

    A few well-developed strategies are stronger than many shallow ones.

  5. Choosing strategies you can trace across MULTIPLE parts of a passage, rather than a single isolated line, is important because:

    • A single line is easier to analyze closely in timed writing
    • Graders score one example per device, so patterns add little
    • It supports a more developed, well-evidenced analysis
    • Repeated examples distract from the writer's central claim

    Tracing a strategy across the passage allows for deeper, more convincing analysis.

  6. Why should a rhetorical analysis essay start by identifying the rhetorical situation?

    • It lets the writer skip the thesis, since the situation names the claim
    • It is useful for synthesis essays, in which sources must be compared
    • It grounds the analysis in speaker, audience, purpose, and occasion
    • It shows the grader that the writer can summarize the passage

    Establishing the rhetorical situation grounds the entire analysis that follows.

  7. A rhetorical analysis essay that spends a whole paragraph arguing the topic is wrong (e.g., disagreeing with the writer's stance) is:

    • The correct approach, since an analysis must first show that the writer’s stance is wrong
    • Required for a high score, since graders reward writers who take a clear position on the topic
    • Off-task — this isn't what rhetorical analysis asks for
    • Optional but encouraged, since it shows the writer’s independence and willingness to take a position

    Arguing the topic itself, rather than analyzing the writer's rhetoric, is off-task.

  8. Explaining WHY a specific word was chosen over an alternative demonstrates:

    • Overinterpretation of one detail
    • Unnecessary attention to minor details
    • Strong, precise rhetorical analysis
    • Summary of the passage's wording

    Explaining specific word choices over alternatives shows precise, strong analysis.

  9. Which best completes a device-to-effect analysis: 'The anaphora of "we must"...'?

    • “…is used three times in the second paragraph, in the first sentence of each section.”
    • “…is a rhetorical device in which a phrase is repeated at the beginning of successive clauses.”
    • “…appears in the second paragraph of the speech, where the speaker first mentions the audience.”
    • '...builds a mounting sense of urgency, compelling the audience toward collective action.'

    This explains the specific effect on the audience, completing the device-to-effect move.

  10. Analyzing a persuasive speech, a student instead explains why they personally disagree with the speaker's cause. This essay:

    • Correctly fulfills the task, since the student has shown a clear and personal engagement with the topic
    • Fails to fulfill the rhetorical analysis task
    • Is the strongest possible approach, since a personal view is the most direct form of analysis
    • Does not need a thesis, since a personal response to the speaker’s cause serves in its place

    This confuses rhetorical analysis with an argument essay about the topic itself.

  11. A rhetorical analysis thesis that only restates the passage's topic, without naming strategies or purpose, is:

    • Adequate for a rhetorical thesis
    • Strong, since it stays on the topic
    • Underdeveloped for this essay type
    • Appropriate when the passage is short

    A strong thesis must go beyond topic restatement to name purpose and strategies.

  12. Which is a valid organizational approach for rhetorical analysis?

    • Either strategy-based or chronological structure, if reasoning is clear
    • Strategy-based structure alone, since chronological order becomes summary
    • Chronological structure alone, since strategy-based essays ignore the order
    • Thematic structure organized around the writer's own opinions of the passage

    Both structures are valid as long as the essay's reasoning is clear and well-organized.

  13. Discussing 5+ rhetorical devices shallowly, with one sentence each, compared to 2-3 devices in depth, is generally:

    • A stronger approach, since it shows a wider range of knowledge
    • Equally effective, since graders credit each device identified
    • Required by the exam, which scores the number of devices named
    • A weaker approach than fewer, well-developed strategies

    A few well-developed strategies produce stronger analysis than many shallow ones.

  14. Which best reflects analyzing a shift in strategy across a passage's structure?

    • The essay opens with logos-heavy statistics before pivoting to pathos-driven anecdotes in the closing paragraphs
    • The essay discusses the opening paragraph in depth, treating it as the section where the argument is set out
    • The essay compares the passage with other writers' texts on the same topic, in order to judge its fairness
    • The essay lists the devices in order of appearance, noting each one with a short definition and example

    Tracking how strategies shift across the passage shows sophisticated structural analysis.

  15. For a timed rhetorical analysis, the best approach to strategies is usually:

    • list 5 or more strategies briefly
    • analyze 2-3 strategies in depth
    • focus on a single device in depth
    • summarize the passage first

    Depth of analysis beats breadth of identification.

  16. A defensible rhetorical analysis thesis should be:

    • a statement of fact that everyone accepts, so that the writer’s analysis can build on common ground
    • a summary of the passage that identifies each of its main points and the order in which they appear
    • arguable - a reasonable reader could interpret the choices differently
    • a personal opinion about the topic that the writer supports with evidence from the passage

    It makes a claim about the writer's choices that requires support.

  17. A strong body paragraph in a rhetorical analysis essay:

    • identifies a choice, provides textual evidence, and explains the effect on the argument
    • quotes the passage at length so that the grader can see the evidence behind the claim
    • names the devices the writer uses and defines each one in the paragraph's opening
    • restates the thesis in the first and last sentences with one example between them

    Claim-evidence-analysis is the core structure.

  18. A passage's author, writing to a hostile audience, begins by praising the audience's commitment to safety before criticizing a policy. Which analysis best explains the strategy?

    • The praise is an example of hyperbole that wins the audience’s sympathy by exaggerating its virtues
    • The praise is a distraction that keeps the audience from seeing the criticism until it is too late
    • The praise establishes common ground so the criticism seems a shared concern rather than an attack
    • The author is changing the subject so that the audience will not notice that the policy is flawed

    Opening with shared values lowers resistance, positioning the criticism as consistent with the audience's own commitments.

  19. Which topic sentence for a rhetorical analysis body paragraph is strongest?

    • “In the second paragraph, Kim shifts from statistics to a personal anecdote, which makes her essay more interesting for a general audience.”
    • "By shifting from statistics to a personal anecdote in the second paragraph, Kim humanizes the issue and encourages empathy from a general audience."
    • “Kim's shift from statistics to anecdote shows that she uses both logos and pathos in the second paragraph to persuade her readers.”
    • “By including a personal anecdote after the statistics in the second paragraph, Kim proves that her argument is emotional rather than logical.”

    It names a specific choice, explains the effect and links it to the audience.

  20. A student writes, "The author uses a metaphor, which makes the essay better." What is the primary weakness?

    • It identifies a device and so shows that the student can recognize rhetorical strategies in the passage
    • It does not explain how the metaphor works or its effect on the audience
    • It uses too much evidence, so that the writer’s own commentary is lost among the quotations
    • It states a claim, but the claim is too broad to be supported by any single piece of evidence

    Naming a device is not analysis; the student must explain the effect.

  21. Which of the following best describes the difference between summary and analysis in a rhetorical analysis essay?

    • Summary reports what the text says; analysis explains how and why the writer's choices produce an effect
    • They are the same, since both explain what the passage says in the writer’s own words
    • Analysis is longer than summary, and graders reward essays that spend most of their time on analysis
    • Summary identifies the tone of the passage, while analysis identifies the devices that create it

    Rhetorical analysis explains the relationship between choices and effects.

  22. A writer opens a speech with a long list of historical wrongs and then asks the audience to act now. Which assessment best explains the structure's effect?

    • It confuses the audience, since a long list makes the speaker’s point difficult to follow
    • It undermines the speaker’s purpose, since a list of past wrongs seems to excuse inaction now
    • The accumulation builds urgency so the call to action seems the natural response
    • It establishes a neutral tone, since the list presents the facts without any evident emotion

    The list generates momentum that the appeal then channels.

  23. A student argues that an author uses ethos by mentioning her twenty years as a nurse. Which addition would most deepen the analysis?

    • Counting the number of years mentioned and comparing it with the experience of other authors
    • Quoting the sentence again so that the grader can see the exact wording of the writer’s claim
    • Explaining how the experience makes her claims about staffing more credible to readers who distrust administrators
    • Defining ethos as an appeal to the credibility of the writer and giving two other examples

    The analysis should connect the choice to its effect on the audience in context.

  24. A rhetorical analysis essay discusses an author's tone as 'passionate.' How could the student improve this?

    • Specify the tone more precisely, such as 'indignant but controlled,' and show how diction creates it
    • Replace it with “good,” which is a simpler word and describes the writer’s attitude toward the topic
    • Remove the discussion of tone, since the essay should concentrate on the passage’s evidence
    • State it again in the conclusion so that the reader is certain to remember the writer’s point

    Precise tone words supported by textual evidence show insight.

  25. Which sentence best shows a line of reasoning that connects evidence to the thesis?

    • “The writer's use of second-person address makes readers feel personally involved, which helps her persuade them throughout the passage.”
    • "The writer's use of second-person address invites readers to imagine themselves in the scene, making the abstract policy feel personally consequential."
    • “By addressing readers as ‘you,’ the writer creates a conversational tone, which shows that the passage is informal in style and purpose.”
    • “The writer's second-person address invites readers to imagine themselves in the scene, a strategy that appears in the third paragraph and the conclusion.”

    It explains how the device works and its effect on readers.

  26. A student's analysis claims the author is 'trying to persuade the audience' without describing how. This is most accurately characterized as:

    • A sophisticated analysis that places the passage in its larger social and historical context
    • A thesis that identifies the writer’s purpose and previews the strategies that the essay will examine
    • A summary of the conclusion that reports what the writer says in the passage’s last paragraph
    • A general statement that does not analyze specific choices

    Analysis requires attention to specific rhetorical choices and effects.

  27. A writer shifts abruptly from formal diction to colloquial language. What is the best way to analyze this shift?

    • Ignore it, since a change of diction is a matter of style and not a rhetorical choice
    • Identify the shift, describe its effect on tone and relate it to the writer's relationship with the audience
    • Say that it is a mistake, since a writer who shifts diction has lost control of the passage’s tone
    • Say that it is a metaphor, since the shift compares the formal and the casual registers

    Shifts in diction signal changes in attitude or relationship worth analyzing.

Unit 9: The Argument Essay (26)

  1. Which is considered valid evidence in an argument essay?

    • Rumors and unverified claims, since persuasion matters more than accuracy
    • Historical examples, current events, literature, or personal experience
    • Invented statistics, since graders have no way to verify them
    • Passages quoted from the prompt, since they need no explanation

    A wide range of evidence types are valid, as long as they're specific and relevant.

  2. A 'qualified' thesis ('X is true, except when...') in an argument essay often demonstrates:

    • Weak reasoning, since a thesis with exceptions shows the writer is unsure
    • More sophisticated thinking than an absolute, all-or-nothing claim
    • A breach of the task, since the prompt requires agreeing or disagreeing
    • A lack of commitment, since graders prefer one clear, firm stance

    Nuanced, qualified positions often show more sophisticated thinking than absolute claims.

  3. Addressing a counterargument in the argument essay, then explaining why your position still holds, primarily demonstrates:

    • Awareness of the issue's complexity
    • A logical fallacy, since raising an objection gives the reader a reason to doubt the thesis
    • Weakness in your position, since the writer has shown that a reasonable person could disagree
    • An unnecessary structural step, since the thesis has already been supported by the earlier paragraphs

    Engaging counterarguments shows awareness of complexity and strengthens the essay.

  4. Explaining the broader implications or stakes of an argument is one way to demonstrate:

    • Sophistication of thought
    • Weak reasoning
    • A logical fallacy
    • Poor organization

    Broader implications/stakes are a recognized marker of sophisticated argumentation.

  5. Vivid, effective writing style alone (without complex reasoning) is:

    • Sufficient by itself for sophistication credit, since a graceful style shows mastery of the topic
    • Not equivalent to sophistication — reasoning must also be genuinely complex
    • Irrelevant to the essay entirely, since graders look only at the reasoning and not at the writing
    • Required for a passing thesis, since a thesis must be written in an elevated and polished style

    Sophistication requires substantive complexity of reasoning, not just polished prose.

  6. Making nuanced distinctions ('this is true in some contexts but not others') shows:

    • A weak and indecisive argument, since the writer has not committed to a clear position
    • A logical fallacy, since a claim that is true in one context cannot be false in another
    • Sophistication over an all-or-nothing stance
    • Poor thesis construction, since a claim with conditions is not defensible in a short timed essay

    Nuanced context-dependent claims demonstrate sophisticated thinking.

  7. Ignoring the counterargument entirely in an argument essay tends to make the essay seem:

    • More focused and persuasive overall
    • Strategically wise on a timed exam
    • Cautious and appropriately concise
    • Incomplete or naive in its reasoning

    Ignoring counterarguments weakens the perceived completeness of the reasoning.

  8. Which best shows specific, well-developed evidence rather than a vague generality?

    • Detailing the 1969 moon landing's effect on public trust in science, with specifics
    • “Space exploration has helped society in many ways, and the benefits have reached most countries.”
    • “Science is generally good for people, and its benefits have made life better for everyone.”
    • “History shows that progress happens, and the world has become better over the last century.”

    The specific, detailed example is far stronger than the vague general statements.

  9. An argument essay may take which kind of position on the given claim?

    • Agree with the claim or agree with qualifications, but not disagree outright
    • Disagree with the claim or take a qualified view, but not agree outright
    • Take a neutral stance that weighs both sides without committing to either
    • Agree, disagree, or agree with qualifications — any defensible position

    Any well-supported, defensible position is acceptable.

  10. Why must argument-essay evidence be 'verifiably true or at least reasonably plausible'?

    • Invented 'facts' undermine the writer's credibility
    • Graders verify each example against outside sources
    • Plausible evidence counts for less than documented proof
    • Invented examples distract from the thesis statement

    Invented or implausible 'facts' damage the writer's ethos/credibility.

  11. A basic thesis-evidence-conclusion structure without further nuance is generally scored as:

    • A top-scoring approach, since clear structure helps graders
    • Unscorable, since the rubric needs more complex reasoning
    • Competent but not necessarily the most sophisticated approach
    • A failing response, since a thesis without nuance earns no credit

    Basic structure can be competent, but sophistication requires going beyond it with nuance.

  12. Which best reflects addressing complexity in an argument essay?

    • 'Although some people disagree with this policy, it is the best policy and the evidence proves it.'
    • Naming a few exceptions in the introduction and then ignoring them for the rest of the essay
    • Restating the thesis in different words at the start of each paragraph to keep the claim clear
    • 'While exceptions exist in emergency situations, the general policy remains sound because...'

    Acknowledging exceptions while still defending the general position shows nuanced, complex thinking.

  13. Which best distinguishes the argument essay from the synthesis essay?

    • The argument essay requires provided sources, while synthesis relies on the writer's own evidence
    • The argument essay requires a thesis, while the synthesis essay requires a summary of sources
    • Argument essays require at least three sources, which the writer chooses from memory
    • The argument essay uses the writer's own evidence; synthesis requires citing provided sources

    This is the defining structural difference between the two essay types.

  14. Which best demonstrates addressing the 'stakes' of an argument for sophistication credit?

    • Restating the thesis in stronger language so the reader sees its firmness
    • Explaining what could go wrong for real communities if the policy is NOT adopted
    • Explaining what the policy would cost taxpayers if it were adopted in the coming year
    • Adding examples from history to show that the claim has held in earlier periods

    Explaining real-world stakes/implications is a recognized way to show sophistication.

  15. 'Sophistication' on the AP argument rubric can be earned by:

    • using longer words and more complex sentences so the essay reads as skilled
    • writing a longer essay with more paragraphs than the task requires
    • situating the argument in a broader context or acknowledging complexity
    • citing more examples than the task requires, to support the claim widely

    Nuance, tension, and a compelling style signal sophisticated thought.

  16. A nuanced thesis such as 'Curfews reduce some crimes but at a civic cost' is preferable to a flat one because it:

    • reflects the complexity of the issue and is easier to defend well
    • is safer because it avoids a position and cannot be shown to be false by any single example
    • uses more sophisticated vocabulary, which graders reward in the sophistication row of the rubric
    • is longer, and so allows the writer to show more of the thinking behind the claim

    Qualified, specific claims tend to support stronger reasoning.

  17. Given the prompt "Is it more important to preserve tradition or embrace change?", which thesis best reflects the sophistication expected in an argument essay?

    • "While tradition provides continuity, a community that refuses change risks becoming irrelevant, so the healthiest societies preserve traditions that serve their values and revise those that no longer do."
    • “Tradition and change are both valuable, so societies should find a balance between preserving the old ways and welcoming the new ones.”
    • “While change can bring progress, a community that abandons its traditions risks losing its identity, so societies should protect their traditions.”
    • “Although tradition matters, change is more important, since societies that refuse to change have often been overtaken by those that adapt.”

    A nuanced thesis acknowledges complexity and makes a defensible, reasoned claim.

  18. A student's essay argues that homework should be limited and supports this with only personal anecdotes. How could the essay best be improved?

    • Add varied evidence, such as research and examples from other schools, and explain how they support the claim
    • Add more personal anecdotes, so that the writer’s view is supported by a larger number of cases
    • Remove the claim, since a thesis supported by anecdote alone cannot be defended in a timed essay
    • Change the topic to one on which the writer has access to more reliable statistical evidence

    Strong arguments use multiple kinds of evidence and commentary.

  19. A writer concedes that 'online classes are convenient' and then argues that 'convenience is not the same as learning.' This move best demonstrates:

    • Circular reasoning, assuming the claim as its proof
    • False dilemma between convenience and learning
    • Qualification and refutation of an opposing idea
    • Summary of the opposing view without comment

    Granting a point and then limiting its force is a sophisticated argumentative move.

  20. Which of the following best illustrates the use of specific, relevant evidence in an argument about public transportation?

    • A claim that “everyone knows” transit is good for cities, followed by a statement of its popularity
    • A quotation about trains from a novel that describes the pleasure of traveling across the countryside
    • A comparison of commute times and costs in two cities with different transit investment
    • A statement that transit exists in most cities and that many people use it in their daily lives

    Specific and relevant evidence supports a particular claim.

  21. A student argues that a school should extend the library's hours, but the essay never addresses cost. Which revision would best strengthen the argument?

    • Remove the evidence on usage so that the essay is focused on the writer's claim and not on support
    • Anticipate the objection about cost and respond with an estimate or an alternative funding approach
    • Add emotional appeals about students' stress so that the reader feels the library's importance
    • Argue that cost is secondary, since the value of longer hours outweighs the expense involved

    Addressing a likely objection strengthens the argument.

  22. Which sentence from an argument essay most effectively uses commentary?

    • “The policy has benefits that are shown in the data, and these benefits are available to many students.”
    • “Many students are affected by the policy, and the effects are described in the sources the writer cites.”
    • "This difference matters because it shows the policy's benefits reach the students who are least likely to be reached by existing programs."
    • “There are students who attend the schools where the policy has been tried, and they number in the thousands.”

    Commentary explains the significance of evidence.

  23. A writer begins an argument with a definition of a key term and then uses that definition throughout. What is the strategic purpose?

    • To confuse the audience so that readers accept the writer’s claim without noticing how it is defined
    • To fill space in an essay that has too little material to reach the length that is expected
    • To establish a precise meaning on which the argument depends
    • To add humor to a serious argument so that the reader’s attention is held through the middle of the essay

    Defining terms prevents misunderstanding.

  24. Which of the following would most weaken an argument essay's credibility?

    • Acknowledging the complexity of the issue, since a writer who admits difficulty seems indecisive
    • Using precise language, since a writer who is exact seems to be more concerned with words than with ideas
    • Relying on an exaggerated claim without evidence
    • Citing a credible source, since an argument that depends on others’ authority seems to lack original thought

    Overstated claims erode trust.

  25. An essay argues that the voting age should be lowered to 16 and supports this by noting that 16-year-olds can work and pay taxes. What is the best way to deepen the reasoning?

    • Add evidence about the average age at which teenagers start working, along with a statistic on how many 16-year-olds pay income taxes
    • Explain that voting is a right and not a privilege, and cite the Twenty-sixth Amendment as the reason the age should be changed
    • Explain the principle behind the claim, such as taxation implying representation, and address differences between work and voting
    • Acknowledge that many teenagers are less informed than adults, and then argue that this disadvantage is outweighed by the taxes they already pay

    Reasoning should state the principle that connects the evidence to the claim.

  26. A student writes: "Some might say technology isolates us, but it also connects us." What does this sentence do?

    • Develops a full rebuttal of the counterclaim, with evidence for each part of the writer’s response
    • Acknowledges a counterclaim and responds, though it needs development to be persuasive
    • Provides evidence that technology connects people, in the form of a study of social networks
    • Concludes the essay by summarizing its argument and restating the thesis for the reader

    It begins a concession-rebuttal but remains thin without evidence.

Unit 10: Grammar, Conventions & Multiple-Choice Strategy (24)

  1. 'Running quickly to the store.' with no subject or complete thought is a:

    • Sentence fragment
    • Comma splice
    • Run-on sentence
    • Correct sentence

    This lacks a complete subject-verb thought and cannot stand alone — a fragment.

  2. 'I went to the store I bought milk' with no punctuation at all connecting the clauses is a:

    • Run-on sentence
    • Sentence fragment
    • Correct sentence
    • Parallel structure

    Independent clauses joined with no punctuation or connector at all form a run-on.

  3. Which correctly demonstrates subject-verb agreement despite intervening words?

    • 'The box of old books is heavy.'
    • 'The box of old books are heavy.'
    • 'The boxes of old book is heavy.'
    • 'The box of old book are heavy.'

    'Box' (singular) is the true subject, so it takes 'is,' regardless of the intervening 'of old books.'

  4. A multiple-choice reading question asking for a passage's main claim tests:

    • Close reading of the passage's overall argument
    • Grammar and punctuation, since the main claim is identified by the way each sentence is constructed
    • The reader’s personal opinion, which should be set out clearly and need not match the passage’s claim
    • Vocabulary memorization, since the claim is usually found by defining the key words in the first paragraph

    Main-claim questions test comprehension of the passage's overall argument.

  5. A writing multiple-choice question asking for the 'best transition' tests:

    • Spelling and word choice, since a transition is correct when each word in it has been spelled properly
    • Historical facts about the subject, since the best transition depends on what happened earlier in the passage
    • Vocabulary definitions, since the right transition is the one whose literal meaning is closest to the previous sentence
    • Revision skill — choosing language that fits the passage's logic

    Writing questions test a student's ability to revise for clarity, logic, and fit.

  6. A question asking 'which choice best maintains the established tone' requires:

    • Judging the sentence with the blank, since tone is set locally
    • Checking the surrounding sentences' tone, not just grammar
    • Choosing the most formal option, since it suits most texts
    • Checking grammar and punctuation, since tone follows correctness

    Tone-matching questions require attention to the surrounding passage's tone.

  7. A question asking which choice would be 'LEAST effective' requires:

    • Choosing the best-written answer, since the stem does not change the task
    • Reading the passage first, since the stem repeats what the choices say
    • Reading the question stem carefully — the correct answer is the WORST option
    • Eliminating the longest option, since the worst answer tends to be wordy

    Some questions invert the usual logic and ask for the least effective/worst choice.

  8. 'Everyone must bring their own laptop' mixing a singular antecedent ('everyone') with a plural pronoun ('their') is an example (in the strict formal usage tested) of:

    • A comma splice, in which two independent clauses are joined by a comma without a conjunction
    • A run-on sentence, in which two independent clauses run together without any punctuation
    • A pronoun-antecedent agreement issue
    • Correct parallel structure, since both parts of the sentence use the same grammatical pattern

    'Everyone' is singular, so strict formal usage pairs it with a singular pronoun form.

  9. Fixing a comma splice by just deleting the comma with nothing else added typically creates:

    • A grammatically correct sentence, since two independent clauses may be placed side by side
    • A sentence fragment, since one clause no longer has a verb of its own after the comma is gone
    • Correct parallel structure, since each clause now follows the same grammatical pattern as the other
    • A run-on sentence instead of a correct one

    Removing only the comma, with no replacement punctuation, creates a run-on.

  10. A question asking where to best place a sentence within a paragraph tests:

    • Punctuation and conventions
    • Vocabulary and word choice
    • Tone and level of formality
    • Organizational logic and flow

    Placement questions test understanding of a paragraph's logical organization.

  11. Why is it important to read the multiple-choice question stem carefully before answering?

    • Most questions ask for the best option, so the stem adds little to the choices
    • Some questions ask for the least effective option or a deletion, reversing the usual logic
    • The stem names the passage's main topic, which the answer choices do not mention
    • Stems differ by section, so reading questions need a stem but writing questions do not

    Careful reading prevents missing inverted questions (e.g., 'least effective,' 'should be deleted').

  12. 'Neither the teacher nor the students was ready' should actually use which verb to agree with the nearer subject?

    • 'was,' agreeing with the earlier singular subject 'teacher'
    • 'was,' agreeing with the singular pronoun 'neither'
    • 'are,' agreeing with the combined subject 'teacher and students'
    • 'were,' agreeing with the nearer plural subject 'students'

    With 'neither...nor,' the verb agrees with the subject closer to it — 'students' (plural) takes 'were.'

  13. A colon is correctly used when:

    • the clause before it is complete and it introduces an explanation, list, or appositive
    • it joins two independent clauses in a casual way where a writer wants a less formal effect
    • it replaces a comma in a series so that the items in the list stand out more clearly
    • it ends a question that the writer has asked for the purpose of introducing the next paragraph

    'She had one goal: to finish.' The clause before the colon stands alone.

  14. On a multiple-choice 'writing' revision question, the best answer is usually the one that is:

    • clearest and most concise
    • longest and most formal
    • most varied in vocabulary
    • most detailed

    AP MC writing items reward economy and precision.

  15. Which choice correctly punctuates the sentence? "The mayor, who had promised reform _ lost the election."

    • The mayor, who had promised reform, lost the election.
    • The mayor who had promised reform, lost the election.
    • The mayor, who had promised reform lost the election.
    • The mayor who had promised reform; lost the election.

    A nonrestrictive clause set off with a comma at the start requires a closing comma after it.

  16. Which sentence contains a misplaced modifier?

    • Walking down the street, Maria thought the trees looked beautiful.
    • Maria walked down the street and admired the trees.
    • As Maria walked down the street, the trees looked beautiful.
    • Walking down the street, the trees looked beautiful to Maria.

    'Walking down the street' appears to modify 'the trees' rather than Maria.

  17. Which choice correctly completes the sentence? "Neither the principal nor the teachers _ aware of the change."

    • was
    • is
    • were
    • has been

    With 'neither ... nor' the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'teachers,' which is plural.

  18. Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?

    • The committee reviewed; the proposal and approved it.
    • The committee reviewed the proposal; it decided to approve it.
    • The committee reviewed the proposal; and approved it.
    • The committee; reviewed the proposal.

    A semicolon joins two independent clauses.

  19. In the sentence "Between you and me, the plan is flawed," the pronoun 'me' is correct because:

    • It is the subject of the sentence, since it names the person who is described as being between
    • It is a possessive pronoun, since it refers to something that belongs to the speaker
    • It is a reflexive pronoun, since it refers back to the speaker who is making the statement
    • It is the object of the preposition 'between'

    Prepositions take object-case pronouns.

  20. Which of the following best corrects the faulty parallelism? "The coach praised their dedication, speed, and that they never gave up."

    • The coach praised their dedication, speed, and that they persevered.
    • The coach praised their dedication, being fast, and perseverance.
    • The coach praised their dedication, speed, and perseverance.
    • The coach praised dedication, speed and that they persevere.

    Items in a series should share the same grammatical form.

  21. On a multiple-choice question asking for the best way to combine two sentences, which strategy is most effective?

    • Identify the relationship between the ideas and choose the option that expresses it concisely and correctly
    • Choose the longest option, since it keeps the most detail from both of the original sentences
    • Choose the option that keeps the original order of both sentences, since that preserves the author's meaning
    • Choose the option with the most commas, since punctuation shows the ideas are properly joined

    Look for logical relationship and economy of expression.

  22. Which sentence uses 'its' or 'it's' correctly?

    • The committee issued it's report, and its clear the results are mixed.
    • The committee issued its report, and it's clear the results are mixed.
    • The committee issued its' report, and its' clear.
    • The committee issued it's report and it's clear.

    'Its' is possessive; 'it's' means 'it is.'

  23. A multiple-choice question asks which revision improves the logical flow between two sentences. Which strategy is best?

    • Choose the transition that sounds most formal, since the exam rewards a polished academic tone over logical fit
    • Choose the shortest transition, since concise wording is preferred in revision questions regardless of the relationship
    • Choose the transition that signals contrast, since contrast is the relationship tested most often in revision questions
    • Determine what relationship (contrast, cause, example) the second sentence has to the first and pick the transition that matches

    The correct transition expresses the actual logical relationship.

  24. Which sentence has correct comma use with a coordinating conjunction?

    • The speech was long but, the audience stayed.
    • The speech was long but the audience, stayed.
    • The speech was long, but, the audience stayed.
    • The speech was long, but the audience stayed.

    A comma precedes the conjunction joining two independent clauses.

Unit 11: GrAmSS (179)

  1. Irving frames "Rip Van Winkle" as papers left behind by the fictional historian Diedrich Knickerbocker, and appends a postscript in which Knickerbocker vouches for the tale. The most significant effect of this frame is to:

    • Convince readers that the events actually occurred in the Hudson Valley by appealing to a respected historian’s sworn statement
    • Provide the biographical background of Rip’s family, so that readers can understand why he behaves as he does in the village
    • Shift the narrative to the first person so that a participant can describe the events and so persuade readers that they happened
    • Establish a tragic tone that the comic events of the story will later contradict, so that the ending gains an ironic force
    • Lend a mock-scholarly authority to a fanciful legend, which gently satirizes the claims of historical writing
    • Introduce a second plot, concerning the historian’s own life, that is resolved by the revelation of Rip’s long sleep

    The pedantic, sworn-to-be-true frame is itself humorous; it parodies historical authority while giving a folk legend an air of credibility. It does not seriously try to convince readers the events happened.

  2. Irving writes that the changes of states and empires "made but little impression on him," but "there was one species of despotism under which he had long groaned, and that was—petticoat government." The effect of this sentence is primarily to:

    • Condemn the American Revolution as a form of tyranny that has ruined Rip’s village and destroyed the peace he enjoyed before it began
    • Reveal that Rip was secretly a political revolutionary who disguised his views by playing the part of a lazy and ignorant man
    • Mock Rip's narrow priorities by treating a domestic grievance as equal to a political revolution
    • Praise Dame Van Winkle for the strength of character that allows her to manage the household while her husband neglects his duties
    • Suggest that Rip understands politics better than his neighbors, since he has recognized the tyranny that exists in his own home
    • Establish the story’s setting in the years before the Revolution, so that the reader will understand why Rip does not mind the king

    The mock-heroic comparison elevates a household squabble to the level of political despotism, and the narrator's gentle irony reveals Rip's self-centered point of view.

  3. Rip is described as willing to do any amount of work for his neighbors but unwilling to do the work of his own farm. The best interpretation of this contrast is that:

    • Irving shows that Rip is a social creature who values his neighbors, so his neglect of the farm is a deliberate rejection of his wife's authority and not a matter of temperament
    • Irving contrasts voluntary and compulsory work to suggest that Rip is lazy only when others demand his labor, which makes him a comic figure and nothing more
    • Irving presents Rip's willingness to help neighbors as proof that he is a good man, and his neglected farm as a minor flaw that the narrator forgives
    • Irving uses the contrast to criticize the village economy, in which neighborly favors replace paid labor and the farms in the district decline as a result of the exchange
    • Irving contrasts Rip's generosity toward others with his selfishness at home to show that he values the approval of neighbors over the welfare of his own family
    • Irving distinguishes between work that offers social companionship and work that offers only obligation, making Rip's idleness a matter of temperament and not simple laziness
