    Rip happily helps neighbors but avoids his own labor; the contrast characterizes him as sociable and easygoing, not merely lazy, which makes him sympathetic.

  4. The narrator remarks that a tart temper "never mellows with age, and a sharp tongue is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use." The second clause is notable chiefly for:

    • Its use of dialect to reveal the narrator’s social class and so to distance him from the Dutch villagers he describes with such amusement
    • Its use of understatement to minimize the seriousness of Rip’s problem, so that his wife’s temper appears a trifling inconvenience
    • Its use of a metaphor that turns a proverb-like generalization into a witty comment on Dame Van Winkle
    • Its use of apostrophe to address the reader directly and so to ask for sympathy with Rip in his unhappy domestic situation
    • Its use of allusion to a historical figure whom the reader is expected to recognize as a model of a sharp-tongued woman
    • Its use of personification of the tongue as a living creature, which gives the sentence a violent and almost frightening tone

    The tongue as an 'edged tool' that sharpens with use is a metaphor delivered as a witty aphorism; humor, not dialect or apostrophe, drives the line.

  5. Which statement best explains the significance of the sign at the village inn changing from a portrait of King George III to one of General Washington?

    • It shows that Rip has awakened in a different country, since the portrait of Washington is the emblem of a new nation across the ocean
    • It proves that Rip has been asleep for exactly twenty years, since the sign was painted on the day that he fell asleep
    • It suggests that the villagers are loyal to the British crown, since they have retained a portrait of a leader in the inn
    • It dramatizes how thoroughly the Revolution has changed the world Rip wakes into, without requiring the narrator to explain the change
    • It indicates that the owner of the inn has become wealthy, since he can afford to repaint the sign with a new portrait
    • It warns Rip that he is in danger from the village authorities, who have replaced the king’s portrait to frighten any visitor

    The altered sign is a concrete, nearly wordless way to show political transformation; Irving relies on a symbol rather than exposition.

  6. When Rip declares himself "a poor quiet man, a native of the place, and a loyal subject of the King, God bless him!", the crowd reacts with hostility. The irony of the moment is that:

    • Rip is actually a spy for the British, and the crowd’s suspicion is justified by words that he has spoken without any knowledge of its effect
    • Rip is deliberately provoking the villagers by declaring his loyalty, for he wishes to test whether the people have changed in his absence
    • The villagers misunderstand Rip because he speaks Dutch, and the crowd takes his words for a threat that he has not intended
    • The king mentioned is a character in the story whom the villagers have known, and they resent Rip’s calling him a good ruler
    • Rip speaks with innocent sincerity in a language of loyalty that has become dangerous without his knowing it
    • Rip is being sarcastic about the Revolution, and the crowd’s hostility is the natural reaction to a joke made at its expense

    His speech would have been unremarkable twenty years earlier; now it marks him as a Tory. The irony arises from the gap between his intention and the way it is received.

  7. When Rip says "I'm not myself—I'm somebody else," which interpretation is most consistent with the rest of the passage?

    • It is an attempt to deceive the crowd by giving a false name, in the hope that the villagers will let him alone and go away
    • It reveals that Rip has lost his memory of his earlier life, and so he is unable to say who he is or where he belongs
    • It is a joke aimed at the villagers, intended to ease the tension of the moment by making light of his own confusion
    • It expresses his genuine bewilderment at a world in which both his surroundings and his identity have been displaced
    • It shows that Rip has become suspicious of his dog, which no longer seems to him the animal that he knew before
    • It proves that someone else has taken Rip’s place in the village, and that the stranger he meets is in fact himself

    Every familiar marker of identity (people, houses, politics, even his appearance) has changed, so Rip's confusion is literal and comic and underscores the theme of time and change.

  8. Which of the following best describes how Irving uses the character Peter Vanderdonk, the village historian, near the end of the story?

    • He challenges Rip’s account and exposes him as a fraud, since no one in the village can recall the legend that Rip describes
    • He becomes Rip’s main antagonist, for he resents the attention that Rip’s story has attracted from the village’s inhabitants
    • He represents the new American government, which regards Rip’s story as dangerous and wishes to prevent its being spread
    • He interprets Rip’s dream through philosophy, and shows that the long sleep is a symbol of the colony’s age under the king
    • He becomes Rip’s business partner, and together they use the legend to attract visitors to the inn and the village
    • He confirms Rip's story by appealing to legend, which helps resolve the plot while keeping the tone playful

    Vanderdonk ties Rip's story to the local legend of Hendrick Hudson's crew, giving the tale a folkloric resolution.

  9. Rip's final position as a village patriarch who tells his story to visitors mainly suggests that:

    • Rip has become an important political leader, whose stories about his sleep persuade the villagers to adopt the new government
    • The Revolution had little effect on the village, since the same people live there and the same customs are observed
    • Rip has become wealthy through the sale of his story, and he enjoys the comforts that his years of idleness had denied him
    • Irving believes that storytelling is a form of work, and that Rip has at last found an occupation worthy of his talents
    • The old, comfortable order can survive in memory and storytelling even after historical change
    • Rip has accepted the new government enthusiastically, and he now regards the Revolution as the best event of his lifetime

    Rip becomes a living link to the pre-Revolutionary past, valued for his stories, which reflects the story's gentle nostalgia.

  10. Compared with Dame Van Winkle, the narrator's treatment of Rip's idleness is best characterized as:

    • Harshly critical, treating Rip's idleness as a serious fault
    • Neutral and clinical, reporting Rip's idleness without judgment
    • Indulgent and affectionate, even while it acknowledges Rip's faults
    • Admiring and heroic, presenting Rip's idleness as a principled stand
    • Ironically disapproving of Rip's neighbors for enabling him
    • Indifferent to Rip, focusing mainly on Dame Van Winkle's temper

    The narrator forgives Rip's faults with humor, while Dame's temper is the object of satire; tone is indulgent, not clinical.

  11. The description of the strange men playing ninepins in the mountains, whose faces and silence seem unnatural, primarily serves to:

    • Show that Rip has been drinking too much, so that the strange scene is understood as a drunken fancy and not as a real event
    • Demonstrate that Rip has joined the Revolution, since the men are soldiers whose silence and odd dress are military discipline
    • Provide comic relief that contradicts the rest of the story’s serious tone, and so lets the reader laugh at Rip’s credulity
    • Reveal that the men are villagers in disguise, who have staged the scene in order to play a joke on Rip while he is asleep
    • Establish a realistic setting for the plot, in which the men are ordinary travelers who have stopped to rest in the mountains
    • Create a supernatural, eerie atmosphere that makes Rip's long sleep plausible within the world of the legend

    The silence, odd costumes and thunder-like rolling of the balls create a folkloric, uncanny mood.

  12. The principal irony in Rip's twenty-year sleep is that:

    • He becomes famous during his absence, since the villagers talk of his disappearance and add to the legend that they tell
    • He sleeps through a battle in which he had fought, and so misses the one event that would have given his life a meaning
    • He returns to find that his farm has prospered in his absence, so his idleness has proved more useful than industry
    • The great historical events of his time pass him by while he is absent for a nap, and he returns with no sense of loss
    • He wakes up as a different person, who has been changed by the long sleep and now wishes to atone for his earlier neglect
    • He sleeps through a single night, though the villagers insist that he has been absent for twenty years

    He misses the entire Revolution and returns relatively unscathed; the humor lies in the contrast between historical magnitude and Rip's obliviousness.

  13. Irving's narrator describes the inn's "rubicund portrait of His Majesty George the Third" as faded and weatherworn by the time Rip returns. If the portrait is treated as a symbol, it most plausibly represents:

    • Rip's affection for the king
    • The wealth of the innkeeper
    • The author's disapproval of kings
    • The beauty of the Catskill landscape
    • The passage of a single season
    • The fading of the old colonial order

    A symbol of royal authority that has been replaced highlights the transition between regimes.

  14. Which sentence best captures the story's attitude toward change?

    • It portrays change as a catastrophe to be resisted, and so it encourages the reader to hold fast to old customs and loyalties
    • It celebrates revolution as the end of all injustice, and presents Rip’s sleep as a missed opportunity to take part in it
    • It portrays change as an illusion, since the village in the end seems no different from the one that Rip had left
    • It condemns Rip for ignoring change, and shows that his idleness has cost him the chance to take part in the nation’s history
    • It presents change as a punishment for idleness, since Rip’s sleep is the penalty for his neglect of the farm and the family
    • It treats change with humor and wistfulness, as something that comes whether or not one is paying attention

    Irving's tone is amused and a little nostalgic rather than angry or triumphant.

  15. In the village's political argument that greets Rip, the crowd shouts questions such as whether he is "Federal or Democrat." Rip's baffled reaction primarily emphasizes that:

    • The language of politics has changed in his absence so that even simple loyalty questions seem foreign
    • Rip holds strong opinions on both parties, though his long absence makes them hard to explain
    • Rip had voted in secret before his sleep, so the question touches a matter he would rather avoid
    • The villagers are mocking him, since they know that a man who has been absent so long cannot answer the question
    • Rip does not understand English, and so he is unable to follow the questions that the crowd is shouting at him
    • Rip is a lifelong Democrat, and his hesitation shows surprise that anyone should ask him

    The unfamiliar party vocabulary shows the gap between his world and the new republic.

  16. The narrator's habit of using mock-formal diction to describe homely matters is best exemplified by:

    • Describing Rip’s dog as a dignified courtier who is skilled in the arts of the royal court and the etiquette of its ceremonies
    • Using dialect for Rip’s speech so that the reader hears the accent of the Dutch settlers and recognizes his place in the village
    • Reporting dialogue in short sentences, which gives the narration the swift movement of a play and the sharpness of conversation
    • Using one-word paragraphs to mark the story’s turning points, so that the reader’s attention is directed to each important event
    • Describing a household dispute in terms of despotism and government
    • Omitting description of the setting, so that the reader’s attention remains fixed on the characters and on their speech

    Elevated diction applied to trivial subjects produces mock-heroic humor.

  17. Dame Van Winkle's death is reported near the end of the story in a way that most clearly:

    • Elicits deep sympathy for Dame Van Winkle, whose death is described in language that stresses her suffering and the family’s loss
    • Suggests that Rip caused her death by his neglect, and so makes the narrator’s later affection for him seem questionable
    • Treats her as a figure of comic menace whose absence relieves Rip, without the narrator expressing sorrow
    • Shows that Rip is cruel, since he does not mourn for his wife but seems pleased that she is no longer there to scold him
    • Makes the ending tragic, since the wife’s death comes at a moment when Rip might have been reconciled with her
    • Implies that she has secretly been a good wife, since the narrator mentions her death in a tone of regret and respect

    Her death is reported briefly and without lament; the tone aligns with Rip's relief.

  18. Which feature of "Rip Van Winkle" most strongly marks it as a tale of the American literary tradition rather than a purely European folktale?

    • Its use of magic, since the folktales of the old world were full of enchanted sleepers and spirits
    • Its use of a frame narrator, since European tales had long been presented as the work of an invented and learned compiler
    • Its use of a comic tone, since the humor of the story is drawn from a tradition of German and Dutch folklore
    • Its blending of an old-world legend with the specific history of the Hudson Valley and the American Revolution
    • Its focus on a husband and wife, since the quarrel between a henpecked man and his wife is a common figure of European comedy
    • Its use of a mountain setting, since the enchanted mountain is a familiar feature of the folktales of northern Europe

    Irving adapted a European folktale type to a distinctly American setting and political history.

  19. Why might Irving have chosen to make Rip's reaction to the Revolution one of mild confusion rather than strong opinion?

    • It shows Rip to be a coward, who fears the consequences of expressing an opinion in a village that has been divided by war
    • It is the realistic choice, since a man who had slept for twenty years could have no opinion about politics
    • It reveals that Irving opposed the Revolution, and wished to suggest that its changes were of little real importance to the people
    • It allows the narrator to treat the historical upheaval with gentle humor, emphasizing the continuity of ordinary life
    • It makes the story a tragedy, since a man who cannot understand the change in his world is shown to be helpless
    • It shows that Rip is secretly wise, since he has seen that politics is less important than a quiet and contented life

    A bewildered, apolitical protagonist lets Irving examine historical change through a comic, human lens.

  20. The narrator's description of Dame Van Winkle's household, with the wife's loud "curtain lecture" at night, primarily functions to:

    • Introduce a subplot about the village’s opinion of Rip’s marriage, which the narrator will resolve by describing the neighbors’ views
    • Establish the domestic conflict that motivates Rip's flight to the mountains
    • Show that the family is wealthy, since the wife’s long lectures are those of a woman with servants and a large household
    • Foreshadow Rip’s death, since the scene suggests that he will not long survive in a house governed by such a temper
    • Provide a contrast with Rip’s daughter, whose gentle manner is set against the harsh temper of her mother in the household
    • Introduce the story’s frame, in which the narrator explains how the tale came to be written down and preserved

    Rip's retreat to the woods is motivated by his wife's scolding, setting up the central event.

  21. In a rhetorical analysis of the story, which statement most accurately describes the narrator's persona?

    • Naive and unreliable, since the narrator accepts the legend without question and reports it in good faith to the readers
    • Hostile to the characters, since he portrays the village and its inhabitants in an unflattering and often contemptuous manner
    • Detached and scientific, since he records the facts of Rip’s story as an observer who has no feeling about them
    • Knowing and amused, adopting the pose of an antiquarian historian while slyly undercutting that pose
    • Mournful and nostalgic only, since the narrator’s chief concern is to lament the loss of the village’s earlier customs
    • Argumentative and didactic, since he uses the story of Rip to teach the reader a lesson about industry and thrift

    The Knickerbocker persona is a comic, self-aware antiquarian.

  22. The sentence "A tart temper never mellows with age" is most closely related to which of these generalized aims of the story?

    • Teaching a moral lesson about hard work, since the sentence shows what comes to a woman who is unwilling to hold her tongue
    • Describing historical events in the language of a chronicle, so that the reader may place the story in its period
    • Providing a realistic portrait of marriage in the colonial period, based on the narrator’s observation of village households
    • Foreshadowing the Revolution, since the sentence compares a domestic quarrel with the strife between the colonies and the crown
    • Offering gentle satire of human types through proverb-like observation
    • Explaining Rip’s drinking, since a man who lived with so sharp a tongue might be expected to seek relief in liquor

    Aphoristic generalizations about human nature are part of the satiric voice.

  23. Rip's dog Wolf is said to be as much afraid of Dame Van Winkle as Rip is. The detail is most useful for:

    • Showing that Wolf is a poorly trained dog, whose timidity makes him a poor companion for a hunter and a source of embarrassment
    • Foreshadowing Wolf’s disappearance, since the dog is described in a way that suggests he will not be seen again
    • Showing that Wolf is brave, since he alone dares to stay in the house when Dame Van Winkle’s anger is at its height
    • Suggesting that Dame is secretly kind, since the dog’s attachment to the household indicates that she treats animals gently
    • Extending the comic portrait of Dame Van Winkle's domestic power to the household animals
    • Describing the setting of the farm, so that the reader may picture the yard and outbuildings of the Van Winkle property

    The shared fear unites man and dog against the wife and builds the comedy.

  24. Which of the following would be the strongest evidence that Irving's story is more concerned with how people experience historical change than with the change itself?

    • Rip's personal bewilderment and the focus on his small-scale experiences rather than battles or leaders
    • The presence of a historian character, Peter Vanderdonk, who records the events that Rip describes and verifies them for the village
    • The mention of Washington, whose portrait appears on the inn’s sign and whose name is known to everyone in the village
    • The setting in the Catskills, whose mountains and valleys give the story its distinctive atmosphere and its air of legend
    • The description of Dutch customs, which shows the village’s way of life before the Revolution and after it had ended
    • The inclusion of a frame narrator, who introduces the story and assures the reader in a postscript that it is true

    The story keeps the Revolution offstage and follows an ordinary man's reaction.

  25. What function does the long first-person-like introduction describing the Catskill Mountains play?

    • It contains the story’s central conflict, since the mountains are described as the source of the troubles that Rip later suffers
    • It reveals the narrator’s identity, so that the reader may judge his reliability before the story of Rip begins
    • It establishes a mythic, atmospheric setting that makes the legend feel timeless
    • It introduces Rip’s wife, whose temper is compared with the changing weather that the narrator describes among the hills
    • It argues for the independence of the colonies, since the mountains are presented as a symbol of the land’s freedom
    • It explains the plot of the story in advance, so that the reader will know what to expect from the events that follow

    The romantic description of the mountains sets up the folkloric tone.

  26. Twain introduces the bluejay tale by having Jim Baker claim that jays have a command of slang and grammar. This claim is best understood as:

    • A scientific observation, offered to show the narrator has studied bird habits with care
    • A serious argument that animals possess a form of speech like human language
    • Comic exaggeration that anthropomorphizes the birds and establishes the tall-tale mode
    • A literal report of bird behavior that Baker offers as fact about jay communication
    • An attack on human grammar, suggesting people use language less skillfully than birds
    • A sign that Baker is unreliable, so the reader must doubt his other statements

    The absurd praise of jay language is a tall-tale exaggeration, not a literal claim.

  27. The simile that the jay's smile "faded gradually out of his countenance like breath off'n a razor" is effective because it:

    • Combines a precise, unexpected visual comparison with dialect, which conveys both the jay's embarrassment and Baker's voice
    • Uses formal diction to contrast with the humor, so that the elevated language makes the jay’s embarrassment seem more absurd
    • Relies on abstract imagery, which leaves the reader to supply the details and so to share in the speaker’s humor
    • Appeals to patriotic feeling, since the razor is a familiar emblem of the frontier’s spirit of independence and self-reliance
    • Is a literal description of the jay’s expression, which Baker has observed and which he reports with a naturalist’s precision
    • Foreshadows the jay’s death, since a razor suggests the danger that awaits the bird in the final scene of the tale

    A fogging razor surface fading is a vivid comparison phrased in Baker's dialect ("off'n").

  28. Twain presents the story as told by Jim Baker rather than directly by the narrator. The most important effect of this frame is:

    • It makes the story more scientific, since a miner who has lived among jays is an authority on their conduct
    • It reduces the humor, since Baker’s plain manner is less lively than the narrator’s own style would have been
    • It allows Twain to avoid the use of dialect, since a character’s speech may be reported in standard English
    • It lets a character with a distinctive voice deliver the exaggerations, adding humor and a sense of oral tradition
    • It removes the narrator’s opinions, so that the story is presented as a plain account of what Baker has seen
    • It changes the genre to tragedy, since the character’s earnest manner gives the jay’s labor a serious and moving tone

    The tale gains authority and comedy from Baker's deadpan, dialect-rich storytelling.

  29. Baker's repeated pronouncement that the jay is better than a human in some respects (using "human" traits) functions mainly as:

    • A scientific hypothesis, which Baker proposes in order to explain why the jay’s behavior is so much like that of a person
    • A moral lesson on kindness to animals, which Baker hopes the narrator will remember when he next meets a jay
    • A criticism of Baker himself, whose own foolish habits are the real subject of the comparison with the bird
    • A claim about literary style, in which Baker suggests that jays are better storytellers than most human writers
    • A symbol of the Old West, in which the jay’s self-reliance and independence represent the spirit of the frontier
    • Satire of human behavior through animal comparison

    By giving birds human foibles, the story mocks human pride and behavior.

  30. The central comic situation in the story arises because:

    • A jay learns to speak and begins to bargain with Baker over the price of the acorns that he has carried to the cabin
    • Baker captures a jay and then keeps it in the cabin, where the other birds come to look at it and to laugh
    • A jay's determined effort to fill a hole fails in a way that grows more absurd as more jays arrive
    • The jays steal a miner’s gold from the cabin and carry it up to the hole, where it is later discovered by Baker
    • The cabin collapses under the weight of the acorns that the jay has dropped, and the jays flee in confusion
    • A jay defeats an owl in a contest of strength, and the jays gather to celebrate his victory in front of Baker

    The acorns keep falling through the hole into an empty cabin, and the jay's persistence and the others' amusement drive the humor.

  31. The phrase "sweating like an ice-pitcher" is best classified as:

    • A colloquial simile built on a paradoxical image
    • A formal metaphor suggesting a cool temper
    • An allusion to a famous story about a pitcher
    • A pun on two meanings of the word pitcher
    • Personification of a pitcher that perspires
    • Hyperbole that exaggerates the amount of sweat

    It compares the bird to a pitcher whose cold surface beads with water, in a homespun idiom.

  32. Which of these best describes Twain's tone in the bluejay passage?

    • Deadpan humor that treats an absurd story as sober fact
    • Bitter satire of miners and their ways, which the narrator uses to show his contempt for the people of the West
    • Elevated and solemn, in the manner of a heroic tale in which the jay’s labor is treated with great respect
    • Nostalgic and sentimental, since the narrator recalls the pleasures of life in a mining camp and mourns their passing
    • Fearful and suspenseful, since the story depends on the narrator’s uncertainty about what the jays may do next
    • Didactic and instructive, since the narrator presents the story as a lesson in patience and in the value of labor

    The humor depends on the straight-faced delivery.

  33. The detail that the jays gather in large numbers to look at the hole and laugh primarily serves to:

    • Provide the setting, by showing that the cabin stands in a region where jays are numerous and the winters are mild
    • Show that the jays are cruel to their companion, since they enjoy his failure and take pleasure in his distress
    • Illustrate predation, since the jays gather to feed on the acorns that have fallen around the cabin and in its yard
    • Prove that the hole is real, since a large number of witnesses is able to confirm its existence to Baker
    • Intensify the humor by giving the gathering a social, human-like quality
    • Foreshadow an attack, since the gathering of so many jays suggests that they mean to do harm to the miner

    The crowd of jays behaving like jeering spectators emphasizes the comedy and anthropomorphism.

  34. Which statement best explains the effect of Baker's dialect (for example, "off'n") on the reader?

    • It confuses the plot, since the reader must work to understand each sentence and so loses the thread of the story
    • It makes the story less funny, since the humor depends on language that is more formal and precise than Baker’s
    • It establishes a folksy, authentic oral voice that supports the tall-tale conventions
    • It suggests that Baker is a well-educated man, whose speech is a deliberate imitation of the frontier’s dialect
    • It sets a tragic tone, since the speech of the working classes is associated with suffering and hardship
    • It tells readers that the setting is the East Coast, since the dialect belongs to the working people of that region

    Dialect creates character and local color in a frame narrative.

  35. The jay's attempt to fill a hole that cannot be filled can be read as a comic image of:

    • The success of hard work, since the jay persists until at last he accomplishes what he has set out to do
    • The destruction of nature by human settlement, since the cabin and the hole are signs of the miners’ presence
    • Human futility and stubborn effort in the face of obvious failure
    • The cruelty of owls, which prey upon smaller birds and have caused the jay to labor so hard at his task
    • The rhythm of nature, in which creatures perform the same tasks again and again according to the seasons
    • The cycle of life, in which the work of one generation is taken up and completed by that which comes after it

    The jay's labor, observed with comic detachment, is a parody of human persistence.

  36. Hawthorne names the protagonist's wife Faith and has Brown say, "With Heaven above and Faith below, I will stand firm against the devil." The most significant effect of this naming is that:

    • It identifies Faith as the story’s villain, since her name suggests that she has misled Brown into leaving his home
    • It proves that the story takes place in a dream, since the name is so exactly suited to the theme that it cannot be real
    • It allows the story to operate on two levels, so Brown's loss of trust in his wife also reads as a loss of religious faith
    • It establishes that Faith is a spiritual guide, whose advice Brown ought to follow whenever he is in doubt
    • It shows that Brown is a religious hypocrite, since he speaks of Heaven while he is about to go and meet the devil
    • It suggests that Faith will lead Brown to the forest meeting, where he will see that she is the devil’s servant

    The allegorical name makes the personal and spiritual losses inseparable; the reader cannot easily tell which one Brown is describing.

  37. As Brown leaves, Faith's pink ribbons are mentioned in the first paragraph and a pink ribbon later flutters down in the forest. The ribbon functions primarily as:

    • A clue that Faith has secretly followed him into the forest, so that the reader suspects that she is part of the plot
    • A sign that Brown has found his way out of the forest, since the ribbon marks the path that leads him back to the village
    • A concrete symbol that Brown interprets as proof of Faith's corruption, though its meaning remains open to question
    • A symbol of the devil’s power over the village, since the ribbon is left by the traveler as a mark of his triumph
    • Evidence that the events were a dream, since a ribbon could not remain in the air after Brown had seen it
    • A decoration with no thematic importance, which Hawthorne mentions to give the scene an air of realistic detail

    The ribbon sets off Brown's conclusion that Faith is lost, but the story never confirms it, which preserves ambiguity.

  38. The traveler Brown meets in the forest carries a staff "which bore the likeness of a great black snake, so curiously wrought that it might almost be seen to twist and wriggle itself like a living serpent." The description most directly suggests:

    • That the traveler is a hunter, whose staff is carved to resemble the animals that he pursues in the forest
    • A comic detail that lightens the story’s mood, since the staff’s behavior is more amusing than frightening to the reader
    • An allusion to the serpent of Eden that identifies the traveler with the devil and connects the story to the theme of temptation
    • A literal threat of violence, since the snake is real and the traveler means to use it against Brown
    • That the traveler is lame, since he needs the staff for support and has carved it in a form that interests him
    • That the forest contains dangerous animals, and that Brown ought to be on his guard as he continues on his way

    The twisting snake-staff echoes the Garden of Eden and signals the traveler's identity.

  39. The traveler claims to have helped Brown's father and grandfather in acts of cruelty in Puritan history. The purpose of this claim in the story is to:

    • Prove that Brown’s ancestors were innocent, since the traveler’s claim is shown to be false by the village’s records
    • Provide historical detail about Salem, so that the reader will understand the events of the period in which the story is set
    • Undermine Brown's confidence in the moral purity of his community and ancestors
    • Show that the traveler is a historian, who knows the village’s past better than any of the people who live in it
    • Reassure Brown that the journey is safe, since the traveler has been the friend of his family for several generations
    • Introduce a subplot about Brown’s father, which the author will develop in the later pages of the story

    By linking Brown's forebears to violence, the traveler erodes the idea that Puritan society is purely good, pushing Brown toward doubt.

  40. When Brown sees Goody Cloyse, who taught him his catechism, in the forest, he reacts by hiding. The moment is important because:

    • It shows that Brown is brave, since he hides in order to observe what the old woman means to do in the forest
    • It proves that Goody Cloyse is a witch in fact, since she is seen to speak with the traveler as an intimate friend
    • It shows the traveler’s kindness to the old woman, whom he helps to travel faster by giving her his staff
    • It is the climax of the story, since Brown’s discovery of the old woman is the event that decides his later actions
    • It introduces Faith to the reader, since the old woman speaks of her in the conversation with the traveler
    • It begins a series of discoveries that the most pious figures in his life are also present at the devil's meeting, intensifying his doubt

    Each respected figure Brown sees compounds his fear that virtue is universally false.

  41. Brown cries, "My Faith is gone! ... There is no good on earth; and sin is but a name. Come, devil! for to thee is this world given." The passage most clearly demonstrates:

    • His resolution to resist evil, which he expresses in the language of a man who has overcome his doubt
    • His decision to return to Faith, which he announces in the hope that she will forgive him for having left her
    • A sincere conversion to the devil’s cause as a matter of conviction, which he accepts with calm and with resolve
    • A sudden swing from rigid belief to total cynicism, revealing that his faith was fragile
    • A comic exaggeration of the despair of a man who has seen very little, and has been frightened by a dream
    • That Brown is dreaming, since the extravagance of the speech is the mark of a man who is not awake

    The absolute swing from piety to despair indicates the shallowness of his faith, which depended on assuming everyone else's goodness.

  42. The devil's address to the converts, "Evil is the nature of mankind," is most useful as a window into the story's theme because it:

    • Proves the story is a sermon, since the devil’s words state a doctrine that the author wishes his readers to accept
    • States the doctrine of universal human depravity that Brown, and perhaps the Puritan community, has been trying to deny
    • Shows that the devil is truthful, and so that everything he has told Brown about the village is certainly true
    • Is Hawthorne’s own statement of belief, which he gives to the devil so that it will be better remembered by the reader
    • Gives the story a happy ending, since the converts accept the devil’s teaching and are reconciled to one another
    • Proves that Brown is guilty of the sins that the devil describes, and that he deserves to be counted among the converts

    The devil voices the Calvinist idea of innate sinfulness; the story explores the effect of this knowledge, not necessarily its truth.

  43. Hawthorne never confirms whether Brown dreamed the forest meeting. Which reading best explains the effect of this ambiguity?

    • It reveals that Hawthorne could not decide on an ending, and so left the reader to choose between two possibilities
    • It proves that the events were real, since a dream would have been described as one by a careful narrator
    • It makes the effect of the experience on Brown more important than whether the events were literally real
    • It shows that Brown is lying about what he saw in the forest, in order to cover his own wrongdoing
    • It proves that Faith is guilty, since a narrator who denies the dream must regard the vision as true
    • It turns the story into a mystery to be solved, so that the reader’s task is to find out what really happened

    The consequence for Brown's life is the same either way; the ambiguity shifts attention to the psychological and moral effect.

  44. In the closing paragraphs Brown is described as "a stern, a sad, a darkly meditative, if not a distrustful, soul." The stacking of adjectives with the qualifier "if not" is best described as:

    • A neutral list of traits that the narrator reports without comment on their effect on Brown
    • A comic exaggeration of Brown’s change, offered to make fun of the village’s gloomy mood
    • An escalating series whose final qualification points to the extent of his lasting damage
    • An indirect compliment to Brown, since the traits were qualities the Puritans held in high regard
    • An example of understatement, since the narrator’s words are weaker than the facts they describe
    • A shift to first-person narration, in which the narrator voices his own judgment of Brown’s character

    The sequence intensifies, and "if not a distrustful" suggests a more severe condition than the earlier words.

  45. After the night in the forest, Brown shrinks from the minister's blessing and snatches a child away from Goody Cloyse. These actions primarily show that:

    • His suspicion has isolated him from the community he once trusted
    • He has become a devoted churchgoer who listens to sermons with pleasure
    • The minister is a harmful man whose blessing carries a hidden curse
    • He has forgiven the villagers, and his withdrawal shows humility
    • He has become a village leader who protects children from old women
    • He is rewarding the child, whom he regards as the sole innocent soul

    His distrust turns ordinary gestures of piety into occasions of fear, which isolates him.

  46. The statement that "they carved no hopeful verse upon his tombstone, for his dying hour was gloom" contributes to the story's effect by:

    • Providing a happy ending, since the villagers’ choice of an inscription shows how highly they regarded his piety
    • Revealing that Brown is a hero, whose death is remembered by the village as that of a man of great courage
    • Establishing that Brown died young, since the absence of a hopeful verse suggests that his life was cut short
    • Contradicting the rest of the story, since the villagers’ treatment of Brown shows that they trusted him
    • Showing that the doubt is lifelong and that the community, though unaware of the cause, perceives it
    • Providing a comic tone, since the villagers’ refusal to carve a verse is a joke at the expense of a gloomy man

    The grim epitaph confirms that his night in the forest shaped his entire life.

  47. The setting of Salem village during the era of witch accusations is most important to the story because:

    • It provides a happy contrast with the forest, so that the reader is made to feel the safety and warmth of the village
    • It makes the story a documentary of the trials, since the events are drawn from the records of the period
    • It names the villain, whose identity is revealed by the historical setting and by the details of the time
    • It explains Faith’s name, since it was common among Puritan women of the period to be called after virtues
    • It limits the story’s relevance to the past, since the fears it describes belong to a world that has disappeared
    • It evokes a historical atmosphere of suspicion and hidden guilt that parallels Brown's internal crisis

    The Puritan background of fear of secret sin amplifies the story's psychological themes.

  48. Hawthorne's description of the forest path as dark and narrow, with trees closing in, functions chiefly to:

    • Provide a realistic map of the village and the forest, so that the reader can follow Brown on his journey
    • Show that Brown is lost, since he has strayed from the path and cannot find his way back to the village
    • Foreshadow rain, which falls in the later part of the story and adds to the gloom of the setting
    • Externalize Brown's moral wilderness and his growing fear and isolation
    • Contrast with the light of the village, whose brightness is the symbol of the safety that Brown has left
    • Introduce a monster, which waits for Brown in the forest and attacks him as he makes his way along the path

    The setting reflects the inner state of the character, a hallmark of allegory.

  49. Faith's last words to Brown in the forest scene are "Look up to Heaven, and resist the Wicked One." Which interpretation is best supported?

    • They prove she is a witch, since a woman who speaks in the forest at night must be one of the devil’s servants
    • Her appeal suggests she may remain faithful at the crucial moment, a possibility that the story deliberately leaves unresolved
    • They are spoken by Brown, who cries out in the hope that Faith will hear and will come to him
    • They show that Faith has been taken by the devil, and that her words are a plea for her husband’s help
    • They prove that the events were real, since a voice in a dream would not be so clearly heard
    • They mean that Brown has been forgiven for his sins, and that the devil’s power over him has ended

    Her last-minute resistance is undercut or confirmed by Brown's morning doubt; Hawthorne leaves it unsettled.

  50. An analysis of the story's structure would most reasonably note that:

    • The story is a series of unrelated incidents, each of which presents a different aspect of the village’s character
    • The journey into the woods and return to the village forms a descent-and-return pattern in which the hero is not restored
    • It is told in reverse order, beginning with Brown’s old age and returning step by step to the evening of his departure
    • It follows a standard romance structure, in which the hero is tested and in the end restored to his place
    • It begins with the resolution, in which Brown’s doubts are settled, and then turns back to explain how they arose
    • It is an epistolary story, told through letters that Brown wrote to his wife on the night that he went away

    Brown returns, but changed and unable to rejoin the community's trust.

  51. The traveler's remark, "Faith kept me back a while," when Brown explains his lateness, is ironic because:

    • The traveler is surprised by Brown’s lateness, since he had expected Brown to arrive before the time they had agreed
    • Faith is the traveler’s name, and Brown has used it to show that he knows the identity of the man he is meeting
    • Brown is lying about the cause of his delay, since the real reason is that he is afraid of the journey
    • It reveals that Faith is present in the forest, and that she has prevented Brown from keeping his appointment
    • Brown means his wife's name, while the phrase also suggests that his faith is what delays his entering into evil
    • It is a clear statement of the story’s theme, which the traveler is able to understand and to explain to Brown

    The double meaning of 'Faith' (wife and belief) is a central pun.

  52. Hawthorne's narrator describes the congregation in the forest as including both the respectable and the notorious. This detail most directly emphasizes:

    • That Salem is a pleasant town whose citizens live in peace
    • The idea that sin is universal and not limited to obvious sinners
    • That Brown is the one good man, invited because he is innocent
    • That the devil has little power over the righteous villagers
    • That the ceremony is a trial where the converts are judged
    • That the community is united in virtue, standing together

    The mixture shows evil as common to all, challenging the notion of a moral dividing line.

  53. Which of the following best describes the role of the minister and Deacon Gookin in the story?

    • They are villains who have planned to lead Brown astray, and who use their reputations for piety to deceive him
    • They represent the community's respected moral authorities, whose apparent presence at the devil's gathering shakes Brown's trust
    • They are heroes who attend the meeting in order to discover the devil’s plans and to protect the village
    • They are comic figures, whose behavior in the forest is meant to amuse the reader and to relieve the story’s gloom
    • They are narrators, whose reports of the meeting give the reader a second account of what Brown saw in the forest
    • They are imaginary characters that Brown invents in his dream, and that have no counterpart among the villagers

    Their presence turns the symbols of religious authority into symbols of hypocrisy.

  54. In what way does the story's ending most strongly critique Brown's response to what he saw?

    • It shows that he was right about the village, since the people whom he had trusted were found to be hypocrites
    • It shows that evil is not real, since the forest’s events are only a dream and have no effect on the village
    • It implies that his rigid assumption of others' perfection made him unable to live with human imperfection
    • It praises his skepticism, since a man who doubts his neighbors is more careful than one who accepts them
    • It shows that he was a hero, who had the courage to face the devil and the wisdom to withdraw
    • It rewards him with wisdom, since the night in the forest taught him a truth that others in the village had not learned

    Brown's inability to reconcile belief with human flaws is the story's implied criticism.

  55. The devil is described as bearing a resemblance to Brown himself. This detail most plausibly suggests that:

    • The traveler is Brown’s father, who has returned from the grave to lead his son to the meeting in the forest
    • The traveler is a relative of Brown’s who has lived in another part of the colony and who has come to visit
    • Brown is the devil, and the story’s events are an account of what he does under another name in the forest
    • The evil he confronts is not wholly external but connected to his own nature
    • Brown is lying about the traveler, whom he has invented to excuse his own conduct in the forest at night
    • The story is a comedy, since a traveler who looks like Brown is a humorous device and not a serious one

    Resemblance hints that temptation is internal; Brown is complicit in the evil he sees.

  56. The narrator confesses that on seeing the house he felt "a sense of insufferable gloom" that he could not explain. This admission is significant because:

    • It establishes the narrator as an emotionally impressionable, possibly unreliable, interpreter of events, shaping how readers view what follows
    • It proves that the house is haunted, since a feeling of gloom that cannot be explained is the sign of a ghost
    • It is an objective account of the house’s appearance, which the narrator gives in order to inform the reader accurately
    • It shows that he is a skeptic, who is able to resist the house’s effect and to judge it with a clear mind
    • It reveals the house’s owner, whose identity the narrator guesses from the feeling that the building produces in him
    • It resolves the plot by explaining the cause of the gloom, so that the reader need not wonder what lies behind it

    The narrator's subjective reaction colors the entire account and invites readers to question his perception.

  57. Poe describes the house's "vacant eye-like windows" and a barely visible fissure running from roof to foundation. Together these details most likely:

    • Give a realistic description of a ruined house, so the reader has an accurate picture of its condition
    • Personify the house and foreshadow its collapse while linking it to the Usher family's decay
    • Contrast with the bright, welcoming interior, which makes the narrator's first impression seem unfounded
    • Introduce a comic note, since the house looks so odd that the narrator cannot take it seriously
    • Show that the house is new, since such a fissure appears in recently constructed buildings
    • Represent the narrator's wealth, since a rich man would be the one to visit such a house

    The house is figured as a living face and its fissure presages its destruction, mirroring the family's end.

  58. The title's phrase "House of Usher" refers both to a building and to a family line. This double meaning is important because:

    • It is a pun intended to be comic, since the name suits both the house and the family in an unexpected way
    • It is a mistake that Poe corrects later, when he explains that the family and house are distinct
    • It means the family is wealthy and respected, since the house bears its name in the manner of a noble line
    • It shows that the house is a hotel, in which the Usher family has lived for several generations
    • It refers to the building, since the family has died out and no one remains to bear the name of Usher
    • It suggests that the physical house and the family's bloodline decay together and share a fate

    The collapse of the house and the extinction of the family are simultaneous.

  59. Roderick Usher's belief in the "sentience of all vegetable things" and the house's stones primarily serves to:

    • Deepen the atmosphere of morbid superstition and suggest the house exerts an influence over its inhabitants
    • Prove the supernatural is real, since a man who believes that stones can feel must have seen evidence of it
    • Introduce a scientific theory that Poe took from the writers of his own time and presents without comment
    • Show that Usher is a botanist, whose studies have led him to believe that plants have feelings like those of animals
    • Establish a comic tone, since a belief of this kind is absurd and the narrator reports it with amusement
    • Reveal the narrator’s beliefs, since he shares Usher’s opinion and is persuaded by what he has seen at the house

    Usher's belief in the house's life underlines his obsession and fear.

  60. In the poem "The Haunted Palace," the splendid palace is overrun by a "hideous throng." In context, the poem is best read as:

    • A description of Usher’s real home, whose towers and windows the narrator has seen and recognizes in the poem
    • A comic song that Usher composed to amuse his guest, and whose gloomy imagery is meant to be taken as a joke
    • A historical ballad that tells how an ancient king lost his palace and his throne to an invading army
    • A hymn that praises the house and its family, which Usher sings in a moment of pride in his ancestry
    • An unrelated interlude that gives the narrator a rest from the story’s tension before the climax approaches
    • An allegory of Usher's mind descending from sanity into madness

    The palace corresponds to a head and mind, and the ruin to the loss of reason.

  61. Poe withholds the narrator's name and gives little background about him. The most reasonable effect of this choice is to:

    • Focus attention on the atmosphere and on Usher's decline while making the narrator a vehicle for the reader's perceptions
    • Make the narrator a villain, whose silence about himself conceals his part in the disaster that overtakes the house
    • Conceal the plot, so that the reader cannot guess the ending until the narrator has fled from the house
    • Make the story a comedy, in which an anonymous visitor is the victim of a series of mishaps and misreadings
    • Suggest that the narrator is dead, and that the account is that of a ghost who recalls his last visit
    • Shift the narration to Usher, whose private thoughts and personality become the real center of the story's scenes

    An anonymous observer allows readers to experience the unfolding horror directly.

  62. Madeline's illness, described as cataleptic, plays a key role in the plot because:

    • It shows that she is an ordinary invalid, whose weakness is of no importance to the plot or to the story’s theme
    • It makes plausible her premature burial and her eventual return, which brings about the story's climax
    • It is a comic detail that relieves the story’s gloom, since the narrator regards her condition as a joke
    • It proves she is a ghost, since a woman who appears to die and then returns cannot be a living person
    • It signals the family's wealth, since her long illness is shown to require the care of several expensive physicians
    • It is a symbol of Roderick’s recovery, since her illness grows worse as his own condition becomes better

    The catalepsy provides the mechanism for a living burial and return.

  63. When the narrator reads aloud from the romance "Mad Trist," the sounds described in the story are heard from within the house. The narrator's use of this device most directly:

    • Provides comic relief, since the coincidence of the noises in the story and in the house is absurd and amusing
    • Shows that the narrator has been dreaming, since the sounds he hears are the product of his own half-sleeping mind
    • Proves that the house is a stage, on which the events of the romance are acted out for the narrator’s benefit
    • Blurs the boundary between fiction and reality, heightening suspense as the unseen events draw nearer
    • Resolves the mystery of the house by revealing that the noises are made by a servant who wishes to alarm Usher
    • Shows that Usher invented the sounds, in order to make the narrator believe that his sister has come back

    The synchronous noises make the story-within-the-story appear to enter the narrative, intensifying dread.

  64. Madeline's appearance at the door, bloody and trembling, causing Roderick's death by terror, is an example of:

    • A gothic climax in which long-suppressed fear and guilt finally materialize
    • A comic reversal, in which the figure of a woman believed dead appears unexpectedly and frightens a man who has been mourning her
    • A realistic scene, which the narrator describes with the accuracy of a physician who has observed the death of a patient
    • An anticlimax, in which the story’s tension is released in a quiet moment that brings the narrative to a close
    • A flashback to an earlier time in the family’s history, which explains the cause of Usher’s fear of his sister
    • A parody of romance, since the scene imitates the events of the “Mad Trist” in a manner meant to be funny

    The scene fulfills the story's atmosphere of terror and guilt.

  65. In the final image, the house splits along the fissure and the tarn closes "over the fragments of the 'House of Usher.'" This conclusion most strongly emphasizes:

    • The narrator’s rescue from the collapsing house, which he escapes in time to see its fall and to tell the story
    • The simultaneous destruction of the family and its home, closing the story's pattern of decay with finality
    • The restoration of order after the catastrophe, since the tarn closes over the house and its troubles are ended
    • The beauty of the tarn, whose dark and still waters reflect the house and give the scene its final image
    • A comic punishment of the Usher family, whose pride has led them to neglect the building that bears their name
    • Roderick’s survival, since the narrator sees him escape from the house before the walls fall into the water

    The collapse unites symbol and plot, as the House of Usher ends in both senses.

  66. Poe's emphasis on a single, unified emotional effect in the story is best illustrated by:

    • The consistent use of gloomy setting, diction and imagery from the opening to the final line
    • The use of multiple narrators, each of whom adds a different view of the house and its inhabitants to the account
    • A sudden shift to comedy in the middle of the story, which relieves the tension before the climax is reached
    • A twist ending that is unrelated to the rest of the story and leaves the reader with a final surprise
    • A variety of settings, which the narrator describes in turn as he travels between the house and the countryside
    • The use of dialect, which gives the characters’ speech a regional flavor and makes the story seem more realistic

    Every detail contributes to a pervasive mood of dread.

  67. The narrator's first-person account of Roderick's behavior most likely invites readers to question:

    • Whether Roderick is a real man, since the narrator alone describes him and no servant ever speaks of him
    • Whether the house exists, since the narrator’s description of it seems more like a dream than a real building
    • Whether the story is true to history, since the details of the house and family do not match any known record
    • Whether the tarn is real, since the narrator says that it is black and still and has no visible source
    • Whether Madeline is a ghost, since the narrator does not see her again after she has been placed in the vault
    • How much of the horror is in Roderick and the narrator's minds rather than in the supernatural

    Subjective narration leaves open the distinction between psychological and supernatural horror.

  68. Which of the following best explains why Usher's artwork and improvised music are described in the story?

    • They show that he is a celebrity in his community, whose paintings and songs are admired by the people of the region
    • They reveal his extreme sensitivity and nervous temperament, deepening the portrait of his mental state
    • They are a diversion that Poe includes to relieve the monotony of the narrator’s long stay at the house
    • They prove the house is haunted, since the pictures and the music are produced by spirits that live within it
    • They serve as comic relief, since the pictures are strange and the music is so odd that it amuses the narrator
    • They are used to solve a puzzle, since the narrator finds in them a clue to the cause of Madeline’s illness

    His morbid art and music reflect his fragile psyche.

  69. The comparison of the house's appearance to a decayed structure whose "minute fungi overspread the whole exterior" suggests:

    • That the house was recently built, since fungus appears on new timber before it has been seasoned and painted
    • That the house is clean and well kept, since the narrator notices no sign of damage when he first looks at it
    • That nature is benevolent, since the fungi spread over the house like a covering and protect its walls from the weather
    • That the house is a hospital, since the narrator compares its condition to that of a building where sick people stay
    • That the narrator is wealthy, since he is able to observe the house’s condition without being troubled by its cost
    • That outward appearance hides slow internal rot, paralleling the family's condition

    Surface integrity masks deep decay, a motif in the story.

  70. Keats opens the poem with the bitter cold, the owl and the hare, and the Beadsman's numb fingers and frosted breath. This opening most plausibly serves to:

    • Introduce a comic subplot about the Beadsman, whose cold hands and breath amuse the reader before the main story begins
    • Describe the poem’s climax, in which the lovers escape from the castle into the cold of the winter night
    • Establish a setting of austere cold and piety that will contrast with the warmth and sensuous richness of Madeline's chamber
    • Introduce Porphyro, whose journey through the cold to the castle is the subject of the stanzas that open the poem
    • Demonstrate Keats’s disdain for religion, since the Beadsman’s devotion is shown to be cold and useless to him
    • Provide a realistic weather report, so that the reader will know the season and the conditions at the time of the poem

    The chilly, ascetic opening sets up a contrast with the warm, sensuous interior that follows.

  71. The Spenserian stanza that Keats uses has nine lines, with eight iambic pentameter lines followed by a longer final line. The effect of the longer last line is most likely to:

    • Create a sense of closure and a slower, weightier cadence at the end of each stanza
    • Introduce a comic note at the end of each stanza, so that the poem’s serious subjects are relieved by a touch of wit
    • Break the pattern of rhyme, so that the reader is made to notice the final line as an exception to the rest
    • Create the impression of speech, since the last line is longer and so more like the rhythm of a person talking
    • Make the poem seem unfinished, since the extra length of the line leaves the stanza without a firm conclusion
    • Reduce the stanza’s musicality, since a longer line is harder to read aloud and breaks the rhythm of the verse

    The extended final line (an alexandrine) provides a concluding sweep.

  72. In the lines describing the Beadsman's frosted breath, "Like pious incense from a censer old, / Seem'd taking flight for heaven," the simile achieves which of the following?

    • It uses the visible breath to merge the physical cold with the religious ritual, elevating a mundane detail
    • It insults the Beadsman by comparing his breath to smoke, and so suggests that his prayers are empty and false
    • It describes a literal fire that the Beadsman has lit in the chapel, and by whose light he is able to pray
    • It anticipates the lovers’ escape, since the breath that seems to fly toward heaven foretells their flight
    • It is a comic exaggeration, since the Beadsman’s breath cannot be compared with the smoke of incense in any serious way
    • It serves as a transition to Madeline, since the incense moves toward the castle and the room where she lies

    The breath becomes incense, joining sensory observation with spiritual imagery.

  73. The legend of St. Agnes' Eve, in which a maiden who performs certain rituals will dream of her lover, matters to the poem's plot because:

    • It sets the poem's date, since the feast day fixes the season but does not affect what the characters do
    • It makes the poem a devotional work, whose main aim is to honor the saint and her festival
    • It condemns Madeline's superstition, suggesting her faith in the legend has led her astray
    • It motivates Madeline's actions and makes possible Porphyro's plan to enter her chamber
    • It explains Porphyro's ancestry, since his family first established the festival of the saint
    • It explains the family feud, since the legend tells how the two houses became enemies

    Madeline's belief in the ritual keeps her from seeing Porphyro as real, enabling the plot.

  74. Porphyro's preparing a lavish feast of delicacies beside Madeline's bed is described in rich sensory detail. The most likely purpose of this lavish description is:

    • To satirize luxury, since the feast is an excess that Keats presents as foolish and unsuited to the lovers’ situation
    • To provide recipe details that will interest the reader, who may wish to prepare the dishes that are described
    • To introduce a villain, since the preparation of so large a feast suggests that Porphyro has plans to deceive her
    • To heighten the poem's sensuous, romantic atmosphere and contrast the warmth of love with the cold outside
    • To show that Porphyro is wealthy, since the quantity and variety of the food are signs of his rank and his means
    • To advance a legal argument, since the feast is offered as evidence that Porphyro has the right to enter the room

    Keats's sensuous imagery is central to the poem's Romantic mood.

  75. Which of the following best describes the relationship between the lovers' families in the poem?

    • An old alliance that makes their marriage welcome to both houses
    • A feud that makes their love dangerous and requires secrecy
    • A business partnership that makes their marriage a useful match
    • A guardianship that lets Madeline's aunt decide whom she may marry
    • A kinship that makes their love improper and requires secrecy
    • A feud that has ended and makes their love safe and public

    The family hostility raises the stakes of Porphyro's presence.

  76. The poem ends with the lovers fleeing into a storm and then returns to the Beadsman and Angela, both of whom die. What is the likely effect of returning to them at the end?

    • It provides a comic coda, in which the deaths of the two old people are treated as a joke after the lovers’ flight
    • It shows that Madeline has died, since the poem’s last lines announce the end of her life and of her story
    • It reintroduces the cold, ascetic world of the opening, framing the lovers' escape in a contrast of youth and age, warmth and death
    • It reveals that Porphyro is the Beadsman’s son, who has come back to the castle after many years of absence
    • It suggests that the poem is a dream, since the return to the first scene shows that the story has ended
    • It introduces new characters, whose arrival at the castle prepares the reader for a sequel to the lovers’ story

    The frame returns to the opening's cold piety, reinforcing contrast and transience.

  77. In the poem, Madeline's reaction on waking to find Porphyro present, is best described as:

    • Anger at Porphyro, whom she accuses of having entered her room without permission and of having broken her sleep
    • Indifference, since she regards the visit as a part of her dream and takes no notice of what he says
    • Terror and flight, since she is alarmed by a stranger’s presence and runs from the chamber in order to call for help
    • Recognition and rejection, since she knows him as the enemy of her family and will not accept his love
    • A mixture of confusion and tenderness, in which she compares the real lover to the dream
    • Amusement at his scheme, which she finds so absurd that she cannot take it seriously or respond with any feeling

    She is dismayed that the dream has faded but accepts the real Porphyro.

  78. Which poetic device is most responsible for the poem's sense of richness and sensuous warmth?

    • Vivid sensory imagery appealing to sight, taste, smell and touch
    • Satire, which exposes the faults of the characters and shows the reader how the poem’s society ought to be reformed
    • Irony, in which the speaker says one thing and means another in order to show how the lovers’ plan has failed
    • Understatement, in which the speaker’s restraint allows the reader to feel the scene’s emotion without being told of it
    • Colloquial diction, which brings the speech of ordinary people into the poem and gives it a natural and easy flow
    • A repeated refrain, which returns at the end of each stanza and gives the poem its rhythm and its mood

    Keats's imagery is lush and sensory throughout.

  79. As a Romantic poem, "The Eve of St. Agnes" most clearly reflects which of the following Romantic values?

    • Emotion, imagination and the intensity of individual experience
    • Reason, restraint and the authority of classical convention
    • Public duty, social order and the claims of the community
    • Satire, wit and the correction of social folly through ridicule
    • Realism, detail and the careful observation of ordinary life
    • Progress, science and the improvement of society by industry

    Romanticism privileges feeling and imagination.

  80. Both Hawthorne's "Young Goodman Brown" and Poe's "The Fall of the House of Usher" leave readers uncertain about whether the horror is supernatural or psychological. Which statement best explains how each author achieves this ambiguity?

    • Both authors state outright that the events were imaginary, and each uses the dream to explain what has happened
    • Both use omniscient narrators who explain the events, so that the reader knows exactly what has occurred in each story
    • Both rely on comic exaggeration, so that the horror in each tale is softened and the reader is not frightened
    • Both resolve the uncertainty in the final paragraph, where a character explains that the cause was natural
    • Hawthorne never confirms the forest events were real, while Poe filters events through a narrator whose perceptions are colored by dread
    • Neither author uses symbolism, since the stories’ effects depend on plain narration and on the order of the events

    Hawthorne's open question ("Had Goodman Brown fallen asleep...?") and Poe's subjective first-person narrator each preserve the ambiguity by different means.

  81. Which pairing best contrasts the narrative frames of "Rip Van Winkle" and "Baker's Bluejay Yarn"?

    • Both are told in the third person by Rip and the miner, who describe the events they have seen in plain speech
    • Irving’s frame is a letter and Twain’s is a diary, and each of them is presented as the writer’s private record
    • Irving's frame is a mock-scholarly historian's papers, while Twain's is a character's oral tale told in dialect
    • Both stories are narrated by their main characters, who describe what happened to them in a manner that is meant to amuse
    • Irving’s narrator is Rip himself, and Twain’s is a jay who recounts the events in the speech of the frontier
    • Neither story uses a frame, since each begins directly with the events and ends with the end of the action

    Both stories use storytellers, but Irving's persona is a pedantic historian and Twain's is Jim Baker, a talker in dialect.

  82. Which of the following texts relies most heavily on dialect to establish the voice and characterization of its narrator?

    • "The Eve of St. Agnes"
    • "The Fall of the House of Usher"
    • "Baker's Bluejay Yarn"
    • "Young Goodman Brown"
    • "Rip Van Winkle" in its frame narration
    • The Haunted Palace

    Twain's Jim Baker speaks in a Western dialect that supports the oral tall-tale tradition.

  83. Hawthorne, Poe and Irving all use setting to reinforce theme. Which pairing correctly matches setting to function?

    • Hawthorne’s village is comic; Poe’s tarn is cheerful; Irving’s mountains are a realistic part of the setting
    • All three settings are neutral backdrops that serve to identify the place of the action and have no further purpose
    • Hawthorne’s forest symbolizes industry; Poe’s house, wealth; and Irving’s mountains, the freedom of the new republic
    • Irving’s mountains symbolize wealth; Hawthorne’s forest, the frontier; and Poe’s house, the pride of a noble family
    • Poe’s house is a real historical site that Poe visited, and the details of its description are drawn from life
    • Hawthorne's dark forest externalizes moral doubt; Poe's decaying house mirrors a family's ruin; Irving's mountains create a folkloric otherworld

    Each author's setting is symbolic or atmospheric, extending the story's meaning.

  84. Compare the endings of "Rip Van Winkle" and "Young Goodman Brown." Which statement is most accurate?

    • Rip is reintegrated into a community that values his stories, while Brown is permanently alienated by what he believes he has learned
    • Both endings are happy, since each protagonist is restored to the community and to the people who had known him
    • Both protagonists die, and the villagers remember each of them with respect and with a sense of loss
    • Both end with a return to the forest, where the hero finds the peace that he had been unable to find at home
    • Rip is exiled while Brown is welcomed, since the village rejects the one and gives the other a place of honor
    • Both end with the revelation that the events were a dream, and that the heroes have lost nothing by their journeys

    Irving's ending is gently comic and restorative, whereas Hawthorne's is bleak and isolating.

  85. Which of the following best explains why Keats's poem is often paired with the prose works in this unit as an example of Romanticism?

    • It is a historical novel, set in a medieval castle and based on events recorded in the chronicles of the period
    • It is a satire in prose, in which the vices of the aristocracy are exposed in an elaborate and comic allegory
    • It shares with them an interest in imagination, atmosphere and intense experience, though in verse form
    • It was written by the same author as “Usher,” and the two works are by a single hand and share its style
    • It is a realistic account of an American town, whose people are described with care and with attention to detail
    • It is a hymn, intended to be sung in churches on St. Agnes’ Eve in memory of the saint

    The unit connects Romantic and Gothic works that foreground imagination, mood and heightened feeling.

  86. In which of the following ways do the narrators of "The Fall of the House of Usher" and "Rip Van Winkle" differ most significantly in their reliability and function?

    • Poe's narrator is an eyewitness who stays calm and rational throughout, while Irving's is a historian who gets caught up in the events he describes
    • Irving's narrator is a participant whose perceptions shape the story, while Poe's is a detached observer who reports the events from a distance
    • Both narrators are outsiders who report events secondhand, but Poe's relies on documents and letters while Irving's relies on local legend
    • Both are observers who comment on events from a distance, though Poe's narrator is more serious and Irving's is more humorous
    • Poe's narrator is a participant whose emotional perceptions shape the account; Irving's is an amused, self-conscious historian who comments on events from a distance
    • Both narrators are participants in the events, but Poe's is a friend of the Usher family and Irving's is a villager who knew Rip personally

    Poe's narrator is immersed in the events, while Irving's is a comic storyteller who stands outside them.

  87. A student argues that all five texts in the unit deal with the tension between appearance and reality. Which choice offers the best textual support for this claim across at least three texts?

    • Brown's discovery behind the pious facade, the cracks in Usher's seemingly solid house, and Keats's contrast between ascetic piety and sensuous warmth
    • The cold weather in three of the texts, which the authors describe in similar terms and which affects their characters
    • The use of first-person narration in three texts, which allows the narrators to describe things as they seem to them
    • The mention of animals in three texts, which are shown to behave in ways that differ from what one would expect
    • The presence of a female character in three texts, each of whom is found in the end to be other than she seemed
    • Three texts that have the word “house” in the title or in the first paragraph and describe it in detail

    Each cited example shows a surface that conceals something different beneath.

  88. Which of the following best describes the different uses of irony in "Rip Van Winkle" and "Young Goodman Brown"?

    • Irving's irony is verbal and works through the narrator's mock-formal diction; Hawthorne's irony is mainly situational and appears chiefly in the final paragraph
    • Both authors use gentle, comic irony, but Hawthorne's is aimed at the Puritan community while Irving's is aimed at Rip's wife and her temper
    • Irving's irony is darker because Rip loses twenty years of his life, while Hawthorne's is lighter because Brown returns safely to his wife
    • Irving uses dramatic irony, since readers know more than Rip does, while Hawthorne uses verbal irony, in the traveler's remarks to Brown
    • Irving's irony is directed at the narrator himself, who is a fool, while Hawthorne's is directed at Brown, who is a villain
    • Irving's irony is gentle and comic, arising from Rip's obliviousness; Hawthorne's irony is darker, as in the name Faith and the 'virtue' of the community

    The tone of the irony differs: Irving's is comic and Hawthorne's is moral and bleak.

  89. Which of the following would best support the claim that Poe's "House of Usher" prioritizes mood over plot?

    • The narrator is a close friend of Usher, whose shared history with him explains why he agrees to visit the house
    • Extended descriptions of the setting and Usher's behavior precede the minimal action that makes up the climax
    • The story is told in the third person, which allows the reader to know what each character is thinking and feeling
    • The story has multiple settings, which the narrator describes in turn as he moves from place to place
    • The plot has many twists, each of which surprises the reader and leaves the story’s outcome in doubt
    • The narrator changes in the middle of the story, so that the reader sees the events from two different points

    Atmosphere is built through lengthy description before a brief, intense climax.

  90. Which of the following is the best example of personification in the unit's texts?

    • Irving’s description of Rip as lazy and goodhearted, a man who would do anything for others but his own work
    • Hawthorne’s description of the village as small and quiet, with a single street and a meetinghouse at its center
    • Poe's description of the house's "vacant eye-like windows"
    • Keats’s mention of the moon shining through a window, which casts a pale light upon the floor of Madeline’s chamber
    • Twain’s mention of miners who have left the cabin empty and gone elsewhere in search of a better claim
    • Hawthorne’s description of the minister as a man of grave bearing, whose sermons are known to the whole village

    Giving a house eyes is personification.

  91. In the context of the unit, which choice best describes a Gothic element shared by Hawthorne's and Poe's stories?

    • A brooding atmosphere in which hidden guilt and dread overshadow ordinary reality
    • A comic reversal in which a frightening event proves to have a harmless and amusing explanation at the end of the tale
    • A happy ending in which the central characters are reconciled to their families and restored to their former lives
    • An epistolary structure in which the events are revealed through letters, diaries and other private documents
    • A rural setting with farm animals and cheerful villagers, which stands in contrast to the story’s darker events
    • A focus on political reform, in which the characters’ private troubles are the result of the failures of government

    Both use dark settings and psychological terror.

  92. If a student wanted to show how an author uses a symbol to develop theme, which pairing would be strongest?

    • Irving’s mention of a dog and a barn, which appear in the opening paragraphs and recur in the story’s ending
