    • Hawthorne's pink ribbon and the question of Faith's integrity
    • Poe’s mention of a candle and a table, which appear in the narrator’s first view of Usher’s room
    • Keats’s mention of the weather and a shoe, which appear in the stanzas that describe the lovers’ flight
    • Twain’s mention of a pitcher and a gate, which appear in the narrator’s opening account of Baker’s cabin
    • Hawthorne’s mention of a stream and a tree, which appear in the forest’s landscape as Brown goes along the path

    The ribbon is a recurring object whose meaning is central to the theme of faith and doubt.

  93. Which statement best distinguishes Twain's use of humor from Irving's?

    • Twain's humor is gentle and affectionate, whereas Irving's is harsh satire aimed at the weaknesses of the people he describes
    • Twain's humor arises from deadpan exaggeration in a dialect voice, whereas Irving's arises from mock-formal diction and gentle irony
    • Twain's humor depends on mock-formal diction and gentle irony, whereas Irving's arises from deadpan exaggeration in a dialect voice
    • Twain's humor relies on mock-scholarly footnotes and learned asides, whereas Irving's arises from dialect and deadpan exaggeration
    • Irving's humor is based on bawdy wordplay and puns, while Twain's depends on the comic situations in which his characters are placed
    • Both rely on deadpan exaggeration in a dialect voice, though Twain's targets are institutions and Irving's are individual people

    Voice and diction differ: oral deadpan versus mock-scholarly irony.

  94. Which of these claims about narrative point of view across the unit is most accurate?

    • The unit includes a framed omniscient historian, an anonymous first-person observer, a limited third-person view, and a character narrator
    • The unit consistently uses first-person narration, in which a participant tells of the events and offers a view of their meaning
    • The unit consistently uses third-person omniscient narrators, who know what each character thinks and explain it to the reader
    • The unit includes a framed omniscient historian, an anonymous first-person observer, and two protagonists who narrate their own stories
    • The unit uses frames in each prose work, since each begins with a narrator who introduces the story and ends with a comment
    • The poems have narrators with distinct voices, while the prose works present events directly without any narrating persona

    The works use varied perspectives: Irving's frame, Poe's first person, Hawthorne's limited third, Twain's character narrator.

  95. What do Brown's and Rip's returns to their villages have in common?

    • Both return to find their wives alive and waiting, so that each is able to take up his earlier life without change
    • Each returns changed in a way that alters his relationship to a community that did not experience the same event
    • Both return as heroes whose absence has given them a new authority among the people who had known them
    • Both return to find their villages unchanged, so that each is struck by how little time has passed in his absence
    • Both regret leaving their homes, and each resolves to stay near the village and his family for the rest of his life
    • Both are accused of a crime by the villagers, and each must prove his innocence before the town is satisfied

    Both protagonists return after an extraordinary experience; their relationship to the community has been altered.

  96. Which of the following best describes the thematic role of the supernatural in "Rip Van Winkle" compared with "Young Goodman Brown"?

    • In both it is purely comic, since each author uses the supernatural to amuse the reader and to make light of fear
    • In both it is realistic, since the events are given natural explanations at the end and the characters are not deceived
    • In Irving it is a folkloric device that makes comic social commentary possible; in Hawthorne it is a vehicle for moral and psychological exploration
    • In Irving it is tragic, since Rip’s sleep costs him his family, while in Hawthorne it is a source of comedy
    • In Hawthorne it is a minor detail, which gives the story its setting but has no bearing on Brown’s conduct
    • In neither does it matter, since the stories’ themes would be the same if no supernatural event had occurred

    The supernatural functions differently: whimsy versus moral allegory.

  97. In both "The Haunted Palace" and "The Eve of St. Agnes," the poems rely on imagery that appeals to the senses. How does the effect of that imagery differ?

    • The Haunted Palace's imagery moves from horror to splendor as an allegory of recovery, while St. Agnes's imagery builds cold and austerity
    • The Haunted Palace's imagery turns from splendor to horror as an allegory of mental decay, while St. Agnes's imagery builds warmth and sensuous richness
    • Both poems use imagery of warmth and splendor, but St. Agnes's imagery turns into horror by the final stanza while the Haunted Palace's does not
    • The Haunted Palace's imagery is mainly auditory and abstract, while St. Agnes's imagery is mainly visual and literal, with little emotional effect
    • St. Agnes's imagery builds warmth and sensuous richness, while the Haunted Palace's imagery is used to satirize wealth and rank in the court
    • Both poems use imagery of decay, but the Haunted Palace's decay is physical while St. Agnes's decay is emotional and spiritual

    Poe's poem charts a decline; Keats's builds romantic abundance.

  98. Across the unit, which choice best identifies a shared concern about human nature?

    • That human beings act on reason, and their conduct matches the reasons that they give
    • That human beings struggle to reconcile ideals with the imperfections of themselves and others
    • That human beings are born good, and their faults arise from the conditions in which they live
    • That human beings avoid conflict, and each text shows how a quiet and orderly life may be kept
    • That nature is hostile to human beings, who are punished in each text for their attempts to master it
    • That technology improves society, and each text shows the new age is better than the old

    Brown's loss of trust, Usher's fear, Rip's evasions and the lovers' risk all involve gaps between ideal and real.

  99. A student writes that Hawthorne's story is a critique of Puritan society and not just a story of individual doubt. Which detail most strongly supports the student's claim?

    • Faith's pink ribbons, which fall from the sky in the forest and which Brown takes as proof that his wife has joined the devil
    • The presence of respected church leaders at the devil's gathering and the traveler's references to violent acts by the community's forebears
    • The description of a staff that resembles a living serpent, which the traveler carries and later gives to the old woman
    • The forest's darkness, which Hawthorne describes in great detail and which frightens Brown as he goes along the narrow path
    • The use of the word “Faith” as his wife's name, which gives the story a second, allegorical meaning about belief and doubt
    • The return of Brown to his village, where he is shown to be a stern and gloomy man who distrusts his neighbors for a long life

    The implication that the community's pillars are complicit in evil shifts the focus to the society.

  100. In “Rip Van Winkle,” Dame Van Winkle is repeatedly described as a “termagant.” In context, the word most closely means

    • A thrifty and careful housekeeper
    • A woman of great wealth and rank
    • A fearful woman who avoids all conflict
    • A violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman
    • A traveling seller of household goods
    • A woman skilled in folk medicine

    The narrator uses termagant (with virago) for her scolding, domineering temper.

  101. “The opinions of this junto were completely controlled by Nicholas Vedder.” In “Rip Van Winkle,” the word “junto” most closely means

    • A single powerful landowner whose authority extends over the whole village and whose word is accepted as law
    • A noisy annual festival at which the villagers gather to sing, to dance and to drink in the inn’s yard
    • A small group joined together for a common purpose
    • A court that settles village disputes by hearing both parties and by reaching a judgment in accordance with custom
    • A traveling troupe of actors who entertain the villagers with plays on their way through the Hudson Valley
    • A line of soldiers on parade who march through the village on the days when the militia is called out

    The village sages at the inn form a small clique that gathers to talk politics.

  102. The inn’s sign is described as “a rubicund portrait of His Majesty George the Third.” The word “rubicund” most closely means

    • Pale and thin
    • Newly painted
    • Cracked and faded
    • Ruddy or reddish
    • Golden and grand
    • Stern and unsmiling

    Rubicund describes a ruddy, reddish complexion.

  103. Irving writes that men “under the discipline of shrews at home” are apt to be “obsequious and conciliating abroad.” The word “obsequious” most closely means

    • Openly rebellious
    • Physically weak
    • Cleverly cruel
    • Overly eager to please
    • Suspicious of strangers
    • Careless with money

    The point is that henpecked men behave in a servile, people-pleasing way in public.

  104. Rip’s “patrimonial estate had dwindled away.” The word “patrimonial” most closely means

    • Recently purchased by the owner, who paid for the land with the savings of his earlier years in the village
    • Owned by the village as a whole, and used by the farmers for grazing their cattle and for cutting wood
    • Inherited from one’s father or ancestors
    • Held in common by neighbors who divide the produce of the land among them at the end of each season
    • Taxed by the crown at a rate that the owner could not meet, and so reduced by the sale of its parts
    • Mortgaged to a merchant in the town, who has taken the land in payment for the debts that Rip has incurred

    Patrimonial refers to what is inherited from a father; his inherited land has shrunk through neglect.

  105. Rip has an “insuperable aversion to all kinds of profitable labor.” The word “insuperable” most closely means

    • Unreasonable in degree
    • Difficult to describe
    • Increasingly severe
    • Likely to fade in time
    • Superior to similar ones
    • Impossible to overcome

    An insuperable aversion cannot be overcome.

  106. In “Young Goodman Brown,” Goody Cloyse says, “Ah, forsooth, and is it your worship indeed?” The word “forsooth” most closely means

    • Forgive me
    • Truly or in truth
    • Before noon
    • At last
    • Gently
    • Without doubt a sin

    Forsooth is an archaic intensifier meaning “in truth.”

  107. In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” the house stands beside a “tarn.” The word “tarn” most closely means

    • A narrow stream
    • A small mountain lake
    • A stone wall
    • A walled garden
    • A marshy field
    • An underground cellar

    A tarn is a small lake, here a black, still one beside the house.

  108. In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” the “Beadsman” is introduced counting his rosary in the cold chapel. The word “Beadsman” most closely means

    • A man paid to pray for others, using prayer beads
    • A seller of jewelry who travels from castle to castle with a stock of beads, rings and ornaments for sale
    • A servant who guards the castle’s gate and keeps watch over the lord’s guests when they arrive for the feast
    • A soldier loyal to a noble family, who carries a rosary of beads in order to protect himself in battle
    • A traveling minstrel who plays and sings at festivals, and who is paid in gifts of food and drink
    • A monk who has left his order and now lives by begging, and who is known in the neighborhood for his poverty

    A beadsman prays for the souls of his patrons and tells his beads.

  109. In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” the Beadsman’s breath is “Like pious incense from a censer old.” The word “censer” most closely means

    • A person who judges others harshly, and who is known for his willingness to criticize the faults of his neighbors
    • A heavy chain by which a lamp or a lantern is hung in the roof of a church or in the hall of a castle
    • A small bell rung during the service to mark the moments of the ritual and to call the people to prayer
    • A prayer book carried by the priest, who reads from it at the altar during the celebration of the mass
    • A container in which incense is burned
    • A candle stand that holds the lights burning before the saint’s image in the chapel on the evening of her feast

    A censer swings and holds burning incense in religious ritual.

  110. In “Rip Van Winkle,” which word from the story is best defined as “inherited from one’s father”?

    • Rubicund
    • Obsequious
    • Insuperable
    • Conciliating
    • Peevish
    • Patrimonial

    Patrimonial refers to paternal inheritance.

  111. Identify the speaker of: “I am a poor quiet man, a native of the place, and a loyal subject of the King, God bless him!”

    • Nicholas Vedder
    • Peter Vanderdonk
    • Judith Gardenier
    • The stranger with the keg
    • Rip Van Winkle
    • Diedrich Knickerbocker

    Rip says this in the village after his sleep, not knowing that a king no longer rules.

  112. To whom is Rip speaking when he says, “I am a poor quiet man, a native of the place, and a loyal subject of the King, God bless him!”

    • The crowd of villagers who have surrounded and questioned him
    • His daughter Judith, who stands near him in the crowd and has asked him who he is and where he has come from
    • The innkeeper alone, who has come out of the tavern and demands to know what sort of person he is
    • The ghostly crew of the ninepins players, whom he meets again as he returns to the mountain and tells his story
    • The historian Peter Vanderdonk, to whom he has gone for advice about how to prove his identity to the village
    • His dog Wolf, which has followed him into the village and which he addresses in a gentle and bewildered tone

    He is answering the hostile townspeople who ask which party he supports.

  113. Identify the speaker of: “Faith kept me back a while.”

    • Goodman Brown
    • The devil
    • Deacon Gookin
    • The minister
    • Goody Cloyse
    • Faith

    Brown explains his lateness to the traveler; the line puns on his wife’s name.

  114. Identify the speaker of: “Ah, forsooth, and is it your worship indeed?”

    • Faith
    • Goodman Brown
    • The minister
    • Goody Cloyse
    • Deacon Gookin
    • The devil

    Goody Cloyse greets the traveler as though recognizing a respected acquaintance.

  115. Identify the speaker of: “Come, devil! for to thee is this world given.”

    • The traveler
    • Faith
    • Goodman Brown
    • Deacon Gookin
    • Goody Cloyse
    • The minister

    Brown cries this out in despair after he thinks Faith is lost.

  116. Identify the speaker of: “Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!”

    • The narrator
    • Roderick Usher
    • Madeline
    • A servant of the house
    • The physician
    • Sir Launcelot Canning

    Usher shrieks this to the narrator as the sounds from the romance seem to come true.

  117. In “Rip Van Winkle,” what does Rip carry up the mountain for the stranger he meets?

    • A bundle of firewood
    • A stack of ninepins
    • A sack of acorns
    • A fowling piece
    • A lantern
    • A keg

    The stranger in antique Dutch dress asks Rip to help him carry a keg of liquor.

  118. In “Rip Van Winkle,” what are the odd figures in the mountain hollow doing when Rip first sees them?

    • Drinking and singing
    • Digging for treasure
    • Praying around a fire
    • Dancing in a circle
    • Playing ninepins in silence
    • Arguing about politics

    They play ninepins without speaking; the only sound is the rolling balls, like distant thunder.

  119. In “Rip Van Winkle,” who is the village historian who recognizes the legend of the mountain?

    • Nicholas Vedder
    • Derrick Van Bummel
    • Brom Dutcher
    • Diedrich Knickerbocker
    • Jan Gardenier
    • Peter Vanderdonk

    Peter Vanderdonk, the oldest inhabitant, tells that Hendrick Hudson’s crew returns every twenty years.

  120. In “Rip Van Winkle,” whom does Rip recognize first in the changed village as a family member?

    • His son Rip Jr., who looks exactly like him as he was in youth and who is lounging against a tree
    • His wife, who is still living and who greets him with the same scolding that he had heard when he left
    • His friend Nicholas Vedder, who is seated before the inn and who recognizes him by his old manner of speaking
    • His brother, who keeps the inn and who has been waiting for him since the morning he failed to return
    • His neighbor Brom Dutcher, who calls out to him from the road and asks where he has been for so long
    • His grown daughter, Judith Gardenier, carrying a child

    Judith Gardenier, now married with a baby, welcomes her father home.

  121. In “Young Goodman Brown,” what does Faith wear in her cap that Brown later sees fall from the sky?

    • A silver cross
    • A white veil
    • A blue shawl
    • A gold locket
    • Pink ribbons
    • A green wreath

    The pink ribbon floating down convinces Brown that Faith has gone to the forest meeting.

  122. In “Young Goodman Brown,” what does the traveler give to Goody Cloyse that makes her suddenly vanish?

    • His staff
    • A letter
    • A bottle
    • A cloak
    • A ring
    • A coin

    She seizes the staff, which looks like a snake, and flies away on it.

  123. In “Young Goodman Brown,” the traveler claims to have known Brown’s father and grandfather. Which of the following does he say Brown’s ancestors did?

    • Fought against the Indians as soldiers
    • Signed the Declaration of Independence
    • Served as ministers of Salem village
    • Built the village meetinghouse
    • Helped persecute Quakers
    • Sailed from England on the Mayflower

    The traveler says Brown’s grandfather helped scourge a Quaker woman and his father burned an Indian village.

  124. In “Young Goodman Brown,” what is Brown’s state of mind when he returns to Salem village the next morning?

    • Relieved and cheerful about the people he meets
    • Guilty and eager to confess to the people he meets
    • Angry and confronting the people he meets in public
    • Suspicious and recoiling from the people he meets
    • Doubtful of the dream but trusting the people he meets
    • Accepting and forgiving toward the people he meets

    He shrinks from the minister, Goody Cloyse and Faith, as if they all were part of the forest meeting.

  125. In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” what does the narrator read to Roderick Usher during the storm?

    • A romance called the “Mad Trist”
    • A poem by Roderick himself
    • A medical text about catalepsy
    • A letter from Madeline
    • A prayer book
    • A history of the Usher family

    The narrator reads the “Mad Trist” of Sir Launcelot Canning, whose sounds seem to match noises in the house.

  126. In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” why do Usher and the narrator place Madeline in the vault?

    • They want to hide a murder, and the vault is a place where the body will not be found by the servants
    • The family tradition requires burial inside the house, and the vault is where all the Ushers have been placed
    • They believe she has died and wish to keep her body for a time
    • The physician has recommended it, for he believes that the cool air of the vault will protect the body from decay
    • They plan to move her to another house for burial, and the vault is a temporary place of rest on the way
    • Roderick wants to prove his theory of the sentience of the house by placing his sister within its stones

    Madeline suffers from catalepsy and appears dead; Usher wants to entomb her temporarily in the vault.

  127. In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” what happens to the house at the end?

    • It burns to the ground
    • It splits and sinks into the tarn
    • It is abandoned and left empty
    • It is sold to a distant relative
    • It collapses in the storm but is rebuilt
    • It becomes a hospital

    The narrator flees and watches the fissure widen until the house falls into the tarn.

  128. In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” what does Porphyro bring into Madeline’s chamber?

    • A casket of jewels
    • A bundle of letters
    • A feast of delicacies
    • A basket of flowers
    • A flask of perfume
    • A cloak for the cold

    He sets out a banquet of fruits, sweets and wine while she sleeps.

  129. In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” what is Angela’s role in Porphyro’s plan?

    • She warns the Baron of his arrival, and so brings about the discovery that the lovers must flee from the castle
    • She tries to marry Madeline to a rival of Porphyro’s, whom she regards as a more suitable husband for the girl
    • She hides Madeline in the chapel, where the lovers are afterward united in the presence of the Beadsman
    • She leads him secretly to Madeline’s chamber
    • She poisons the guests at the feast, in order to give Porphyro a chance to enter the castle unobserved
    • She declares him a trespasser and calls the servants, who drive him from the castle before he can speak to her

    Angela, the old nurse, reluctantly helps him hide near Madeline’s room.

  130. In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” the legend says that a maiden who goes to bed without supper will

    • See her future husband in a dream
    • Receive a gift from the saint
    • Hear the voice of her mother
    • Be protected from illness
    • Wake with the gift of prophecy
    • Meet her enemy in a vision

    Maidens hope to dream of their lover on St. Agnes’ Eve.

  131. In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” what do Madeline and Porphyro do at the end of the poem?

    • They marry in the chapel
    • They are discovered and punished
    • They stay in the castle
    • They flee into the stormy night
    • They return to Porphyro’s castle by daylight
    • They part forever

    They slip past the sleeping revelers and out into the storm.

  132. In “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn,” who tells the story of the jay and the cabin?

    • Mark Twain’s narrator’s mother
    • A traveling preacher
    • Jim Baker
    • The jay himself
    • A schoolmaster
    • Tom Sawyer

    Jim Baker, a California miner, tells the narrator about jays.

  133. In “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn,” what does the jay try to fill with acorns?

    • A hollow log that stands at the edge of the clearing, and into which the jay drops the acorns one by one
    • A hole in the roof of an empty cabin
    • A rain barrel behind the cabin, which the jay believes is the storehouse where the miner keeps his supplies
    • A nest in the branches of a pine, which the jay has built for the winter and which he wishes to stock
    • A well near the cabin, whose depth the jay is unable to judge from the edge, and which swallows each acorn
    • A mine shaft on the hillside, which opens into a chamber that is too large for the jay’s acorns to fill

    The jay drops acorns into the hole in the roof, but the acorns disappear into the empty cabin.

  134. In “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn,” why do the other jays come to look at the hole?

    • They want to nest in the cabin, and they have come to see whether the hole is large enough for their use
    • They have heard of the first jay’s odd task
    • They hope to steal acorns that the first jay has gathered, and they gather round the hole to see where they are
    • They are chasing a hawk that has entered the cabin, and the hole is the place through which the bird escaped
    • They want to warn Baker that the jay has damaged the roof of his cabin, and that he should take care
    • They are lost, and have followed the first jay to the cabin in the hope that he will show them the way

    News of his labor spreads among jays, and a crowd gathers to laugh at his predicament.

  135. Based on “Young Goodman Brown,” which of the following would Faith most likely agree with?

    • Brown should join the traveler on his journey, since the errand is a harmless one and will be over by morning
    • Brown should trust the minister less, since he has been heard to speak in a manner unbecoming to his office
    • Brown should stay at home on the night of the journey
    • Brown should leave the village and take her with him, since the place has become hostile to honest people
    • The forest is a place of safety, and it is better for Brown to go there than to remain at home at night
    • Salem is a wicked town, and no one who lives in it can be sure of avoiding the temptations that surround him

    Faith begs him to put off his journey and sleep in his own bed.

  136. Based on “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn,” Jim Baker would most likely disagree with which statement?

    • Jays can express themselves with great force
    • Jays have a sense of humor of their own
    • Jays understand a good deal of human talk
    • Jays are expressive and feel what they say
    • Jays are less intelligent than other animals
    • Jays enjoy a joke at another bird's expense

    Baker insists that jays are remarkably expressive, so he would reject the claim that they are dull.

  137. Which of the following statements about “Rip Van Winkle” is accurate?

    • The story is told in the first person by Rip, who describes his own experiences to the villagers in a plain style
    • The story is presented as the papers of Diedrich Knickerbocker
    • The story takes place in New England, in a village whose customs are those of the Puritan colonists
    • Rip is a leader of the Revolution, whose long absence is due to his service in the army of the colonies
    • The story ends with Rip’s death, which comes on the day he returns to the village and sees his daughter
    • Rip’s wife lives to see him return, and she welcomes him with the same scolding that she had given before

    A postscript and headnote attribute the tale to Knickerbocker.

  138. Which of the following statements about “Young Goodman Brown” is accurate?

    • It is narrated by Brown himself
    • It is set in the nineteenth century
    • It ends with Brown's death in the woods
    • It is set in Puritan Salem Village
    • Faith walks with Brown into the forest
    • Brown is a minister in the village

    Hawthorne sets the tale in seventeenth-century Salem Village.

  139. Which of the following statements about “The Fall of the House of Usher” is accurate?

    • The narrator is Madeline’s husband
    • The narrator is Roderick’s physician
    • The narrator is a friend of Roderick’s youth
    • The narrator is Roderick’s brother
    • The narrator is Madeline’s twin
    • The narrator is the owner of the house

    The unnamed narrator was a boyhood friend of Usher who is summoned by a letter.

  140. Which of the following statements about “The Eve of St. Agnes” is accurate?

    • It is a narrative in free verse
    • It is a play in blank verse
    • It is written in Spenserian stanzas
    • It is a sonnet sequence
    • It is composed in ballad meter
    • It is written in heroic couplets

    Keats uses nine-line Spenserian stanzas ending in an alexandrine.

  141. Which of the following statements about “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn” is accurate?

    • It is told by a jay, who describes the events in a voice that is a mixture of human speech and birdsong
    • It is set in New England, in a village where the people speak in the dialect of the region’s farmers
    • It was written as a lecture, which Twain delivered to an audience in the course of a tour of the Western states
    • It is told in a Western vernacular by a miner
    • It is a poem, in which Baker’s story is told in a series of rhymed couplets with a regular rhythm
    • It is told in formal, ornate language, which the narrator adopts in order to give the story an air of dignity

    Twain gives Baker a colloquial Western voice and has him present the story as true.

  142. “Rip Van Winkle” is set in the years surrounding the American Revolution. Which detail best shows the change in the village?

    • The village has a new church, which was built after the Revolution and which replaces the old meetinghouse
    • Rip’s house is repaired, and the garden that his wife had kept is now in better condition than it had been
    • The Catskill Mountains have moved, and the villagers say that the hills are not where they stood before
    • The villagers wear different hats, and Rip’s own hat is a mark of the fashion that has gone out of use
    • The inn is closed, and the villagers meet in a private house to discuss the news of the day and the war
    • The tavern sign changes from King George to General Washington

    The sign is a concrete marker of the transformation from colony to republic.

  143. Hawthorne’s Puritan setting in “Young Goodman Brown” most directly supports which theme?

    • The conflict between outward piety and hidden sin
    • The value of free enterprise, since the story shows that a man who works for himself is better than one who serves others
    • The danger of exploring the frontier, since Brown’s journey into the forest leads him into peril and into error
    • The hopefulness of democratic reform, since the story presents the new world as a place of freedom from the past
    • The power of love to cure fear, since Brown’s affection for Faith is shown in the end to have restored his trust
    • The rise of industrial society, since the story shows how the old village is changed by the new age and its habits

    The Puritan community stresses piety, and the story suggests hypocrisy and doubt beneath it.

  144. “The Fall of the House of Usher” is an example of which literary tradition?

    • Gothic fiction
    • Realism
    • Naturalism
    • Regionalism
    • Transcendentalism
    • Modernism

    Poe uses the decaying mansion, madness, and supernatural dread typical of the Gothic.

  145. “The Eve of St. Agnes” is a poem of which literary movement?

    • Romanticism
    • Neoclassicism
    • Realism
    • Modernism
    • Metaphysical poetry
    • Naturalism

    Keats is a major second-generation English Romantic poet, and the poem emphasizes sensuous imagery.

  146. “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn” is an example of which literary tradition?

    • American regionalism and frontier humor
    • Gothic fiction, in which a decaying setting and a sense of dread combine to produce a mood of terror in the reader
    • Transcendentalism, in which the writer’s interest is in the individual’s relation to nature and to the divine spirit
    • Romantic nature poetry, in which the writer describes the beauty of the landscape in a style marked by feeling
    • Puritan sermon, in which the writer instructs the congregation on the dangers of sin and the need for repentance
    • Neoclassical satire, in which the writer exposes the follies of society in a formal style governed by reason

    Twain uses Western dialect and tall-tale humor.

  147. One can infer about Irving’s attitude toward Rip’s neighbors from the portrait of the inn’s “junto” of village sages that

    • He admires their wisdom and means readers to treat their judgments as the story’s authority
    • He fears their influence on the village and wishes to warn readers against idle gossip
    • He pities them for the poverty that forces them to rely on a few old newspapers
    • He is indifferent to the sages and includes them to complete the local setting of the inn
    • He finds their self-importance amusing, since their solemn politics rest on a few old newspapers
    • He regards them as dangerous radicals who have prepared the way for the Revolution

    The sages’ gravity is mock-heroic: Nicholas Vedder’s silent pipe-smoking governs their opinions, and Irving is gently amused.

  148. By commenting that Rip would “rather starve on a penny than work for a pound,” the narrator chiefly emphasizes that Rip’s idleness is

    • A calculated strategy by which he hopes to avoid paying taxes to the crown
    • A habit he has recently acquired in imitation of the village’s wealthier men
    • A condition brought on by illness that the villagers misread as laziness
    • A settled principle of his temperament, which no practical reward can overcome
    • A deliberate protest against the authority of his wife and the village council
    • A form of religious scruple that the narrator treats with respectful seriousness

    The narrator treats the trait as built into Rip’s nature, so even a large payment cannot change it.

  149. In the phrase “petticoat government,” the narrator is suggesting that Rip

    • Opposes all forms of government and therefore resents the Revolution as much as he had resented the king’s rule
    • Believes that women should hold political office in the new republic, and regards his wife as a fit ruler
    • Has joined the Revolution in order to escape his wife’s authority, and sees the war as a means of freedom
    • Considers his wife a traitor to the cause of the colonies, whose quarrels with him are a form of rebellion
    • Understands domestic power as a form of tyranny, and so mixes small and large subjects for comic effect
    • Regards the king’s ministers as no better than a household of women, and so as unfit to govern the colonies

    Rip’s grievance is the scolding at home; the narrator’s mock-political phrase makes it comic.

  150. The chief effect of the opening paragraphs describing the Catskill Mountains is to

    • Provide the geographical details that a reader needs to find the village on a map
    • Argue that the mountains are the most important natural feature of the Hudson Valley
    • Introduce a conflict between the villagers and the mountain’s inhabitants
    • Establish a legendary, almost enchanted setting in which the later events will seem natural
    • Contrast the beauty of nature with the ugliness of the village’s politics
    • Prepare readers for a realistic description of the Dutch colonial economy

    The mountains change color with the weather and are described with a lyrical, storybook quality that prepares for the supernatural.

  151. The final paragraph of “Rip Van Winkle,” in which Rip tells his story to visitors, primarily reveals that

    • Rip has regained the wealth that he lost through his neglect of the farm
    • Rip has become a bitter critic of the new government and its officials
    • Rip has ceased to believe that his story is true
    • Rip has learned from his experience that industry is the highest virtue
    • Rip has become a local legend whose idleness is now honored as a form of wisdom
    • Rip regrets the years that his sleep has taken from his family

    He sits on the bench outside the inn, a respected patriarch in the new village, free of his wife and his farm work.

  152. The speaker of “Come, devil! for to thee is this world given” can best be described as

    • A man who has just resolved to resist evil and defies the devil to tempt him
    • A skeptic who mocks the devil’s power in order to show that it is imaginary
    • A minister delivering a sermon on the danger of despair in a Puritan community
    • A man in despair who gives himself up to evil after concluding that goodness is a delusion
    • A traveler who feels that he has lost his way and calls for any guide
    • A man in a fever whose words have no connection to what he has seen

    Brown cries out when he believes Faith has fallen, and he abandons his resistance.

  153. Which of the following would the minister and Deacon Gookin, as Brown first knows them, probably not approve of?

    • A villager’s attendance at the evening prayers in the meetinghouse
    • A villager’s decision to walk alone in the forest after dark to attend a secret meeting
    • A villager’s habit of reading scripture to his family at night
    • A villager’s support for the minister’s sermons on sin and judgment
    • A villager’s loyalty to the village’s ancient customs and laws
    • A villager’s willingness to listen to the counsel of the community’s elders

    Their public piety makes them ostensible opponents of the forest meeting, which is what makes their presence there shocking.

  154. Which of the following best paraphrases the meaning of the sentence “A stern, a sad, a darkly meditative, a distrustful, if not a desperate man did he become, from the night of that fearful dream”?

    • Brown became a more careful man, a better husband and a firmer believer in his faith
    • Brown became a respected leader who used the dream to make his community better
    • Brown remained as cheerful as he had been, though the dream gave him an interest in scripture
    • Brown’s experience in the forest left him gloomy, suspicious and distant for the rest of his life
    • Brown grew steadily more fearful of the forest, which he never entered again in his life
    • Brown became a desperate man because he had committed a crime on the night of the dream

    The sentence lists traits of lasting disillusionment; the dream permanently altered his view of the people around him.

  155. In context, “vacant eye-like windows” suggests that the house

    • Has recently been abandoned and shows signs of having been looted by the people who lived near it before
    • Appears to gaze back at the narrator, lifeless yet watchful, which prepares for its sentient menace
    • Is being rebuilt after a fire and has no glass in its frames, which the builders will supply in the spring
    • Is a modern building designed by an architect with an interest in symmetry and in the effects of light
    • Offers a bright and welcoming view of the surrounding countryside, which the narrator enjoys on his arrival
    • Contains a collection of paintings of eyes that Roderick has assembled, and which can be seen from outside

    The simile gives the house a blank, staring look and begins the story’s identification of house and family.

  156. The speaker gives explicit symbolic significance to the house in the sentence in which the narrator says that “the mansion and the family” are

    • Expected to be rebuilt by the last surviving member of the family
    • Divided by a legal dispute that has lasted several generations
    • Identified in the peasantry’s mind as a single entity, the “House of Usher”
    • Known to the narrator through Roderick's letters rather than by sight
    • Described by the narrator as a refuge from the hostile countryside
    • Compared by the family physician to a hospital in need of repair

    The name “House of Usher” refers to both the building and the family line, and Poe makes the identification explicit.

  157. In the lines describing the “Haunted Palace,” the palace is compared to

    • A real castle that once stood in the narrator’s homeland
    • A ship that wanders the sea after a great storm
    • A church whose bells ring at the death of the king
    • A garden that withers when the seasons change
    • The human head and mind, whose ruin the poem allegorically traces
    • A battlefield where the monarch’s armies were defeated

    Usher’s ballad is an allegory of a mind that falls from reason into madness.

  158. It can be inferred that the narrator’s attitude toward Roderick’s theory that the stones of the house are sentient is

    • Quick acceptance of the theory because he has seen the stones respond
    • Amused contempt for a delusion that he thinks will be cured by company
    • Scholarly curiosity about a theory that he has met in earlier reading
    • Indifference, since he gives the theory little notice in his account
    • Uneasy skepticism that is overcome by the evidence of the house’s effect on him
    • Open hostility, because he takes the theory as a sign of Roderick's deceit

    He narrates the theory with doubt but grows more susceptible to the house’s atmosphere.

  159. In lines in which Keats describes “the sculptured dead” in the chapel, the speaker seeks to convey a feeling of

    • Chill, stillness and mortality that makes the lovers’ warmth seem more vivid by contrast
    • Warmth and comfort that the chapel provides to those who pray in it, even in the coldest season of the year
    • Excitement and anticipation at the approach of the festival, which the people of the castle are preparing to celebrate
    • Bitterness at the way the dead have been neglected by the living, who no longer visit the chapel or pray for them
    • Amusement at the ornate carving that decorates the tombs, which the speaker finds excessive and a little foolish
    • Joyful reverence for the saints whose images are painted on the walls, and whose presence is felt by the Beadsman

    The opening stanzas stress cold and death, which sets off the warmth of the main story.

  160. The “Beadsman” in the first stanzas is best described as

    • A figure of renunciation whose cold devotion contrasts with the sensuous love that follows
    • A servant of the Baron who watches over Madeline and reports her movements
    • A traveling pilgrim who seeks shelter in the castle for the night
    • A priest who conducts the marriage of the lovers at the end of the poem
    • A guest at the feast who denounces the revelers for their worldliness
    • A madman whose prophecies foretell the lovers’ downfall

    He prays for others’ sins and then fades from the poem; his asceticism is the foil for Madeline and Porphyro.

  161. In the stanza in which Madeline undresses, the speaker’s attitude toward her is best described as

    • Tender and reverent, treating her innocence with a sensuous delicacy
    • Hostile and critical, since she violates the rules of her household
    • Clinical and detached, as in a scientific study of her behavior
    • Satirical, mocking the superstition that leads her to bed supperless
    • Fearful, since the scene seems to threaten her with violence
    • Indifferent, as the speaker is occupied with Porphyro’s preparations

    Keats’s diction (“warmed jewels”) is lush and admiring.

  162. The tall tale’s final scene, in which the jays shriek with laughter at the jay’s hopeless task, suggests that

    • Mockery of another’s foolishness is a human trait that Twain attributes to the jays
    • Jays are cruel animals who enjoy the sufferings of other creatures, and who take pleasure in the failure of their kind
    • The jay has been punished for stealing from the miner’s cabin, and the other jays are gathered to see his penalty
    • Baker is a poor judge of the animals he has lived among, and his account of their behavior is not to be trusted
    • The jays have a language that Baker alone can understand, and the story is his translation of what they said
    • The scene is meant to teach readers to respect the work of birds, however foolish its object may seem

    The jays’ jeering at the stubborn jay is a satire of human behavior in a social group.

  163. The speaker’s account of the hole in the cabin roof is best described as

    • Lyrical, in the manner of a nature poem about the western landscape
    • Defensive, as though Baker expected to be accused of exaggeration
    • Learned, as though the narrator were reporting a scientific observation
    • Deadpan, with the narrator treating a ridiculous event as plain and serious fact
    • Sentimental, inviting readers to pity the labor of the bird
    • Satirical in a bitter way, aimed at the miners who left the cabin

    Twain’s humor depends on the narrator’s straight face while he narrates absurdity.

  164. The “Fall of the House of Usher” is an example of which genre?

    • A realistic novel of manners about a declining aristocratic family
    • Gothic horror, in which setting and psychology are fused to produce dread
    • A pastoral romance set in the countryside of the narrator’s youth
    • A satirical sketch that mocks the gloom of Romantic poets
    • A didactic tale about the moral dangers of excessive learning
    • A travel narrative that records the narrator’s journey through Europe

    Poe’s tale uses a decaying house, a doomed family and an unreliable narrator typical of Gothic fiction.

  165. According to the editors, which pair of criteria governed their choice of stories?

    • Popularity with earlier anthologists and fairness in representing writers from each region
    • Fame of the author and the story's success with the magazine readers of its day
    • Freedom from Gothic effects and an optimistic view of American national life
    • A balance of regions and the inclusion of a story from each decade since 1832
    • Moral lessons suitable for students and a plot that resolves in a single sitting
    • Excellence of the story itself and its value in showing how the American form developed

    The Introduction says the criteria were “double”: a story’s excellence in itself and its representativeness in the story’s development in the United States.

  166. The editors reject “Marjorie Daw” and “The Lady, or the Tiger?” mainly because they

    • Were written before Poe’s work and so cannot show the form’s development
    • Lack the moral or intellectual weight that serious American stories carry
    • Imitate European Gothic fiction too closely to count as American stories
    • Use dialect and local color in ways that the editors find offensive
    • Were unpopular with the readers of the magazines in which they appeared
    • Rely on a long plot of linked incidents rather than a single effect

    They are called pleasant contrivances or jokes without psychological depth; this missing quality is what Canby called “specific gravity.”

  167. Which of the following would the editors most likely regard as having “specific gravity”?

    • A mystery whose clever solution surprises the reader in the final sentence
    • A tale of local scenery whose chief pleasure is in its colorful description
    • A well-bred joke told with great technical polish and a neat ending
    • A fable about animals that teaches a plain moral to young readers
    • A romantic adventure that ends with the union of two lovers
    • A comic story that is also a serious reflection on manners or national character

    The editors say that even when it is funny, the typical American story asks to be taken seriously as a reflection of life, manners or morals.

  168. In the Introduction, the contrast between Irving’s and Poe’s methods is best described as one between

    • A tale of the supernatural and a tale of ordinary domestic life in a village
    • A graceful chronological chain of incidents and a concentrated tale aimed at a single effect
    • A humorous satire of society and a sober defense of its institutions
    • A story told by a participant and a story told by an all-knowing author
    • An early form based on plot and a later form based on character alone
    • A story rooted in local color and a story rooted in historical fact

    Irving’s “Rip Van Winkle” is the orderly tale of linked incidents; Poe’s is the concentrated tale of effect.

  169. The editors’ claim that Poe’s terror is “not of Germany but of the soul” is best understood as

    • The editors’ praise of Poe as the most profound psychologist of the century
    • A criticism of Poe’s imitation of the German Romantics in his early tales
    • Poe’s own statement, which the editors find only partly justified by his actual effects
    • A definition of the Gothic tradition in all its American and European forms
    • A comparison of Poe’s style with that of Hawthorne in “Young Goodman Brown”
    • An argument that Poe’s stories belong to the tradition of realism

    Poe made the claim, but the editors say his effects are mostly physiological and literary, his “madness” more literary than observed.

  170. Which of the following is credited to Poe in the Introduction?

    • The local-color sketch of life in the Western mining camps
    • The character-centered story of a “situation revealed”
    • The fable in which animals speak in a frontier dialect
    • The tale of ratiocination, the parent of the detective story
    • The comic tale of an idle man who sleeps through a revolution
    • The impressionistic tale of men adrift at sea in an open boat

    “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” is the model of the tale of ratiocination, with its amateur detective, dull assistant and false clues.

  171. Which of the following statements best describes how the Introduction compares Poe and Hawthorne?

    • Poe’s darkness is theatrical, whereas Hawthorne’s forest stands for the darkness of the human soul
    • Poe's stories are rooted in realistic detail, while Hawthorne's are fantasy that carries no moral meaning
    • Both authors depend on a single effect, but Hawthorne is far more concerned with plot than with character
    • Hawthorne's story is less serious than Poe's because it relies on a historical setting and on allegory
    • Poe is a New England moralist who writes of conscience, and Hawthorne a Southern writer of horror tales
    • Both write of witchcraft and the devil, and the two differ mainly in the length of their stories

    The editors call Hawthorne’s story “granite” to Poe’s “pine” in specific gravity, a difference of soul versus stage effect.

  172. The phrase “granite to pine” in the comparison of Hawthorne’s story with Poe’s suggests that Hawthorne’s story is

    • Easier to read and more popular with students than Poe’s
    • Older in its sources and more Gothic in its details than Poe’s
    • Shorter and more tightly constructed than Poe’s
    • More flexible in its use of symbol and dialect than Poe’s
    • Heavier in moral and psychological substance than Poe’s
    • More dependent on setting and less on character than Poe’s

    Granite is dense and hard, pine soft; the metaphor ranks Hawthorne’s “specific gravity” above Poe’s.

  173. According to the Introduction, what weakness does “Young Goodman Brown” show as a piece of craftsmanship?

    • Its use of a forest setting that has no connection with its theme
    • Its reliance on a Gothic house in the manner of Poe
    • Its use of dialect that distracts from the story’s meaning
    • Its failure to give Brown’s experience a symbolic significance
    • Its return section is followed by a lame, anticlimactic appendix
    • Its excessive dependence on a single effect in the final scene

    The editors say Poe would never have left the story with an anticlimactic appendix; Hawthorne is not as impeccable a craftsman.

  174. The Introduction says the American story has moved “away from plot” toward what Henry James called a

    • “Central intelligence”
    • “Situation revealed”
    • “Slice of life”
    • “Moral fable”
    • “Local color”
    • “Unity of effect”

    The editors say the form has tended to become less a complication resolved than a situation revealed.

  175. According to the Introduction, Mark Twain’s mastered forms were

    • The tale of effect and the tale of ratiocination
    • The local-color story and the impressionist sketch
    • The novelette and the historical romance
    • The psychological story and the situation revealed
    • The allegory and the Gothic romance
    • The humorous frontier sketch and the fable

    The Introduction says he never wrote a good short story; the forms he mastered were the humorous frontier sketch (“How to Tell a Story”) and the fable.

  176. The editors’ remark that “Baker’s Bluejay Yarn” is “superb in its own kind” most nearly implies that the piece

    • Belongs to the beast-story tradition and should be judged by its own standards, not as a strict short story
    • Is a poor short story that is redeemed by its humor and dialect, and should be judged on those alone
    • Belongs to the single-effect tradition of Poe and should be judged by how well it produces one unified impression
    • Is a satire of the Western mining camps that should be judged by its dialect and frontier detail
    • Belongs to the local-color tradition and should be judged by how realistically it describes the place and its people
    • Belongs to the fable tradition of animals who teach a moral, and should be judged by the lesson it conveys to readers

    Twain’s yarn belongs to the ancient beast-story tradition (cf. Uncle Remus) and is not a short story by Matthews’s definition, yet is excellent in its kind.

  177. Which of the following does the Introduction credit to Bret Harte?

    • Inventing the tale of ratiocination in the first half of the century
    • Introducing the point-of-view experiments of the central intelligence
    • Writing the first story to use the single effect in 1832
    • Creating the impressionist sketch with a nervous, tense style
    • Popularizing the short story and giving it standing as a distinct form
    • Bringing the humorous frontier sketch into the pages of the Atlantic

    After “The Luck of Roaring Camp” (1868) he gave the story status; his characters combine contradictory qualities.

  178. The editors’ treatment of Henry James emphasizes that he

    • Took Hawthorne's moral seriousness and Poe's Gothic machinery and applied them to the lives of ordinary Americans in a realistic setting
    • Kept Poe's concentration and Gothic atmosphere, but replaced the single effect with a long chronological plot in the manner of Irving
    • Took Irving's graceful chronological structure and applied it to psychological situations drawn from observed experience
    • Dropped Poe's concentration but kept his sensational subject matter, applying it to the settings of the local-color writers
    • Took Poe’s concentration, dropped the Gothic machinery, and applied the method to observed experience
    • Took Melville's moral and intellectual weight and Hawthorne's symbolism, and applied them to the local-color settings of the West

    James took Hawthorne’s serious situation and moral preoccupations, kept Poe’s concentration, and discarded the Gothic and sensational.

  179. In the Introduction, the writing of the editors can best be characterized as

    • Confident literary history that praises most writers and criticizes those outside the American tradition
    • Scholarly analysis that treats each story as an independent work and avoids comparing authors or techniques
    • Defensive argument that apologizes for omissions in the anthology and for weak stories in it
    • Confident literary-historical argument that praises and criticizes the writers it discusses
    • Instructional guide that explains to students how to read and write about each story
    • Polemical essay that attacks nineteenth-century magazines for lowering the standards of the short story

    They rank writers (Poe vs. Hawthorne), name weaknesses (Howells, Twain) and defend their selection.

Hard Mode Questions — 106 questions
Unit 1: The Rhetorical Situation (7)

  1. Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed. Which description best captures the rhetorical situation of this passage?

    • A journalist for a local paper neutrally reports a dispute between merchants and the council, quoting both sides evenly
    • A resident writes to all neighbors, urging them to oppose any change to parking in the district before the vote
    • An economist presents a predictive model of retail traffic to the council, asking it to wait for further data
    • A council member defends a closure already approved, explaining to merchants why their objections came too late
    • A business owner addresses the council and skeptical merchants, using a local pilot's results to urge a timely decision

    The writer speaks as a café owner, addresses both the council ("should make ... permanent") and merchants ("Merchants ... predicted ruin"), and ties the argument to a deadline. It is advocacy, not neutral reporting.

  2. Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair. The speaker's address "Brothers and sisters" and the references to "our eyes" and "our wages" most clearly indicate that the primary audience is:

    • Fellow workers whom the speaker hopes to unite and move to act
    • The mill owners themselves, whom the speaker hopes to persuade directly by appealing to their pride in the family they describe
    • A neutral public audience reading a newspaper, who need to be informed about conditions inside the mill before they judge
    • Government regulators reviewing labor practices at the mill, to whom the speaker presents evidence in the hope of an inspection
    • The speaker’s own family and neighbors, whom the speaker wants to reassure that the mill’s troubles will soon pass

    The speaker uses the inclusive 'our' and a salutation of solidarity. The owners are discussed in the third person ('they'), so they are the object, not the addressee.

  3. To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered." The writer's choice to identify her nineteen years of wheat breeding in the second sentence primarily reflects which consideration?

    • Establishing credibility with readers who may doubt a challenge to the newspaper's framing
    • Providing the exigence for the letter by explaining that her own research was criticized in the original headline
    • Demonstrating that gene editing is safe by pointing to how long she has worked with these plants without harm
    • Appealing to the editor’s emotions by showing how much of her life she has devoted to a single crop
    • Narrowing the audience to other scientists who will recognize her credentials and read the rest with sympathy

    Experience is cited to support her authority (ethos) before she disputes the headline. It does not itself prove safety or define the exigence, which is the headline.

  4. You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there. The speaker's use of the phrase "in the weeks ahead" most directly acknowledges which element of the rhetorical situation?

    • The speaker’s expertise, which entitles her to offer advice that the graduates would not accept from other speakers
    • The occasion and audience of graduating students who will soon hear similar speeches
    • The text’s genre as a eulogy, which sets a solemn expectation about how much the audience should remember
    • A constraint on the length of the speech, which obliges her to compress her advice into a few sentences
    • The speaker’s disagreement with other speakers, whose advice she expects to contradict her own in later remarks

    The reference locates the speech in a graduation season and anticipates the platitudes the audience will hear, which the speaker then undercuts.

  5. The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands. The reviewer's primary purpose in the passage is best described as:

    • To summarize the dam’s history for readers unfamiliar with it, so that they can decide whether to see the film
    • To evaluate a documentary's framing and argue that it ignores the dam's human costs while claiming novelty
    • To praise the film’s technical craft while regretting that its subject has already been treated by other films
    • To inform readers of the film’s release date and subject, together with a short guide to how it is organized
    • To persuade readers to visit the dam, whose history the film is said to have neglected, in order to judge it

    The review evaluates and criticizes; the concluding sentences make an argument about what the film should have done.

  6. I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive. The writer's account of expecting "silence" and "a kind of apology" most strongly suggests an audience that:

    • Is made up of professional ecologists who already know that marshes are far more resilient than they appear to visitors
    • Has little experience of marshes and needs to be told that such places are alive with birds and other creatures
    • Prefers an objective scientific report to a personal narrative and would therefore be impatient with the writer’s reflection
    • Shares assumptions about the damage human activity does to wild places, which the writer then complicates
    • Is hostile to conservation and must be persuaded that marshes deserve protection from the effects of human visits

    The essay anticipates readers who would expect a diminished marsh and then surprises them. It does not use technical or hostile language.

  7. Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate. Which of the following best describes the likely purpose of this statement?

    • To manage public reaction to a data incident while limiting acceptance of responsibility
    • To announce a new privacy policy that protects customers' records from a repeat of the incident
    • To tell customers which steps to take now to protect their own accounts and passwords
    • To persuade investors to hold their shares by showing that the company is containing the damage
    • To explain the technical cause of the incident so that experts can judge whether it could recur

    The vague language and avoidance of a clear agent suggest damage control rather than full accountability.

Unit 2: Rhetorical Appeals & Logical Fallacies (7)

  1. Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed. The phrase "They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces" most directly serves to:

    • Establish the writer’s expertise in retail economics so that later statistical claims will be trusted without question
    • Mock the merchants by implying that their worry about parking is trivial and not worth the council’s serious attention
    • Concede the objection's reasonableness in order to present the writer as fair before redirecting the argument
    • Introduce the first piece of statistical evidence about parking, which the rest of the paragraph then builds upon
    • Shift the tone from persuasive to purely informational so that the reader can weigh both sides without pressure

    'Understandably' grants the merchants a reasonable motive, which builds the writer's credibility and prepares the redirect in 'But parking was never the product.' It does not ridicule them.

  2. Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair. The statement "I have noticed how the family eats" most directly establishes:

    • A sincere endorsement of the mill as a family, offered by a speaker who has watched the owners care for the workers
    • An ironic challenge to the owners' metaphor by implying the family relationship is exploitative
    • A logical appeal supported by data on food spending, intended to prove that the owners’ claim is statistically false
    • An appeal to the speaker’s authority as a physician, whose professional judgment gives the observation its credibility
    • A neutral transition that closes one paragraph and opens the next without adding any new idea to the argument

    The speaker accepts the owners' 'family' language and turns it ironic: noticing 'how the family eats' implies that some members consume while others pay.

  3. To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered." Which statement best describes the effect of the sentence "Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is"?

    • It undermines her argument by admitting that the technology is unsafe, which gives the headline writer an opening
    • It shifts the argument from logos to pathos by asking readers to feel sympathy for a scientist who has been misjudged
    • It introduces a fallacy by oversimplifying a complicated question into a choice between safety and precision
    • It signals that the writer is uncertain about her own position and is preparing to retreat from it in the next paragraph
    • It concedes a limit of her position, which strengthens her credibility with a skeptical audience

    Qualifying her own claim shows fairness and anticipates objection. It does not abandon her thesis.

  4. You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there. The opening "It is not. The world is busy" is most likely intended to:

    • Establish the speaker’s authority through statistics about how the world treats graduates, so her advice appears well-founded
    • Insult the graduates by suggesting that the world will not notice them, so that they feel the need to prove themselves
    • Introduce a logical fallacy by treating a single bleak claim as though it were enough to settle the question
    • Surprise the audience by rejecting a familiar claim, and so win attention for a less conventional message
    • Appeal to nostalgia by recalling the speaker’s own graduation, so that the audience will trust her memories

    The deflationary reversal of a commencement cliché captures attention and sets up the speaker's alternative message.

  5. The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands. The statement "the film's opinion ... arrives at 90 seconds per minute" is best understood as:

    • A literal measurement of the film’s pace, offered by the reviewer to show how much opinion the film contains
    • A sarcastic exaggeration that criticizes the film for pressing its viewpoint relentlessly
    • A neutral comparison between the film’s opinion and its facts, meant to help the reader evaluate the balance
    • A statistical claim about how much of the running time is devoted to interviews, as opposed to narration
    • A compliment about the pacing of the film, which keeps its argument moving without ever losing the viewer’s attention

    The impossible rate is hyperbole used sardonically to suggest the film rushes and overstates its opinion.

  6. Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate. The sentence "Mistakes were made" is most significant because of:

    • The use of the past tense, which reveals that the company regards the problem as already resolved
    • The use of passive voice that omits who made the mistakes, which distances the company from responsibility
    • The use of the word “mistakes,” which is too strong and so makes the company sound more guilty than it intends
    • The sentence’s brevity, which gives it a blunt force that no longer sentence in the statement could equal
    • Its appeal to pathos, which invites customers to feel sympathy for the employees who made an honest error

    The passive voice conceals the actor, a common evasive strategy.

  7. Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything." Source B's phrase "the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything" is primarily an appeal to:

    • The authority of library experts who study public services
    • Statistics showing how little a library costs per visitor
    • Fear of losing the library if the council cuts funding
    • Shared values about public space and equality of access
    • Humor that lightens the tone for skeptical readers

    The phrase invokes the ideal of a public commons, a value-based appeal.

Unit 3: Rhetorical Devices & Figurative Language (8)

  1. Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed. The sentence "A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share" relies primarily on:

    • A simile that likens the street to private property, so that its value is measured in what a business could earn from it
    • Hyperbole that inflates the size of the street in order to make the merchants’ parking complaints seem small by comparison
    • A metaphor paired with an antithetical structure that redefines what a street is for
    • An allusion to a historical dispute over public land, which gives the closure the weight of a long civic tradition
    • Understatement that deliberately minimizes the merchants’ concern so that the council will regard it as not worth debating

    The 'pipe' metaphor is rejected and replaced with a new definition in a 'not X; it is Y' construction. That reframing changes the terms of the debate.

  2. Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair. The structure of the sentences "it is our eyes that pay for the oil" and "it is our wages that were cut by a tenth" is best described as:

    • Parallel clauses that contrast the owners' gains with the workers' costs
    • Anaphora that repeats the same opening phrase to build toward an emotional climax about the workers’ suffering
    • A series of rhetorical questions that invite the owners to defend themselves before an audience of the mill’s workers
    • An extended metaphor that compares the mill to a family and then carries the comparison through the whole sentence
    • Asyndeton that removes conjunctions so that the list of the workers’ grievances moves quickly and without pause

    Each clause pairs an owner-side benefit (lamps burning, profits rising) with a worker-side cost in a parallel pattern, which makes the contrast vivid.

  3. To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered." In the phrase "a gamble with the food supply," quoted from the headline, the word "gamble" functions as:

    • A literal description of the field trials, whose results were uncertain enough to be fairly called a risk
    • A loaded metaphor the writer must challenge because it frames the science as reckless
    • An example of understatement that makes a serious danger to the food supply sound like a minor inconvenience
    • A technical term used by breeders to describe the odds that a given cross will produce the desired trait
    • An allusion to a historical event in which an untested crop failed and brought hunger to a farming region

    The letter responds to the connotations of 'gamble' (risk, chance), which is why she then reframes the issue in terms of precision and openness.

  4. You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there. The repeated structure beginning "Show up" in the middle of the passage is an example of:

    • Antithesis, which sets two opposing ideas side by side so that the audience sees how much each differs from the other
    • Anaphora, which accumulates emphasis on a central imperative
    • Hyperbole, which exaggerates the graduates’ responsibilities so that ordinary duties seem as grand as heroic ones
