    • Euphemism, which softens a harsh claim by describing the demands of adulthood in gentler and more polite terms
    • Apostrophe, which addresses an absent person or abstraction as though it could hear and respond to the speaker

    The repetition of the same opening words across successive sentences is anaphora, and it emphasizes the commandment to be present.

  5. The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands. The repetition in "We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion" primarily creates which effect?

    • A deadpan, mocking rhythm that portrays the film's visual style as repetitive
    • A sense of urgency that makes the film’s images seem to move faster as its argument gathers force
    • Admiration for the film’s artistry, as the reviewer lingers on each image to show how deliberately it was made
    • A shift in the reviewer’s tone to sympathy, since the repetition shows that the filmmakers meant well
    • Confusion about the film’s subject, since the repeated images leave the viewer unsure what the film is about

    The pairing of parallel sentences underscores sameness and mockery; the reviewer is not praising the visuals.

  6. I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive. The long opening sentence, with its accumulation of clauses, produces which effect?

    • It confuses the reader with complexity, a deliberate disorientation that mirrors the writer’s own bewilderment at the marsh
    • It creates a tone of urgency, as though the writer were anxious to describe everything before the scene could change
    • It immerses the reader in the scene's layered details, delaying the main point to mimic the slow arrival of spring
    • It states the writer’s thesis immediately, so that the rest of the passage can be read as support for one claim
    • It depicts a rapid sequence of events, so that the reader is carried quickly from one image to the next

    A periodic, cumulative sentence builds an impression of the season and slows the pace; the main clause is 'I came to the marsh in March.'

  7. I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive. The phrase "who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them" is best characterized as:

    • A literal description of birds that arrive at the marsh earlier than the season’s warmth, which the writer reports as fact
    • Personification that humorously attributes a will to the weather
    • An example of apostrophe, in which the writer addresses the weather directly and asks it to welcome the arriving birds
    • A metaphor for human migration, in which the arrival of the birds stands for people who settle in a new country
    • Hyperbole about spring, which exaggerates how late the season is so as to dramatize the birds’ early arrival

    Weather 'agreeing' to welcome is personification; the humor suggests the birds' boldness.

  8. Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate. The phrase "any inconvenience that may have been experienced" is best understood as which of the following?

    • A precise statement of fact in which the company reports exactly how many customers experienced a problem
    • A metaphor for stress in which the customers’ worry about their data is likened to a physical burden
    • A euphemism that minimizes the effect on customers and hedges whether harm occurred
    • Hyperbole about customers’ feelings that inflates their annoyance so as to make the company’s apology seem larger
    • An allusion to a similar incident at another firm, which suggests that the problem is common to the industry

    'Inconvenience' understates a data breach, and 'may have been' hedges even the existence of harm.

Unit 4: Style: Diction, Syntax & Tone (8)

  1. Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed. Which statement best describes the shift in tone from the first four sentences to the final sentence?

    • From open hostility toward the merchants in the opening sentences to a grudging admiration for how they have endured
    • From personal reminiscence about the street’s past to a detached, statistical analysis of what the closure might cost
    • From playful humor at the start of the passage to a solemn, grieving note about the street’s lost businesses
    • From neutral reporting of the pilot’s results to a tone of weary resignation that the council will not act
    • From measured, wry observation to pointed urgency tied to a consequence

    The opening is measured and a little wry ('understandably,' 'never the product'). The last sentence turns urgent with a deadline and consequence ('before... will come due').

  2. Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair. Which statement best characterizes the speaker's tone in the passage?

    • Warmly sentimental toward the owners, whom the speaker credits with sincere though sometimes misguided generosity
    • Angry and chaotic, with sentences that break down as the speaker loses control of the argument in front of the workers
    • Bitterly ironic yet controlled, with a dignified refusal to beg
    • Neutral and academic, as though the speaker were analyzing conditions at the mill for a professional journal
    • Playful and lighthearted, with jokes at the owners’ expense meant to put the audience at ease before the argument

    The irony ('how the family eats') and the restrained, concrete diction ('I do not ask the owners to love us') produce disciplined bitterness, not rage or neutrality.

  3. To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered." Which feature of the passage's diction most contributes to a measured, professional tone?

    • Qualified, precise phrasing such as "I would put it differently" and "I would not claim"
    • Frequent use of slang and everyday idiom that lets the writer sound like an ordinary reader responding to the paper
    • Extended figurative language that compares the breeding of wheat to the work of an artist shaping her materials
    • Short, emphatic fragments that give each point the force of a slogan and keep the pace of the letter brisk
    • Direct address to the reader as “you,” which turns the letter into a personal appeal rather than a professional reply

    Hedged, restrained phrasing signals a measured, evidence-minded voice.

  4. You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there. Which of the following best characterizes how syntax contributes to the passage's effect?

    • Short, declarative sentences create a blunt, almost aphoristic quality that rises into longer, rhythmic imperatives
    • Long, complex sentences throughout create a scholarly tone and slow the reader so that each qualification can be weighed
    • Rhetorical questions dominate the passage and keep the audience in doubt about which answer the speaker intends
    • Sentence fragments show the speaker’s confusion and make the passage seem like an unfinished set of private notes
    • Parenthetical asides convey humor, since the speaker keeps interrupting herself to qualify a point with a joke

    The speaker moves from terse statements to a rhythm of repeated imperatives, which makes the message memorable.

  5. The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands. Which statement best describes the shift in tone in the last four sentences?

    • From sardonic mockery to a firm, serious moral claim
    • From admiration for the film’s craft to disappointment that it did not do more to explore the dam’s history
    • From light humor to confusion, as the reviewer finds that she can no longer state what the film is about
    • From neutral reporting of what the film contains to enthusiasm for the way it treats its subject
    • From sadness over the dam’s history to joy in discovering that the film offers a hopeful ending

    After mocking the film's style, the reviewer turns serious: 'It is not.' and 'It should not need to pretend...' present an ethical stance.

  6. I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive. The shift in the final sentence from description of the marsh to "what it is to be unnecessary to a place" most clearly reflects a change from:

    • Fact to fiction, as the writer leaves the observed marsh and begins to imagine events she did not witness
    • Argument to narrative, as the writer abandons her claim in order to tell a story about her visit
    • Humor to anger, as the writer’s playful opening gives way to a complaint about how the marsh is treated
    • Past to future tense, as the writer turns from what happened to what she hopes will happen on later visits
    • Observation to reflection, adding a note of humility

    The essay moves from what the writer saw to what the experience taught about human place in nature.

  7. Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate. The tone of the statement is best described as:

    • Warm and conversational, with plain words and short sentences that address customers as though they were neighbors
    • Angry and defensive, with sharp phrasing that suggests the company resents being asked to account for itself
    • Humorous, with a light touch meant to make the problem seem small and keep the customers from becoming alarmed
    • Impersonal and guarded, with formal diction that avoids specifics
    • Personal and confessional, with a first-person admission of fault that invites forgiveness from the customers

    The corporate register, passive constructions and abstractions create distance.

  8. Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything." Compared with Source A, Source B's diction is best described as:

    • More technical and abstract, with terms of measurement that make the argument sound like a report
    • More hostile to its opponents, with sharp wording that treats the other source’s view as foolish
    • More formal in its diction, with long sentences and Latinate words that give it an air of authority
    • More ironic in its tone, since it describes the library’s uses in a manner that implies the opposite
    • More concrete and humane, listing specific uses and people

    Source B names tangible needs (printing, childcare, applications); Source A uses a general statistic and a slogan-like contrast.

Unit 5: Claims, Evidence & Commentary (8)

  1. Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed. Which additional evidence would most effectively strengthen the writer's claim that the closure has helped businesses?

    • Sales tax receipts for the four blocks compared with similar commercial streets that remained open to cars over the same period
    • A quotation from a longtime resident who says she enjoys the sidewalk tables and has begun to shop on the street more often
    • The writer’s own estimate of how many pedestrians now walk along the four blocks on a typical weekday afternoon
    • The number of parking spaces lost to the closure, set beside the total number of spaces that remain in the district
    • A description of the street’s commercial history before the pilot, including which shops had opened and closed in earlier decades

    A comparison group across the same period addresses whether the gains came from the closure rather than from general trends. The other options are anecdotal, irrelevant, or the objection itself.

  2. Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair. The juxtaposition of "profits rose by a fifth" and "wages ... cut by a tenth" is most effective because it:

    • Provides a full financial analysis of the mill, so that listeners can judge the owners' ability to pay
    • Uses specific, parallel proportions that let listeners compare gain and loss immediately
    • Appeals to the owners' pity by describing how workers' families have suffered since the cut
    • Relies on a single anecdote rather than data, so that the audience feels the cut personally
    • Contradicts the claim of family by showing that the owners avoid speaking to the workers

    Numbers expressed as fractions, placed in parallel, make the disparity easy to grasp aloud. The passage does not offer a full financial analysis.

  3. To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered." The writer's claim that "Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered" is most vulnerable to which critique?

    • It relies on an emotional appeal that distracts the reader from the lack of any argument about the science
    • It does not distinguish between kinds of alteration that may carry different risks
    • It uses a statistic from an unreliable source, which makes every claim in the letter harder to trust
    • It contradicts her own later statement about precision, since the word “altered” undermines the distinction she draws
    • It is irrelevant to the headline, which concerned a single new crop and not the history of every cultivar

    Equating crossing with gene editing may overlook differences in kind and speed of change; she partially acknowledges this in the next sentence, but the claim as stated is broad.

  4. You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there. Which of the following would most strengthen the speaker's central claim about being remembered for presence rather than credentials?

    • A list of famous universities whose graduates were not remembered, which would show how little a credential can guarantee
    • A brief example of a person remembered for consistent small acts rather than formal achievements
    • A statistic on average starting salaries for graduates of different fields, which would show what credentials are worth
    • An explanation of what a diploma represents, including the years of study and the standards required to earn one
    • A quotation about the importance of success that praises ambition and suggests how graduates can be remembered

    A specific example would support the claim directly; the other options reinforce the value of credentials the speaker discounts.

  5. The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands. The reviewer quotes the phrase "part of the cost of progress." The use of the quotation is most effective in supporting which point?

    • That the dam was not a triumph of engineering, since its builders failed to anticipate the problems it caused
    • That the film adopts a language of rationalization that minimizes displaced families
    • That the engineers were incorrect in their estimates of cost, which rose well beyond what had been promised
    • That the film includes many interviews, which the reviewer treats as evidence that its makers did careful work
    • That progress is unavoidable, so that those displaced must accept the cost as the film’s speakers insist

    The quotation reveals the film's own wording, which the reviewer challenges as a euphemistic justification.

  6. I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive. In the sentence "I had expected, I think, a kind of apology," the phrase "I think" most likely functions to:

    • Show that the narrator does not understand the marsh well enough to say what she expected to find there
    • Indicate tentative, reflective self-examination, which makes the narrator's candor more credible
    • Present an objective fact that the reader could confirm independently by consulting a record of the marsh
    • Create a humorous tone by having the narrator poke fun at her own foolish assumptions about the marsh
    • Introduce a logical fallacy by presenting a personal impression as though it were evidence about the marsh

    The hedge suggests honest self-reflection, building trust in a personal essay.

  7. Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate. Which revision would most strengthen the credibility of the statement for a skeptical audience?

    • Adding more praise for the company’s long record of high standards, so that readers recall how seldom it has failed
    • Stating what data was affected, when it was discovered, who is responsible for the review and when results will be released
    • Using more formal language throughout, so that the statement sounds as authoritative as a report from a regulator
    • Repeating the company’s commitment to privacy in the opening and closing sentences so that readers remember it
    • Shortening the statement to two sentences, so that readers are not given time to notice what it leaves out

    Specifics and accountability build trust; vague reassurance does not.

  8. Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything." Which additional information would most help evaluate Source A's recommendation?

    • The number of books held in each library, which would show whether the collections have grown or shrunk
    • The age of the library buildings, which would show whether the branches need costly repairs before long
    • The names of the library directors, which would show whether the system has been managed by the same people
    • The price of printed books over the decade, which would show whether readers could still afford to buy them
    • Whether digital circulation and database use increased in the same decade

    The claim to shift to screens depends on whether digital use is growing; that evidence addresses the inference.

Unit 6: Organization, Structure & Counterargument (7)

  1. Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed. The final sentence functions most significantly to:

    • Introduce a counterargument that the writer will refute in a later paragraph, so that the piece appears balanced to its readers
    • Summarize the evidence from the first half of the passage so that the council can recall each point before it votes
    • Soften the argument by acknowledging uncertainty about the pilot’s results and inviting the council to gather more data
    • Move from the argument to a specific request with a deadline, and attach a concrete cost to inaction
    • Shift the focus away from the council and toward the merchants, who are now asked to change their own practices

    It states the demand ('make the closure permanent'), sets a timeframe, and names the cost of delay, which turns the argument into a call to action.

  2. Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair. The final sentence ("I ask only that they count us as they count their looms") functions primarily as:

    • A concession that the owners have been generous, preparing the audience for a smaller request
    • A shift to a neutral tone in which the speaker steps back and invites the audience to decide
    • An analogy that reduces the demand to a modest request based on the owners' own values
    • A summary of the evidence offered earlier so that the audience can recall the argument as a whole
    • A rhetorical question that asks whether workers deserve the same care that machines receive

    The comparison to looms frames the request as modest and uses the owners' own standards (maintenance of valuable property) against them.

  3. To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered." The final two sentences primarily serve to:

    • Introduce a new claim unrelated to the earlier ones, so that the letter ends on a point the editor has not yet considered
    • Summarize each point from the letter in order, so that a hurried reader can carry away the whole argument
    • Retreat from her earlier argument by granting that the newspaper’s headline may be right after all
    • Redirect the audience's skepticism from a label toward evidence, offering a constructive stance instead of simple opposition
    • Appeal to the authority of the newspaper by praising its reputation and asking it to correct its own headline

    The conclusion accepts skepticism but reorients it ('aimed at the evidence rather than at the word'), tying back to the headline.

  4. You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there. The final two sentences function primarily to:

    • Provide a list of tasks the graduates should accomplish in their first year, so that the advice ends on specifics
    • Shift to a humorous tone that relaxes the audience after a serious passage and lets the speech end on laughter
    • Introduce a new topic, the value of friendship, which the speaker will take up in the remainder of her remarks
    • Offer a counterargument that the speaker will refute in the next paragraph, so that the speech appears balanced
    • Contrast what graduates may value with what lasting regard depends on, and so state the thesis in memorable form

    The sentences set 'diplomas' against 'mornings you were still there,' delivering the central claim in antithetical form.

  5. The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands. The final sentence ("A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands.") functions primarily to:

    • Introduce a new argument, about the dam’s engineering, which the reviewer has not previously mentioned and does not develop
    • Concede a legitimate position while stating the reviewer's essential objection in a concise, memorable contrast
    • Summarize the film’s plot in two sentences so that readers who have not seen it can follow the review
    • Provide a logical proof that the film’s claim to be “untold” must be false because it repeats earlier films
    • Shift to a humorous tone that lightens the review and leaves the reader with a final joke at the film’s expense

    The sentence grants that admiration is acceptable and then pinpoints the objection, balancing fairness with a pointed conclusion.

  6. I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive. Which statement best describes the structure of the passage?

    • It presents a problem with the marsh’s condition and then offers a solution that the narrator hopes readers will adopt
    • It moves from a precise scene to an expectation that is overturned and then to a reflective conclusion
    • It compares two marshes, one in March and one in a later season, in order to show how much they differ
    • It argues for a policy of protecting the marsh from visitors and gives reasons for the policy in order
    • It moves chronologically through a single day, beginning at dawn and ending at dusk, with each event in sequence

    The movement from observation to anticipated silence, to 'instead,' to an insight is a turn structure.

  7. Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate. The last sentence, "its findings will be shared as appropriate," most likely:

    • Leaves open whether and when information will be released, which weakens the promise
    • Guarantees transparency by promising that each finding of the review will be published in full
    • Provides a timeline by which customers can expect the results of the review
    • Introduces a new argument about the company's reputation that earlier sentences left unprepared
    • Offers a comparison to other companies that handled similar incidents with less care

    'As appropriate' gives the company discretion, making the promise noncommittal.

Unit 7: The Synthesis Essay (3)

  1. To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered." A student writing a synthesis essay on public trust in science uses this letter alongside a poll showing falling trust in agricultural research. Which use of the letter would best demonstrate synthesis?

    • Using the letter as evidence that scientists are losing public trust, then citing the poll to show that the letter's reasoning is persuasive to its readers
    • Treating the letter as a representative scientific voice and the poll as a counterargument, then concluding that trust depends on the quality of research
    • Comparing the writer's credentials in the letter with the poll's findings, and concluding that expertise alone cannot rebuild public trust
    • Using the poll to introduce the problem and the letter to show the scientists' viewpoint, without evaluating whether the letter's approach addresses the poll's concerns
    • Using the letter to illustrate how a scientist attempts to rebuild trust through transparency, then evaluating whether the approach addresses the poll's concerns

    Synthesis puts sources into conversation in service of the writer's argument. Summary, long quotation, or reliance on one source does not.

  2. Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything." A student writes: "Although Source A is right that print circulation has fallen, Source B shows that falling circulation does not mean falling use." What synthesis move does the sentence make?

    • It summarizes both sources equally, giving each the same weight and leaving the reader to reach a conclusion alone
    • It dismisses Source A without evidence so that the writer may rest the whole argument upon Source B
    • It uses one source to qualify the conclusion drawn from the other, positioning the writer's own claim between them
    • It restates Source B in different words, adding no new idea that Source A had not already prepared
    • It introduces a new fallacy by assuming that one source’s evidence must cancel whatever the other source claims

    The sentence concedes part of A, then uses B to complicate A's inference, which is a synthesis move that advances an argument.

  3. Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything." Which statement best identifies the central disagreement between the sources?

    • Whether libraries should continue to exist at all in a period when so much reading has moved onto screens
    • Whether printed books are valuable to readers of any age, or whether only digital texts can serve them
    • Whether a decline in one measure of use (print circulation) should determine how library resources are allocated
    • Whether the sources use accurate statistics, since each of them cites figures that the other does not mention
    • Whether library visitors are satisfied with the services they receive, as both sources report different surveys

    Source A infers budget priorities from circulation; B argues that visits and uses are broader.

Unit 8: The Rhetorical Analysis Essay (6)

  1. Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed. Which sentence would serve best as a thesis for a rhetorical analysis of this passage?

    • The writer uses metaphor, concession and a call to action to persuade the council and the merchants to support a permanent closure
    • By conceding the merchants' concern and then redefining the street's purpose, the writer reframes the debate so that a permanent closure seems the logical conclusion
    • The passage is persuasive because it uses evidence and emotional appeals to move an audience that began by disagreeing
    • The writer argues that Larkin Street should be closed to cars permanently, and he supports his argument with a pilot program
    • The author’s use of a pipe metaphor shows creativity and effectively changes how readers might think about a city street

    A strong thesis names specific choices, explains how they work and ties them to purpose. The first option does all three; the others list devices, make a generic judgment, or restate the argument.

  2. Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair. Which choice best describes how the speaker uses the word "family" in the passage?

    • The speaker rejects the term in the opening sentence and does not return to the idea of a family
    • The speaker uses it literally to describe real relatives who work together in the mill under the owners’ supervision
    • The speaker adopts the owners' term and then reveals its inadequacy by describing unequal consequences
    • The speaker uses it to praise the owners’ kindness and so earns the goodwill of the owners before making a demand
    • The speaker introduces it in the final sentence, where it becomes a sudden turn in the argument

    The word is introduced as the owners' claim and then tested against evidence (eyes, wages), which exposes the metaphor's hypocrisy.

  3. You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there. Which analysis most accurately describes the speaker's use of the second person?

    • It creates distance between the speaker and the graduates, so the advice sounds like a general rule and not a personal wish
    • It indicates that the speaker is uncertain about her own advice and wants the audience to decide whether it applies
    • It signals a shift to a scientific register, in which the speaker reports the habits of people who succeed
    • It reflects the speaker’s disapproval of the graduates, whose assumptions about their futures she wishes to correct
    • It positions the speaker as a direct advisor and makes the imperative mood personal rather than abstract

    Direct address and imperatives create intimacy and urgency.

  4. The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands. Which of the following best explains how diction contributes to the reviewer's critique in the sentence "The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation"?

    • The word “phrase” signals that the reviewer stays neutral about the film's language and reports it
    • The word “spoken” shows that the line comes from an engineer, which the reviewer treats as a bias
    • The word “kind” makes the sentence ambiguous, leaving readers unsure whether the reviewer approves
    • The word “cost” refers to money, so the sentence is a complaint about the dam's budget
    • The comparison of 'cost' to 'consolation' exposes the illogic of treating a loss as a comfort

    The sentence juxtaposes two opposed ideas to reveal faulty logic.

  5. I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive. Which of the following claims about the writer's use of the word "insistence" is best supported by the passage?

    • It shows the writer's irritation at the birds' noise, which interrupts her reflection
    • It refers to the blackbirds' repeated calls, which she finds more persistent than other sounds
    • It conveys the marsh's vitality as a force that does not depend on human approval
    • It suggests a legal demand made by the marsh's caretakers, who ask her to leave
    • It reveals the writer's scientific method of waiting for an observation to repeat

    The 'insistence' of sound and life contrasts with the writer's expectation of apology.

  6. Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate. A rhetorical analysis of the passage would most appropriately focus on:

    • The statement’s use of statistics, which makes the incident seem small by comparing it with the company’s yearly volume
    • The statement’s emotional appeal to children and families, which is meant to make customers feel protective of the firm
    • How passive voice, euphemism and abstraction serve the company's interest in limiting accountability
    • The writer’s use of dialect, which lends the statement a local flavor and makes the company sound approachable
    • The statement’s metaphors, which compare the data incident to a storm that has passed over the company

    The persuasive strategy lies in grammatical and lexical choices that obscure responsibility.

Unit 9: The Argument Essay (2)

  1. Brothers and sisters: the owners tell us that the mill is a family, and I do not doubt it. I have worked beside this family twenty-two years, and I have noticed how the family eats. The mill's lamps burn all night; it is our eyes that pay for the oil. The mill's profits rose by a fifth this year; it is our wages that were cut by a tenth. I do not ask the owners to love us. Love is a luxury no ledger records. I ask only that they count us as they count their looms: as property worth keeping in repair. If an owner wished to rebut the speaker, which response would most directly address the passage's central comparison?

    • Asserting that the speaker is ungrateful for the steady employment the mill has given his family over many years
    • Saying that the lamps are expensive to keep burning, so the owners could not be expected to pay for workers’ eyes
    • Stating that the speaker has worked at the mill for twenty years and has rarely complained about his pay
    • Arguing that wage reductions were necessary to keep the mill solvent despite profits in a single year
    • Claiming that families have disagreements, so a quarrel over wages does not show that the mill is not one

    The central comparison pits rising profits against falling wages. A rebuttal must explain or challenge that relationship, for example by pointing to solvency concerns.

  2. Source A: "Circulation of printed books has fallen twelve percent in a decade, and library budgets should follow readers: toward screens, not shelves." Source B: "Visits to our branches rose in the same decade. People come for printing, for childcare programs, for job applications, and for the one room in town where nobody asks them to buy anything." A student argues that libraries should keep funding in-person programming. Which line of reasoning, drawing on the sources, would be strongest?

    • Libraries have long been important to their communities, and the council should therefore keep their funding at its present level
    • Print circulation measures only one function; Source B's visit data and program uses indicate that libraries serve needs that screens do not replace
    • Source A is written by a critic of libraries, so its circulation figures should be treated with suspicion by the council members
    • Visitors enjoy books and reading, which shows that the community will keep supporting the library's programs through the next decade
    • A decade is long enough that the circulation decline must reflect a lasting change in how people read, so print budgets should shrink

    The strongest reasoning explains why the evidence supports the position, linking specific data to a claim about function.

Unit 10: Grammar, Conventions & Multiple-Choice Strategy (6)

  1. Merchants on Larkin Street predicted ruin when the council proposed closing four blocks to cars. They pointed, understandably, to the parking spaces. But parking was never the product. In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and the only complaint I hear at my own café is that the sidewalk tables are always full. A street is not a pipe for moving vehicles; it is the largest piece of public property most of us will ever share. The council should make the closure permanent, and it should do so before the next budget cycle ends, when the cost of delay will come due in leases not renewed. Which revision of the third sentence ("In the three summers since the pilot began, foot traffic has doubled, two vacant storefronts have filled, and ...") would introduce an error?

    • Changing "has doubled" to "doubled"
    • Replacing the first comma with a semicolon
    • Changing "has doubled" to "have doubled"
    • Changing "filled" to "been filled"
    • Replacing "pilot began" with "pilot had begun"

    'Foot traffic' is a singular subject, so 'have doubled' would be an agreement error. The other changes alter tense, punctuation or voice without creating a grammatical error in context (although some change meaning slightly).

  2. To the Editor: Your headline calls gene-edited wheat "a gamble with the food supply." I have spent nineteen years breeding wheat, conventionally and otherwise, and I would put it differently. Every cultivar on your readers' tables was altered, by crossing, by radiation, by selection; the question has never been whether we change crops, only how precisely and how openly. Precision is not safety, and I would not claim that it is. But the trials your article calls "secret" are published, and their data on off-target edits are available to anyone willing to read a table. Skepticism is healthy. Let it be aimed at the evidence rather than at the word "engineered." Which version of the underlined portion corrects the error in the following revision? "Every cultivar on your readers' tables were altered."

    • Every cultivar ... were altered
    • Every cultivar ... was altered
    • All cultivar ... were altered
    • All cultivars ... was altered
    • Every cultivars ... was altered

    'Every cultivar' is singular, so the verb must be singular: 'was altered.' 'All cultivar' would need a plural noun.

  3. You will be told, in the weeks ahead, that the world is waiting for you. It is not. The world is busy. It is waiting for no one; it is filling itself with whoever shows up. So show up for the work no one has assigned. Show up for the neighbor whose name you have not learned. Show up when it is cold, when it is unnoticed, when the applause has gone home. You will not be remembered for the diplomas that hang in your offices. You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there. In the sentence "You will be remembered, if you are lucky, for the mornings you were still there," the phrase "if you are lucky" is set off with commas because it is:

    • A restrictive modifier that limits the meaning of “remembered” and so cannot be removed without changing the sentence
    • A series item that belongs to a list of three conditions of being remembered and so needs commas on both sides
    • A coordinate adjective that modifies “mornings” together with another and is therefore separated by a comma
    • A parenthetical element that interrupts the main clause
    • The subject of the clause, which is why it needs to be separated from the verb that follows it

    Nonessential interrupting phrases are set off by commas on both sides.

  4. The documentary promises "the untold story" of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before, mostly by the same three engineers, mostly at the same podium. We are shown the concrete in slow motion. We are shown the river in slow motion. The only thing not in slow motion is the film's opinion, which arrives at 90 seconds per minute: the dam was a triumph, its critics were sentimental, and the displaced families, whom we meet briefly, were "part of the cost of progress." The phrase is spoken as though cost were a kind of consolation. It is not. A film may admire a dam. It should not need to pretend that no one stood where the water now stands. Which revision of the first sentence would most improve clarity without changing its meaning? "The documentary promises 'the untold story' of the dam, which is a curious claim for a film whose every sequence has been told before."

    • Replacing “promises” with “promised” to match the past tense
    • Deleting “curious,” which removes the reviewer's skeptical judgment
    • Moving “before” to the start, which shifts the sentence's emphasis
    • Replacing "which is" with a dash before "a curious claim"
    • Replacing “whose” with “who's” so the pronoun refers to the film

    A dash can set off the comment on the claim while keeping the grammar correct. 'Who's' would be an error, and the others alter meaning or tense.

  5. I came to the marsh in March, when the ice had loosened its grip but not yet let go, when the reeds stood in last year's gold and the first red-winged blackbirds, who arrive before the weather has agreed to welcome them, were already shouting their claims from the cattails. I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology: the quiet of a place that has been drained, and filled, and drained again. Instead there was an insistence so complete that I stood for a long time not trying to name it, only learning what it is to be unnecessary to a place that is entirely alive. The sentence "I had expected silence. I had expected, I think, a kind of apology" contains repetition of "I had expected." Which description is most accurate?

    • Faulty parallelism that should be revised, since the second clause repeats the first without adding a new idea
    • A comma splice that joins two independent clauses without a conjunction and should be corrected in revision
    • A run-on sentence in which the clauses are fused without punctuation and so confuse the reader about the point
    • Anaphora that emphasizes the narrator's mistaken assumptions
    • Redundancy that should be deleted for concision, since repeating “I had expected” adds no information to the sentence

    The repetition is deliberate, creating rhythm and underscoring the contrast with what follows.

  6. Mistakes were made in the handling of customer data, and we regret any inconvenience that may have been experienced. Steps are being taken to ensure that such matters are addressed going forward. We want our customers to know that their privacy remains a priority and that the company has always been committed to the highest standards. An internal review has been initiated, and its findings will be shared as appropriate. Which revision of "Mistakes were made" would most directly add an agent?

    • "We made mistakes in how we handled customer data."
    • “Mistakes had been made.” This changes the tense but leaves the doer of the action unnamed
    • “Some mistakes were being made.” This makes the action continuous but still does not say who made them
    • “There were mistakes made.” This begins with an expletive construction and so again leaves the actor out
    • “Mistakes occurred.” This uses an active verb, but the mistakes appear to happen with no one responsible

    Using the first-person active voice names the actor; the others remain passive or agentless.

Unit 11: GrAmSS (44)

  1. In "Young Goodman Brown," Hawthorne has the devil say that Brown's forebears were his friends and co-workers in violence. A careful reader would most reasonably conclude that this claim is meant to:

    • Be accepted as an accurate history of Salem, which the reader can use to judge the village’s character
    • Reveal that the devil is the narrator of the tale, since only he could know what Brown’s family had done
    • Prove that Brown’s father was a villain, so that Brown’s decision to join the meeting is justified
    • Provide a realistic account of Puritan life, in which cruelty toward outsiders was common in every family
    • Show that the traveler is unreliable in every statement, so that nothing he says can be trusted at all
    • Function as a temptation whose truth cannot be verified, so its power depends on Brown's willingness to believe it

    The devil is a tempter whose claims serve his purpose; the story keeps their truth unverifiable, which makes Brown's belief the crucial act.

  2. Which of the following most accurately describes the difference between Hawthorne's ambiguity in "Young Goodman Brown" and Poe's ambiguity in "The Fall of the House of Usher"?

    • Both authors state plainly that the events were imaginary, and each one differs only in how he explains the dream
    • Hawthorne’s story is allegorical and Poe’s is realistic, so that only Hawthorne’s ambiguity has a moral purpose
    • Poe’s ambiguity concerns the moral of the tale, while Hawthorne’s concerns only the order in which things happen
    • Hawthorne’s narrator is first person while Poe’s is third person, which explains why Poe’s tale is more doubtful
    • They are identical in kind, because in each story the central event may be a dream and the narrator says so
    • Hawthorne questions whether events occurred at all, while Poe questions whether the narrator's perceptions can be trusted

    Hawthorne leaves open whether the night happened ("Had Goodman Brown fallen asleep...?"); Poe's first-person narrator is emotionally colored, leaving his perceptions open to doubt.

  3. Which feature of Irving's narration most clearly distinguishes the narrator of "Rip Van Winkle" from a straightforward historian?

    • His use of citations to older Dutch records, which gives each historical claim a source the reader can check
    • His objective tone, which keeps the narrator from commenting on the characters or the events he describes
    • His comic exaggeration and mock-heroic comparisons, which signal that he is performing the role of historian
    • His reliance on documents and eyewitness reports, which he quotes at length to establish what truly occurred
    • His use of the first person, which makes him a participant in the story’s events and not a distant recorder
    • His refusal to describe characters in any detail, which leaves the reader to imagine them from their actions

    The narrator's persona is playful and satirical, undermining the authority he affects.

  4. In "The Fall of the House of Usher," the narrator reads aloud from a romance whose sounds seem to echo within the house. Which interpretation best accounts for the effect of this device on the story's themes?

    • It collapses the distinction between fiction and reality, mirroring the collapse of the narrator's and Usher's grasp of what is real
    • It lightens the tone with humor, offering the reader a break from the dread that has built up through the story
    • It demonstrates that the house is not haunted, since each sound has a natural cause within the romance being read
    • It shows that the narrator is an author, so that the reader understands why he has so much interest in the book
    • It is an unrelated digression that delays the climax and has little connection with the themes of the main plot
    • It proves that Roderick is a liar who has invented his sister’s illness in order to keep the narrator in the house

    The embedded story's events seem to come true, dissolving boundaries between narrative and reality.

  5. In "The Eve of St. Agnes," the final stanzas return to the Beadsman and Angela. Which reading of this return is best supported by the poem's structure?

    • It reveals that the lovers were captured by the household and punished, so that the poem ends in defeat
    • It shows that the Beadsman is the poem’s true hero, since his prayers have made the lovers’ escape possible
    • It frames the lovers' escape within a world of age, death and cold piety, giving the romance a sense of transience
    • It introduces a new conflict between the lovers and the Baron, which the poem leaves unresolved at its close
    • It undermines the lovers’ love as false by showing that those who remain behind are more faithful to the saint
    • It resolves the family feud by showing that the household accepts the lovers’ flight and wishes them happiness

    The coda mirrors the cold opening and places the lovers' warmth against mortality.

  6. Which of the following is the most defensible claim about the use of symbolism in the unit's prose texts?

    • Symbols in these stories point to a single moral that each author intends, although the objects themselves are described realistically in the text
    • Hawthorne's symbols are ambiguous, but Poe's and Irving's objects have fixed meanings that the narrators make explicit to the reader
    • Symbols in these stories are most meaningful when interpreted through the authors' biographies rather than through their context within the text
    • Objects such as the ribbon, the fissure and the tavern sign are symbolic in the unit's poems but are literal details in the prose narratives, where the narrators give readers no reason to look beyond them
    • Objects like Hawthorne's ribbon and staff, Poe's fissure and Irving's tavern sign carry meanings that depend on their context and can be read in more than one way
    • The symbols in the prose texts are interchangeable, since each of them represents the same idea of hidden corruption in a community

    Each symbol is context-dependent and open to interpretation, which is why textual evidence is needed.

  7. A student claims that Irving's story is ultimately about the persistence of private life amid public upheaval. Which detail offers the strongest support?

    • Rip meets the ghosts of Hendrick Hudson’s crew and drinks their liquor, which shows how far the mountain lies from the village
    • Rip’s old inn now carries a portrait of George Washington in place of the king, which shows how the village has changed
    • Rip's primary concern on returning is his family and identity rather than the political upheaval, and he settles into storytelling
    • Rip’s village is Dutch in its customs and speech, which shows that the tale concerns a local community and not the nation
    • Rip’s dog Wolf is the only creature in the story that welcomes him, which shows that Rip’s loyalties are private ones
    • Peter Vanderdonk, the village historian, confirms the legend of the mountain, which shows that local tradition outlasts events

    Rip's focus on personal bewilderment and eventual domestic comfort supports the claim.

  8. Which of the following best explains how Poe's diction in describing the House of Usher contributes to the story's effect?

    • Concrete scientific terms give the description an objective air, so the narrator seems to record the house without feeling
    • Dialect gives the passage a regional flavor, which roots the house in a particular place and in the speech of its people
    • Colloquial phrases create a casual tone, so that the horror of the house seems ordinary to the narrator
    • Abstract, intensifying words like 'insufferable' and 'melancholy' attribute emotion to the setting, so the atmosphere seems to act on the narrator
    • Short, simple words create a sense of speed, which makes the narrator’s approach to the house seem hurried and tense
    • Technical terms from architecture dominate the passage, and the narrator therefore reports the house with a builder’s eye

    Emotionally loaded abstractions produce a pervasive dread that attaches to the setting.

  9. Which statement best describes how Twain's tall tale exploits the conventions of oral storytelling?

    • The narrator hesitates and corrects himself often, so that the story seems to be a hesitant memory and not a performance
    • The narrator uses scientific terms to explain the jay’s behavior, so that the absurd events seem to be a report of fact
    • The narrator refuses to give details of the cabin and the jays, which leaves the audience to imagine the scene for itself
    • The narrator warns the audience not to believe him, which tells them that the story is a joke before it begins
    • The narrator uses archaic diction that gives the tale the dignity of a legend and lifts it above ordinary speech
    • The narrator treats absurd claims with deadpan seriousness, uses dialect and builds toward an increasingly ridiculous scene, as in a told story

    Deadpan exaggeration, dialect and escalation are staples of the tall tale.

  10. Consider the sentence from Hawthorne's conclusion: "Often, awaking suddenly at midnight, he shrank from the bosom of Faith." What does the sentence most suggest about the effect of the forest experience?

    • Brown is cured of his doubts by the forest and returns to Faith with renewed trust
    • Faith is angry with Brown for what he did in the forest, and he draws away from her because of her reproach
    • Brown grows more affectionate toward his wife, as though he had learned how easily he might lose her
    • Brown has forgotten the events of that night, which now seem a strange dream he wishes to avoid
    • Brown's suspicion survives into his intimate life, so the damage is not only public but domestic
    • The sentence describes a nightly habit that reflects a physical illness rather than any change in Brown's outlook

    The detail extends the consequence into the most private area of his life.

  11. In what way does Keats's use of the Spenserian stanza in "The Eve of St. Agnes" most significantly reinforce the poem's content?

    • Its brevity matches the poem’s plain style, since each stanza is short enough to be read quickly and without effort
    • Its elaborate, flowing rhyme scheme and lingering final line match the poem's sensuous, dreamlike richness
    • It imitates the rhythms of ordinary speech, so the poem seems to be a conversation between the speaker and the reader
    • It creates a comic effect, since the long final line seems to deflate the solemn feeling of each stanza
    • It gives a sense of fragmentation, since each stanza ends abruptly and so breaks the continuity of the narrative
    • It prevents any narrative from developing, so the poem is a series of pictures and does not tell a continuous story

    The interlocking rhymes and extended final line support the lush, lingering mood.

  12. Which of the following would be the most persuasive thesis for an essay comparing Hawthorne and Poe?

    • Hawthorne and Poe both use gloomy settings to create atmosphere, but Hawthorne's story is longer and more allegorical than Poe's, which shows his greater ambition
    • Both authors externalize inner turmoil through setting, and both locate evil in the supernatural rather than in human psychology or society
    • Both authors use settings to externalize inner turmoil, but Hawthorne locates the source of evil in social and spiritual hypocrisy while Poe locates it in psychological and familial decay
    • Hawthorne locates evil in the community and Poe in the house, which shows that setting matters more to Poe than to Hawthorne
    • Because Hawthorne wrote about Puritans and Poe about aristocrats, their stories show that evil depends mainly on a character's social class
    • Hawthorne and Poe both depict evil as inherited, so their stories argue that guilt passes from one generation to the next

    A strong comparison identifies a shared technique and a precise, defensible difference.

  13. Irving's phrase "petticoat government" is best understood as which rhetorical choice?

    • A literal description of the colonial government, which was then administered largely by the wives of its officials
    • A symbol of the Revolution, in which the petticoat stands for the colonists’ rejection of their king’s authority
    • An allusion to a historical event, the Petticoat Rebellion, which the original readers of the tale would have known
    • A humorous metaphor that borrows political terms for a domestic situation
    • A euphemism for a crime that Rip’s wife committed against him, which the narrator prefers not to name outright
    • A technical term from the law of the period that describes a household governed by the wife

    The phrase applies the vocabulary of government to the household, a mock-heroic comparison.

  14. Which feature of "Young Goodman Brown" most strongly supports a reading of the story as allegory?

    • The setting in a particular village, which gives the story a historical and local character that a general fable lacks
    • The use of dialogue between the characters, which keeps the action moving and lets each speaker reveal who he is
    • The story’s brevity, which allows the author to keep the reader’s attention fixed on a single sequence of events
    • The story’s historical period, which is carefully fixed by details of dress and speech that the author provides
    • The story’s use of the first person, which makes the narrator a character whose reliability the reader must judge
    • Characters and objects whose names and attributes (Faith, the serpent staff, the ribbon) correspond to abstract moral ideas

    Allegory pairs concrete elements with abstract meanings; the names and symbols here do so.

  15. In "The Fall of the House of Usher," the narrator's decision to flee the house after Madeline's appearance primarily serves which function in the story's structure?

    • It reveals the narrator as a coward who lacks the courage to help his friend, so that it defines his character for the reader
    • It resolves the story's romantic plot, since the narrator's flight leaves Madeline and Roderick to die together in peace
    • It introduces a new conflict between the narrator and the house, which the story leaves unresolved after he escapes it
    • It suggests that the narrator is the hidden villain, since he was present when each event took place and so shares the blame
    • It indicates that the narrator caused the collapse of the house by disturbing the vault in which Madeline had been laid
    • It provides an outside witness to the collapse, allowing the final image to be described while preserving the narrator's role as observer

    He escapes so that he can report the house's destruction, completing the frame.

  16. Which of the following best explains why Irving includes a postscript from the fictional historian in which he affirms the story's truth?

    • It extends the mock-historical frame and gives a final, tongue-in-cheek assurance
    • It corrects the story's errors and gives a more reliable account of the legend
    • It adds a serious political argument about the Revolution that the story had hinted at
    • It reveals that the story is a forgery, so readers must reconsider the historian
    • It changes the ending so that Rip returns to the mountain and leaves his village
    • It introduces a second narrator who disagrees with the first on the story's truth

    The postscript maintains the comic pose of historical authority.

  17. What is the most significant way in which "The Haunted Palace" functions within "The Fall of the House of Usher"?

    • It interrupts the plot with comic relief, since the poem’s imagery is so exaggerated as to seem a parody of grief
    • It introduces a new character, a king whose palace stands for the house and whose fate the story will later repeat
    • It offers a compressed allegory of Usher's mind that foreshadows the house's and his own ruin
    • It describes a historical event, the fall of an ancient dynasty, which Usher says that his family had once suffered
    • It is a hymn praising the house and its family, which Usher composed in a happier time and now sings with pride
    • It explains why Madeline is ill, since the poem tells how her sickness came from a curse laid upon the house

    The poem's descent from splendor to horror mirrors Usher's mental decline and prefigures the ending.

  18. A student claims that Twain's tall tale is, among other things, a satire of human behavior. Which element offers the strongest support?

    • The jay's absurd persistence and the jeering audience of jays mirror human stubbornness and mockery
    • The mention of a cabin that stands empty and abandoned, which shows how the jay’s labor has gone unseen
    • The use of dialect in the narrator’s speech, which shows how the miner’s language differs from the writer’s own
    • The mention of a miner who tells the story, which shows that the tale comes from a man who has seen jays
    • The mention of an owl that watches the jays from a tree, which shows that nature is indifferent to their labor
    • The mention of an acorn, which is the object the jay drops into the hole and which shows his simple purpose

    The animals' behavior is rendered in human terms, which implicitly comments on people.

  19. In "Rip Van Winkle," which statement best describes the relationship between the story's humor and its treatment of historical change?

    • The humor softens the upheaval of the Revolution by viewing it through an ordinary man's bewilderment
    • The humor mocks the Revolution as foolish and vain, so that Rip's sleep seems the wisest way to live through it
    • The humor is unrelated to the theme of historical change, since its jokes concern Rip's marriage and idle habits
    • The humor celebrates war and the heroes of the Revolution, whose deeds the narrator praises in an extravagant tone
    • The humor is bitter and angry, since the narrator resents the changes that the Revolution has brought to the village
    • The humor is absent from Rip's return, which the narrator describes with serious and tragic feeling

    Comedy renders historical change human-scaled and gentle.

  20. Which of the following is the most accurate description of the way Hawthorne handles the question of Faith's fate in the forest scene?

    • He declares that she is lost to the devil, so that Brown’s despair at the end of the scene is entirely justified
    • He confirms that she is saved by her faith, so that Brown’s later doubts are shown to be mistaken and unjust
    • He leaves unresolved whether she is truly present or a figment of Brown's fear, which keeps the story's central uncertainty alive
    • He shows that she is the devil in disguise, which accounts for Brown’s horror at seeing her among the converts
    • He reveals that she is a witch who has deceived her husband, so that his withdrawal from her is justified
    • He ignores her fate in the forest and returns to it only in the last paragraph, where he mentions her briefly

    Brown's last glimpse and the morning's evidence leave Faith's role open.

  21. In "The Eve of St. Agnes," the contrast between the Beadsman's cold, ascetic prayer and Madeline's chamber of warmth and color most directly presents which tension?

    • Between wealth and poverty, as the cold of the chapel contrasts with the rich furnishings of the castle’s great hall
    • Between youth and political power, as the young lovers defy a household governed by older and more powerful men
    • Between city and country, as the lovers’ flight takes them out of the castle and into the wild landscape beyond
    • Between spiritual renunciation and sensuous, earthly love
    • Between science and religion, as the Beadsman’s prayers are set against Porphyro’s scheming and practical resourcefulness
    • Between reason and madness, as Madeline’s dream of her lover disturbs her judgment and leads her to a rash decision

    Keats juxtaposes ascetic devotion with sensual romance.

  22. Which of the following best distinguishes the way the unit's authors use setting to shape theme?
