    • Hawthorne uses a literal wilderness, Poe a symbolic house, Irving a realistic mountain, Keats a historical castle, and Twain a cabin as a serious backdrop
    • Hawthorne uses a symbolic wilderness, Poe a personified house, Irving a folkloric mountain, Keats a richly sensory chamber, and Twain a cabin as comic stage
    • Each author uses setting chiefly to establish mood, so that the themes of the texts are independent of the particular places where events occur
    • Hawthorne and Poe use settings symbolically, while Irving, Keats and Twain use settings to place the action in a particular time and space without shaping theme
    • Irving and Twain use setting to create comedy at the expense of theme, while Hawthorne, Poe and Keats use it to create horror in the reader
    • Setting in the prose texts shapes theme, while setting in the two poems is decorative and has little bearing on the meaning of either poem

    Each setting is tailored to its work's tone and theme.

  23. A student wants to argue that the narrators in the unit shape readers' sympathies. Which pair provides the clearest contrast in narrative stance?

    • Hawthorne’s and Poe’s, because both use a first-person narrator who is a participant in the story’s events
    • Twain’s and Keats’s, because both use dialect to give the narrator an air of rustic honesty and good humor
    • Irving’s and Twain’s, because both are third-person narrators who observe events from a distance without comment
    • Keats’s and Hawthorne’s, because both are poets whose narrators remain apart from the events they describe
    • Irving's amused historian, who invites affectionate laughter at Rip, and Poe's anxious observer, who invites dread
    • Poe’s and Twain’s, because both are historians who present their tales as accurate records of events that took place

    The tone and reliability of the narrators shape how readers feel.

  24. Identify the person being spoken to in: “Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!”

    • The narrator
    • Madeline
    • A servant
    • The family physician
    • Himself alone
    • The house

    Usher is speaking to the narrator, who has been reading aloud to him.

  25. In “The Fall of the House of Usher,” the pronoun “she” in “she now stands without the door” refers to

    • The narrator’s wife
    • A servant
    • A figure from the romance being read
    • Usher’s mother
    • Madeline
    • The house itself

    Usher believes his entombed sister Madeline has come to the door.

  26. In “The Eve of St. Agnes,” the pronoun “his” in “while his frosted breath, / Like pious incense from a censer old, / Seem’d taking flight for heaven” refers to

    • Porphyro
    • Angela’s husband
    • The priest of the chapel
    • The Baron
    • Madeline’s father
    • The Beadsman

    The Beadsman’s cold breath rises like incense as he prays.

  27. Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “a staff, which bore the likeness of a great black snake, so curiously wrought that it might almost be seen to twist and wriggle itself like a living serpent”? I. Simile II. Allusion III. Hyperbole

    • II and III only
    • II only
    • I and II only
    • III only
    • I and III only
    • I, II, and III

    “like a living serpent” is a simile and the snake evokes the serpent of Eden (allusion). The description is vivid but not an exaggeration.

  28. Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “a sharp tongue is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use”? I. Metaphor II. Paradox III. Alliteration

    • I only
    • I and II only
    • II only
    • I and III only
    • III only
    • I, II, and III

    The tongue is metaphorically an edged tool; the idea that use sharpens it is witty but not a paradox in the strict sense, and there is no meaningful alliteration.

  29. Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “the vacant eye-like windows”? I. Personification II. Imagery III. Onomatopoeia

    • II and III only
    • II only
    • III only
    • I and II only
    • I and III only
    • I, II, and III

    The house is given eyes (personification) and the phrase appeals to the visual sense (imagery).

  30. Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “Like pious incense from a censer old”? I. Simile II. Imagery III. Irony

    • I, II, and III
    • II only
    • III only
    • I and III only
    • I and II only
    • II and III only

    The breath is compared to incense with “like,” and the image is visual and olfactory. There is no irony in the line.

  31. Which of the following devices is (are) present in the description of Rip’s reaction to the Revolution: “there was one species of despotism under which he had long groaned, and that was—petticoat government”? I. Irony II. Metaphor III. Understatement

    • II and III only
    • II only
    • I and II only
    • III only
    • I and III only
    • I, II, and III

    The mock-political language is ironic and “petticoat government” is metonymy, a garment standing for a wife’s rule; the line is not understated.

  32. Which of the following devices is (are) present in: “The deep and dark tarn at my feet closed sullenly and silently over the fragments of the ‘House of Usher’”? I. Personification II. Alliteration III. Hyperbole

    • I and II only
    • II and III only
    • II only
    • III only
    • I and III only
    • I, II, and III

    The tarn “closed sullenly,” attributing a mood to water (personification), and “deep and dank” and “sullenly and silently” repeat sounds (alliteration).

  33. Based on the passage, which of the following would Rip Van Winkle most likely agree with?

    • Hard work is the foundation of good character
    • A person should have time to enjoy company and idleness
    • Wives should manage the finances of a household
    • Political change is the most important event in a person’s life
    • Rip’s neighbors are lazy
    • Land ownership requires constant toil

    Rip prefers fishing, hunting and neighborly conversation to farm work and takes political change lightly.

  34. Based on the passage, which of the following would Dame Van Winkle most likely disagree with?

    • Scolding her husband for his idleness
    • The need to repair the fences
    • The importance of providing for the children
    • Doing household chores
    • Rip’s habit of avoiding his farm work
    • The usefulness of a thrifty housekeeper

    She constantly berates Rip for neglecting his duties, so she would oppose his idleness.

  35. Based on the passage, which of the following would Roderick Usher most likely agree with?

    • A friend's visit can relieve an illness of the mind
    • His sister's illness has little effect on his own state of mind
    • The family name matters little, and its line may end with him
    • Music offers little comfort to a mind as troubled as his own
    • The narrator is a stranger whose company he does not welcome
    • The house and its family are bound together in a fatal way

    Usher believes in the sentience of the house and links it with his family’s fate.

  36. All of the following are true of Rip Van Winkle EXCEPT:

    • He enjoys helping his neighbors
    • He avoids household chores
    • He is a favorite with children
    • He is eager to farm his own land
    • He is sociable in the village
    • He sleeps for many years

    Irving stresses his aversion to work on his own farm.

  37. All of the following are true of the village after Rip’s sleep EXCEPT:

    • Nicholas Vedder is still alive
    • The portrait on the sign has changed
    • Rip’s wife is dead
    • His daughter is grown and married
    • The old inn has changed
    • Rip’s gun is rusted

    Nicholas Vedder has died; his gravestone is seen in the churchyard.

  38. All of the following are descriptions of the stranger Rip meets in the mountains EXCEPT:

    • A short, stout old man with a grizzled beard
    • A man in the antique Dutch dress of the previous century
    • A tall, slender man in modern dress
    • A man with a grizzled beard and bushy hair
    • A man carrying a keg who beckons Rip to help him
    • A man who silently signals Rip to follow him up the ravine

    The stranger wears old-fashioned Dutch clothing, so “modern dress” is false.

  39. All of the following are used to characterize the traveler in “Young Goodman Brown” EXCEPT:

    • His carrying a Bible
    • His resemblance to Brown
    • His staff that looks like a snake
    • His fine, grave dress
    • His traveling in the forest at night
    • His claim that he knew Brown’s ancestors

    He carries a staff, not a Bible.

  40. All of the following are true of the house of Usher EXCEPT:

    • It is old and decayed
    • It has a visible fissure
    • It has a vault
    • It is surrounded by a tarn
    • It stands in a cheerful valley
    • It has vacant, eye-like windows

    The setting is bleak and gloomy, not cheerful.

  41. Which of the following lists the events of “Rip Van Winkle” in the order they occur? I. Rip meets the stranger carrying a keg II. Rip returns to a changed village III. Rip sleeps for twenty years

    • I, II, III
    • II, I, III
    • III, I, II
    • II, III, I
    • III, II, I
    • I, III, II

    Rip meets the stranger, drinks the liquor and sleeps, then returns to the changed village.

  42. Which of the following lists the events of “Young Goodman Brown” in the order they occur? I. Brown meets Goody Cloyse II. Brown leaves Faith at the doorstep III. Brown sees the pink ribbon fall

    • I, II, III
    • III, I, II
    • II, I, III
    • II, III, I
    • I, III, II
    • III, II, I

    He leaves Faith, meets Goody Cloyse on the road, then sees the ribbon.

  43. Which of the following lists the events of “The Fall of the House of Usher” in the order they occur? I. The narrator reads the “Mad Trist” II. Madeline is entombed III. The house falls into the tarn

    • I, II, III
    • III, I, II
    • II, III, I
    • II, I, III
    • I, III, II
    • III, II, I

    Madeline is entombed, the narrator reads the “Mad Trist,” and then the house falls.

  44. Which of the following lists the events of “The Eve of St. Agnes” in the order they occur? I. Porphyro enters the castle II. Madeline prepares for sleep III. The lovers flee

    • II, I, III
    • III, I, II
    • I, III, II
    • II, III, I
    • I, II, III
    • III, II, I

    Porphyro hides, Madeline prepares for bed, and they flee at the end.

Press Enter or Space to flip the card. Left and right arrows move between cards. 1 marks it known, 2 marks it still learning.

Unit 1: The Rhetorical Situation

SOAPSTone
A framework for analyzing a text's rhetorical situation: Speaker, Occasion, Audience, Purpose, Subject, Tone.
Exigence
The specific problem, need, or urgency that makes a piece of writing necessary at that moment.
Purpose
What the writer wants the audience to think, feel, or do — always phrased as 'to ___.'
Constraints
Limits on a writer, such as word count, audience expectations, or what's appropriate for the occasion.
Kairos
The opportune moment: fitting the argument to the right time, audience, and circumstances.
Rhetorical triangle
The relationship among speaker (ethos), audience (pathos), and subject/message (logos).
Purpose (phrasing)
Always a verb phrase: 'to convince [specific audience] that/to ___.'
Audience analysis
Identifying the specific readers' values, assumptions, and knowledge so appeals can be aimed at them.

Unit 2: Rhetorical Appeals & Logical Fallacies

Ethos
An appeal to credibility and character — why the audience should trust the speaker.
Pathos
An appeal to emotion, designed to make the audience feel something that moves them toward the writer's position.
Logos
An appeal to logic and reason, using facts, statistics, and clear chains of reasoning.
Ad hominem
A logical fallacy that attacks the person making an argument instead of the argument itself.
Straw man
A logical fallacy that misrepresents an opponent's argument as weaker than it really is, then attacks that weak version.
False dilemma
A logical fallacy presenting only two options when more actually exist.
Ethos / pathos / logos
Appeals to the speaker's credibility, the audience's emotions, and logical reasoning, respectively.
False dilemma (either/or)
Presenting only two options when more exist.
Post hoc, ergo propter hoc
Assuming that because one event followed another, the first caused the second.
Hasty generalization
Drawing a broad conclusion from too little or unrepresentative evidence.
Appeal to authority
Citing an authority as support; a fallacy when the authority is irrelevant or offered as the sole proof.
Deductive vs. inductive reasoning
Deductive: general principle to specific conclusion. Inductive: specific cases to a general (provisional) claim.
Persona
The character a writer projects through language, tone, and stance - not the same as the real author.

Unit 3: Rhetorical Devices & Figurative Language

Anaphora
Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences.
Antithesis
Placing two contrasting ideas in a parallel grammatical structure.
Juxtaposition
Putting two things side by side for effect, such as Baker's earnest tone against a ridiculous tale.
Metaphor
A direct comparison between two unlike things, without using 'like' or 'as.'
Rhetorical question
A question asked for effect rather than to get a literal answer, leading the reader to a conclusion.
Epistrophe
Repetition of a word or phrase at the end of successive clauses.
Chiasmus
A reversal of grammatical structure in successive phrases ('ask not what... what you can do...').
Asyndeton
Omitting conjunctions between items in a list, speeding the pace ('I came, I saw, I conquered').
Polysyndeton
Repeating conjunctions between items ('and... and... and'), slowing the pace and adding weight.
Metaphor vs. simile
A metaphor states a comparison directly; a simile uses 'like' or 'as.'
Extended metaphor
A single comparison developed across multiple sentences or an entire passage.
Allusion
A brief, indirect reference to a person, place, text or idea of historical, cultural, literary or political significance; relies on the reader's knowledge.
Litotes
Understatement by negating the opposite ('not a small problem'), often for dry emphasis.
Verbal irony
Saying the opposite of what is meant, expecting the audience to catch the gap; sarcasm is a pointed form.

Unit 4: Style: Diction, Syntax & Tone

Denotation
A word's literal, dictionary definition.
Connotation
The emotional association attached to a word, beyond its literal meaning.
Syntax
How a writer arranges words and constructs sentences — a rhetorical choice in itself.
Tone
The writer's attitude toward the subject, revealed through diction and syntax; it can shift within a passage.
Diction
A writer's word choice, including the connotations those words carry.
Denotation vs. connotation
Denotation is the literal meaning; connotation is the emotional or cultural association.
Tonal shift
A change in attitude within a text, often marked by 'but,' a paragraph break, or a change in sentence length; it signals a turn in the argument.
Periodic sentence
Withholds the main clause until the end, building suspense and emphasis.
Cumulative (loose) sentence
States the main clause first, then adds modifying phrases and detail.
Selection of detail
What a writer chooses to include or omit; itself a form of argument.
Imagery
Language that appeals to the senses, making an abstraction vivid and felt.

Unit 5: Claims, Evidence & Commentary

Claim of value
An argument that something is good, bad, right, or wrong.
Commentary
Analysis that explains WHY evidence matters and HOW it supports the argument — different from summary.
Line of reasoning
The logical thread connecting a thesis through each piece of evidence to a coherent overall argument.
Claim types
Fact (is it true?), value (is it good?), and policy (what should we do?).
Summary vs. commentary
Summary restates what the evidence says; commentary explains HOW it supports the claim.
Qualifying a claim
Narrowing a claim with words like 'often,' 'in most cases,' or a condition, so it fits the evidence.
Relevance vs. sufficiency
Relevant evidence bears on the exact claim; sufficient evidence is enough, and varied enough, to be credible.

Unit 6: Organization, Structure & Counterargument

Thesis
A specific, arguable claim that someone could reasonably disagree with — the core of an essay's argument.
Concession
Acknowledging a valid point on the opposing side of an argument before pivoting back to your own position.
Rebuttal
Directly refuting an opposing point by explaining why it's flawed or less compelling.
Effective thesis
Specific and arguable; it previews a line of reasoning rather than stating an obvious truth.
Given-new principle
Begin a sentence with familiar information and end with the new point, to create flow.
Concede-then-counter
Grant an opposing point, then explain why it does not defeat the thesis ('While X is true, it does not follow that Y').
Transitions
Words that must name the logical relationship between ideas (however, therefore, for instance), not just decorate.
Modes of arrangement
Chronological, cause-effect, problem-solution, comparison-contrast, and climactic (order of importance).
Coherence
The quality of prose that guides the reader from idea to idea without gaps; aided by repeated key terms and clear referents.

Unit 7: The Synthesis Essay

Synthesis essay
An essay that develops the writer's own argument using at least three provided sources as support.
Source-by-source trap
Organizing a synthesis essay by summarizing each source in turn instead of by the writer's own claims — a major weakness.
Synthesis essay requirement
Build an argument using at least three of the provided sources as evidence, cited clearly.
The summary trap
Walking through sources one by one instead of organizing body paragraphs around your own claims.
Signal phrase vs. parenthetical citation
A signal phrase names the source in the sentence ('Source B argues'); a parenthetical puts it at the end ((Source B)).
Defensible thesis
A clear, arguable, often qualified position that the sources can be used to support.
Using disagreeing sources
Use one source to complicate or answer another within a paragraph built on your claim.

Unit 8: The Rhetorical Analysis Essay

Rhetorical analysis essay
An essay explaining HOW a writer builds their argument and its effect on the audience, not whether the reader agrees.
Device-to-effect move
The core rhetorical analysis skill: identify a specific choice, then explain its effect on the audience.
Rhetorical analysis focus
Explain HOW a writer argues and to what effect - not whether you agree with the argument.
Weak vs. strong analysis thesis
Weak: lists devices ('uses ethos, pathos, logos'). Strong: names what the writer does and to what end.
Device-dropping
Naming a strategy and quoting a line without explaining its effect on the audience and purpose.
Depth over breadth
On a timed essay, analyze 2-3 strategies thoroughly rather than listing many.
Claim-evidence-analysis
The core structure of a body paragraph: identify a choice, quote the text, explain the effect.

Unit 9: The Argument Essay

Argument essay
An essay defending the writer's own position on an issue using the writer's own knowledge, with no provided sources.
Sophistication
Demonstrating nuance, qualification, or broader implications in an argument — beyond a simple thesis-evidence structure.
Refutation vs. concession
Refutation directly answers an opposing argument and shows why it fails; concession grants it partial merit.
Evidence depth
One or two well-developed, analyzed examples usually score higher than many shallow ones.

Unit 10: Grammar, Conventions & Multiple-Choice Strategy

Comma splice
An error joining two independent clauses with only a comma; fix with a period, semicolon, or conjunction.
Sentence fragment
A group of words missing a subject, verb, or complete thought, unable to stand alone as a sentence.
Parallel structure
Items in a list or series sharing the same grammatical form.
Run-on sentence
Independent clauses joined with no punctuation or connector at all.
Colon vs. semicolon
A colon follows a complete clause and introduces an explanation or list; a semicolon joins two independent clauses.
MC writing questions
Usually reward the clearest and most concise option, not the longest or most formal.
Redundancy to cut
'past history,' 'end result,' 'the reason ... is because,' 'in order to' when 'to' works.
MC reading questions
Verify every answer choice against the exact wording and context of the passage.

Unit 11: GrAmSS

Unit 1 exam date and scope
Tuesday 10/6. Great American Short Stories, Literary Devices packet, nonfiction and handouts; only Hawthorne text is "Young Goodman Brown".
Romanticism
A movement reacting against Enlightenment rationalism that values emotion, imagination, nature, the individual, the past and the supernatural.
Neoclassicism / Enlightenment
The order-and-reason outlook (rationalism, restraint, science) that Romanticism pushed against.
Washington Irving
American Romantic author (1783-1859) of "Rip Van Winkle", first published in The Sketch Book under the pen name Geoffrey Crayon.
Diedrich Knickerbocker
The fictional historian whose papers frame "Rip Van Winkle" (Irving's playful fake-history device).
Rip Van Winkle: setting and time frame
A Dutch village in the Catskills; Rip sleeps 20 years from British rule under George III into the new American republic.
Dame Van Winkle
Rip's wife, characterized as a shrewish "termagant"/"virago"; Irving's language invites sympathy for Rip.
Wolf
Rip's dog and loyal companion, part of the sympathetic characterization of Rip as easygoing.
What Irving comments on through Rip's sleep
The changes from colony to independent nation: new flag, political arguing, and a village that no longer recognizes him.
The Eve of St. Agnes: legend
On St. Agnes' Eve (Jan 20), a young woman who follows the rituals may dream of her future husband.
The Eve of St. Agnes: main characters
Madeline (the dreamer), Porphyro (her lover from a hostile family), Angela (the old nurse), the Beadsman (opens and closes the poem).
Spenserian stanza
Nine-line stanza rhymed ABABBCBCC, eight lines of iambic pentameter then a longer last line; used throughout Keats's poem.
John Keats
English Romantic poet (1795-1821); wrote "The Eve of St. Agnes" in 1819 (published 1820).
Edgar Allan Poe
American Gothic and Romantic writer (1809-1849); "The Fall of the House of Usher" (1839).
Roderick Usher
The ill, hypersensitive host whose nerves and mind mirror the decaying house.
Madeline Usher
Roderick's twin sister; entombed while appearing dead; her return precedes the collapse.
House of Usher (double meaning)
Both the physical mansion and the family line; the fissure and collapse show the family's end.
"The Haunted Palace"
Poem inside Usher: a once-fair palace of Thought overrun by "evil things"; it mirrors Roderick's mind.
"Mad Trist" and Ethelred
The romance the narrator reads to Roderick; sounds in it echo real noises, foreshadowing Madeline's return.
Unity of effect
Poe's idea that every detail in a story should build one single emotional impact (in Usher, dread).
Gothic
Genre with gloomy settings, decay, madness, death and the supernatural; strong mood.
Mark Twain
Samuel Clemens (1835-1910); wrote "Baker's Bluejay Yarn" (1880), a humorous tall tale.
Yarn
A tale, especially a long story of adventure or incredible happenings, often exaggerated.
Jim Baker
A middle-aged, simple-hearted California miner who tells Twain that bluejays are the most human and best-talking animals.
Anthropomorphism
Giving animate (living) beings human characteristics, like Baker's talking, swearing bluejays.
Personification
Giving inanimate (nonliving) objects human characteristics, like the house's "eye-like windows".
The bluejay and the knothole
Baker's centerpiece: a jay drops acorns into a hole in a cabin roof that leads into an empty house; five thousand jays laugh when they see the acorns on the floor. Possible metaphor for foolish human effort.
Dialect
Writing that captures a region or group's speech; builds Baker's characterization and humor.
Nathaniel Hawthorne
American Dark Romantic (1804-1864); "Young Goodman Brown" (1835) is his only work on Unit 1.
Setting of "Young Goodman Brown"
Puritan Salem Village, Massachusetts; the story moves from town to the dark forest and back.
Faith (in "Young Goodman Brown")
Brown's wife and the loss of his religious faith; the pink ribbons are her symbol of innocence.
The traveler's staff
A staff shaped like a black serpent; a Biblical allusion to the serpent in Eden, marking the traveler as the devil.
Ambiguity in "Young Goodman Brown"
Hawthorne never confirms whether the forest meeting was a dream or real, leaving the theme of doubt and hypocrisy open.
Foreshadowing
Hints or clues about events that come later.
Symbol
An object, person or action that stands for a larger idea, like Faith's pink ribbons.
Allegory
A story in which characters, settings and events stand for moral, spiritual or political ideas.
Characterization: direct vs. indirect
Direct: the narrator states traits. Indirect: traits shown through actions, speech, thoughts, appearance and others' reactions.
Point of view
Who tells the story (first person, third limited, omniscient); shapes what we know and trust.
Mood vs. tone
Mood: the feeling created in the reader. Tone: the author's attitude toward the subject.
Ralph Waldo Emerson
Leading Transcendentalist (1803-1882); the handout is from "The Transcendentalist".
Materialist vs. transcendentalist (Emerson)
Emerson excerpt: the materialist starts from the external world and respects society and social institutions; the idealist (transcendentalist) starts from consciousness and holds that "Mind is the only reality".
James Truslow Adams and the American Dream
Popularized the phrase in The Epic of America (1931): opportunity for each person according to ability, a fuller life for everyone, more than material wealth.
Pivotal question
An open-ended, text-based question that prompts discussion, not a recall question. Start: To what extent, In what ways, For what reasons, How is/does and why is it significant?
MOT routine
Underline evidence, circle the key word, label the mood, and annotate how the words work together.
Termagant
A violent, overbearing, quarrelsome woman; Irving's word for Dame Van Winkle.
Virago
A domineering, ill-tempered woman; another word Irving uses for Dame.
Insuperable aversion
An impossible-to-overcome strong dislike; Rip's attitude toward profitable labor.
Obsequious / conciliating
Obsequious: fawning, overly eager to please. Conciliating: trying to win over or calm.
Alacrity
Brisk, cheerful readiness or eagerness.
Rubicund
Ruddy; having a healthy reddish color.
Junto
A small group or faction, often political, that joins together in secret or for a shared aim.
Approbation
Approval or praise.
Akimbo
With hands on hips and elbows turned out.
Patrimonial
Inherited from one's father or ancestors.
Connubial
Relating to marriage.
Roysterers
Noisy, boisterous revelers.
Beadsman
A man paid or bound to pray for others' souls; the cold, praying old man in Keats's poem.
Seraph / pinion / ramparts
Seraph: an angelic being of the highest order. Pinion: a wing or flight feather. Ramparts: protective earthen or stone walls of a fortress.
Discordant / throng
Discordant: harsh, disagreeing, out of tune. Throng: a large crowd.
STEAL
Five methods of indirect characterization: Speech, Thoughts, Effect on others, Actions, Looks.
Static vs. dynamic character
Static: does not change much in the story. Dynamic: changes in an important way because of the story's action.
Flat vs. round character
Flat: one or two traits, one-dimensional. Round: complex, with many dimensions like real people.
Literary period order
Puritanism (1620-1770s), Neoclassic (1770s-early 1800s), Romanticism (early 1800s-1870s), Realism (1850s-early 1900s).
Transcendentalism (packet definition)
A 19th-century movement in the Romantic tradition holding that every individual can reach ultimate truths through spiritual intuition, which transcends reason and sensory experience.
Horace Walpole
Credited with founding Gothic fiction with The Castle of Otranto (1764), subtitled "A Gothic Story".
Lyrical Ballads
Wordsworth and Coleridge's 1790s collection that began English Romanticism; Wordsworth's Preface called poetry "the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings".
Jonathan Oldstyle / Salmagundi
Irving's first pen name (1802 letters) and the 1807 magazine that nicknamed New York "Gotham".
Irving's Sketch Book
The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent. (1819-20), the collection containing "Rip Van Winkle" and "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow".
Sunnyside
Irving's home on the Hudson where he lived after returning from Spain; he is buried at Sleepy Hollow cemetery nearby.
Hendrick Hudson (in Rip)
The explorer whose crew, per the villagers, still haunt the Catskills and bowl ninepins, explaining the thunder.
Judith Gardenier
Rip's grown daughter; Rip tells her he is her father, and she takes him in to live with her family.
Peter Vanderdonk
The most ancient inhabitant, descended from a historian of the province, who recognizes Rip and corroborates the legend of Hendrick Hudson's crew.
Union Hotel and the sign of General Washington
The changed inn and sign in Rip's village show the switch from King George III to the new republic.
Federal or Democrat?
The question Rip is asked on his return; he does not understand the new political parties and answers as a loyal subject of the King.
Two tons (Baker's jay)
The jay's exaggerated claim of how many acorns he dropped in the hole; hyperbole that fuels the yarn's humor.
Open door in Baker's yarn
The hole led into a cabin; the door is open and acorns are scattered on the floor, revealing the jay's absurd task.
King Philip's War (in YGB)
The 1675-76 New England conflict alluded to when the traveler says Brown's father burned an Indian village.
Salem witch trials (1692)
The Puritan-era events behind Hawthorne's Salem setting; his ancestor John Hathorne was a judge.
Puritan plain style
Simple, clear writing stressing obedience to God; the main form of Puritan writers per the packet.
Refrain
A word, phrase or line repeated for effect, like "round and round she goes" in Rubin's "The Widow's Walk".
Tall tale
An outrageously exaggerated, humorous story that is obviously unbelievable, like Baker's yarn.
Verbal, situational, dramatic irony
Verbal: says one thing, means another. Situational: outcome differs from what is expected. Dramatic: the reader knows more than the character.
Ambiguity
Deliberately suggesting two or more different, sometimes conflicting, meanings; on purpose it is a device, not vagueness.
Metzengerstein (1832)
Poe's story in the Philadelphia Saturday Courier (Jan 14, 1832) where he first used the single-effect technique on which the modern short story is built.
Single effect (Poe)
The technique of building every detail toward one preconceived impression, with the action focused on the climactic moment and the mood controlled from first to last.
Specific gravity (Canby)
Henry Seidel Canby's phrase for the moral or intellectual weight Hawthorne added to the American short story.
Tale of ratiocination
Poe's detective-style tale of reasoning, the parent of the detective story ("The Murders in the Rue Morgue").
Irving vs. Poe (Introduction)
Irving: an orderly tale of linked incidents in chronological order, graceful, humorous, urbane. Poe: a concentrated tale of a single, preconceived effect.
Journey and return (Intro)
The Introduction says Usher and "Young Goodman Brown" both move from light into darkness and back into light; Poe's darkness is theatrical, Hawthorne's is the darkness of the soul.
Situation revealed
Henry James's phrase for the probing story that Hawthorne began: less a complication resolved than an exposed situation.
Twain and the beast fable (Intro)
The Introduction says Twain mastered the humorous frontier sketch and the fable; "Bluejay Yarn" is superb in its own kind and links to Uncle Remus and Thurber.
Local color
Writing that emphasizes a specific place's speech, customs and landscape; the Introduction credits Bret Harte's "The Luck of Roaring Camp" (1868) with popularizing the short story.
Pestilent / patrimonial / urchin
Pestilent: harmful, troublesome. Patrimonial: inherited from a father. Urchin: a mischievous small child (all describing Rip's farm and son).
Assiduity
Steady, careful diligence (Rip has plenty of it, but only for idle pursuits like fishing).
Jargon (Babylonish jargon)
Confusing, hard-to-understand language; Rip cannot follow the election talk.
Torpor
A state of inactivity or deep sleep; Irving's word for Rip's twenty-year sleep.
Corroborate
To confirm; Peter Vanderdonk corroborates Rip's story.
Prithee / afeard / tarry
I pray thee; afraid; stay or wait (from Faith's plea in "Young Goodman Brown").
Scruples / anathema
Scruples: moral doubts. Anathema: a formal curse or denunciation.
Benighted / wanton
Benighted: in darkness, physical or moral. Wanton: immoral, reckless, unrestrained.
Prolixity / fissure / tarn / cadaverousness
Wordiness; a crack; a small mountain lake; corpse-like paleness (Poe's Usher vocabulary).
Leather-headed
Twain's term for stupid or thick-headed, describing the jays' opinions about the hole.
Nicholas Vedder and the junto
The silent landlord whose opinions control the idle bench-sitters at the inn; he has died eighteen years before Rip's return.
Hendrick Hudson and the Halfmoon
Per Peter Vanderdonk, the explorer and his crew keep a vigil in the Kaatskills every twenty years; the thunder is their ninepins.
Rip's last comic line
Henpecked husbands wish for "a quieting draught out of Rip Van Winkle's flagon" (p. 51).
Goody Cloyse and Deacon Gookin
Respected Salem figures Brown sees in the forest; Cloyse taught him his catechism.
Martha Carrier
A woman at the forest ceremony who "received the devil's promise to be queen of hell"; her name is that of an actual Salem witch-trial defendant.
Quotation: "My Faith is gone!"
Brown's cry when the pink ribbon falls; followed by "There is no good on earth; and sin is but a name. Come, devil!"
Quotation: "We have put her living in the tomb!"
Roderick's confession to the narrator that he heard Madeline moving in the coffin (p. 90).
Quotation: "a perfectly elegant hole!"
The jay's first delighted reaction to the knot-hole in the cabin roof (Baker's yarn).
Two tons
The jay's boast of how many acorns he dropped; hyperbole in Baker's yarn.
"The Custom House" — the found-manuscript device
Hawthorne claims The Scarlet Letter comes from a manuscript and a scarlet "A" left by former Surveyor Jonathan Pue, making the invented novel feel like a rediscovered true story.
"The Custom House" — losing his job
A change in presidential administration replaces Hawthorne as Surveyor; he jokes he was "guillotined," but surviving it frees him to finally write the novel.
Situation revealed (James)
The idea that the modern short story is less a plot complication resolved than a situation uncovered, with the ending an illumination, not a trick.
Tale of effect (Poe)
A concentrated story built for one preconceived impression, with all the action aimed at the climax; first used in "Metzengerstein" (Jan. 14, 1832).
Granite to pine
The Introduction's image for Hawthorne's story versus Poe's: Hawthorne's soul-darkness is far denser in specific gravity than Poe's theatrical Gothic.
Why Twain is different (Introduction)
Never wrote a good short story by the editors' standard; mastered the humorous frontier sketch and the fable. The Bluejay Yarn belongs to the beast-story tradition.

Unit 1: The Rhetorical Situation

Identifying the Rhetorical Situation
A retired general publishes an op-ed in a national newspaper the week after a controversial military budget vote, urging Congress to reconsider. Identify SOAPSTone.
Map the rhetorical situation with SOAPSTone
A retired general publishes an op-ed the week Congress debates the defense budget, urging lawmakers to fund veterans' health care before new weapons systems. Break down the rhetorical situation.

Unit 2: Rhetorical Appeals & Logical Fallacies

Naming and Explaining an Appeal
A nonprofit's ad says: 'Dr. Elena Ruiz, a pediatric surgeon with 20 years of experience, warns that delaying this legislation will cost children's lives.' Identify the appeals at work and their effect.
Analyze an appeal, not just label it
A passage reads: 'I have buried men I trained. I have written the letters home. When I tell you this policy costs lives, I am not speculating.' Identify and analyze the appeal.

Unit 3: Rhetorical Devices & Figurative Language

Analyzing a Repetition Device
'We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills.' Identify the device and its effect.
Explain the effect of syntax and repetition
A passage: 'They took the land. They took the language. They took the names of the children and gave them new ones.' Analyze the rhetorical effect.

Unit 4: Style: Diction, Syntax & Tone

Analyzing Diction and Syntax Together
Compare: (A) 'The company terminated 200 employees.' (B) 'Two hundred families lost their livelihoods overnight.' Explain the rhetorical effect of the difference.
Name a precise tone and track a shift
A passage begins with wry, detached observations about a city council meeting ('another Tuesday, another three-hour debate about parking'), then shifts to: 'But behind the tedium, a family was about to lose its home.' Analyze the tone.

Unit 5: Claims, Evidence & Commentary

Turning Evidence into Commentary
Evidence: 'A 2023 study found that students who read 20 minutes daily scored 15% higher on reading assessments.' Write one sentence of commentary (not summary) using this evidence to support the claim that schools should mandate daily reading time.
Turn summary into commentary
A student writes: 'The author notes that 60 percent of the town's water pipes are over a century old.' Add commentary that connects this evidence to a claim that the town has under-invested in basic infrastructure.

Unit 6: Organization, Structure & Counterargument

Writing a Concession and Rebuttal
Claim: schools should eliminate final exams. Write a one-sentence concession followed by a one-sentence rebuttal.
Build a qualified thesis and outline the reasoning
Prompt: Should high schools start later in the morning? Draft a defensible, qualified thesis and a three-part line of reasoning.

Unit 7: The Synthesis Essay

Synthesizing Two Sources into One Point
Source A: 'Remote work increased reported employee satisfaction by 22%.' Source B: 'Companies with remote policies saw a 30% drop in office lease costs.' Write one synthesis sentence using both sources to support the claim that companies should adopt permanent remote work.
Organize a synthesis paragraph by your claim
Synthesis prompt on whether cities should offer free public transit. You have Source A (ridership data), Source C (a budget analysis), and Source E (an equity argument). Draft one body paragraph organized around your claim.

Unit 8: The Rhetorical Analysis Essay

Writing a Device-to-Effect Sentence
A passage uses short, fragmented sentences ('No warning. No time. Just silence.') to describe a disaster's onset. Write a full rhetorical analysis sentence connecting this syntax to its effect.
Write a strong rhetorical analysis thesis
You are analyzing a commencement speech in which the speaker repeatedly contrasts 'the job you take' with 'the person you become,' uses self-deprecating anecdotes, and ends with a direct charge to the graduates. Draft a thesis.

Unit 9: The Argument Essay

Building a Nuanced Thesis
Prompt: 'Is competition beneficial to society?' Write a qualified, sophisticated thesis (not a simple yes/no).
Use concede-then-counter in an argument
You are arguing that public libraries should expand evening hours. A reader objects that staffing costs are already strained. Write a concede-then-counter passage.

Unit 10: Grammar, Conventions & Multiple-Choice Strategy

Fixing a Comma Splice and Checking Parallelism
Revise: 'The committee reviewed the proposal, they approved it unanimously, and are moving to sign, seal, and finalizing the contract.'
Revise a wordy sentence for the MC 'writing' skill
Revise: 'Due to the fact that the committee was not able to reach a consensus decision, it was decided that the vote would be postponed until a later date.'

Unit 11: GrAmSS

Analyzing Twain's anthropomorphism in "Baker's Bluejay Yarn"
In a well-developed paragraph, explain how Twain uses anthropomorphism and Jim Baker's point of view to advance a theme in "Baker's Bluejay Yarn".
Allusion and setting in "Young Goodman Brown"
In what ways is Hawthorne's use of setting and allusion in "Young Goodman Brown" significant? Answer in one cohesive response with evidence.
Which device? Answering a “which is present” question
Which literary device is present in: “A tart temper never mellows with age, and a sharp tongue is the only edged tool that grows keener with constant use”?
Word in context: vocabulary from Rip Van Winkle
In “Rip Van Winkle”, Irving describes Dame Van Winkle as a “termagant.” What does the word most nearly mean, and how do you know?
Chronology: ordering events in Usher
Put these Usher events in order: the house collapses; the narrator arrives; the narrator reads the Mad Trist; Madeline is entombed; Madeline appears at the door.
Speaker and addressee: “Madman! I tell you that she now stands without the door!”
Identify the speaker and the person being spoken to, and explain what the line shows.

SOAPSTone & the Rhetorical Situation

Speaker
Who is writing/speaking, and what do we know about them?
Occasion
What event or context prompted this text?
Audience
Who is the writer specifically trying to reach?
Purpose
Always phrased as 'to ___' — the intended effect
Subject
What the text is specifically about
Tone
The writer's attitude toward the subject
Exigence
The urgent problem making the writing necessary now

The Three Appeals

AppealTargetsBuilt through
EthosCredibilityCredentials, fairness, careful language
PathosEmotionVivid imagery, anecdotes, charged language
LogosLogicStatistics, data, clear reasoning

Common Rhetorical Devices

Anaphora
Repetition at the START of successive clauses
Epistrophe
Repetition at the END of successive clauses
Antithesis
Contrasting ideas in parallel structure
Chiasmus
Reversed grammatical structure across clauses
Juxtaposition
Placing two things side by side to highlight contrast
Metaphor
Direct comparison, no 'like/as'
Simile
Comparison using 'like' or 'as'
Hyperbole
Deliberate exaggeration for effect
Understatement
Deliberately downplaying for effect
Anadiplosis
Repeating a clause's last word to start the next

Common Logical Fallacies

FallacyWhat it does
Ad hominemAttacks the person, not the argument
Straw manMisrepresents an argument as weaker to attack it
False dilemmaPresents only two options when more exist
Slippery slopeClaims one step inevitably leads to an extreme end
Hasty generalizationDraws a broad conclusion from too small a sample

The Three Essay Types

EssayCore task
SynthesisYour argument, using ≥3 provided sources as support
Rhetorical AnalysisHOW a writer builds their argument, not whether you agree
ArgumentYour position, defended with your own evidence — no provided sources

Fast Facts

  • Always follow "device identified" with "here's its effect" — labeling alone earns little credit.
  • Subject is what a text is about; purpose is what it wants to accomplish — never confuse the two.
  • Commentary explains WHY evidence matters; summary just restates WHAT it says.
  • A comma splice needs a period, semicolon, or conjunction — not just a deleted comma.
  • Parallel structure means every item in a list shares the same grammatical form.
  • On MC questions, always verify your answer against the actual passage text.
Quick ways to lock in the facts you keep forgetting. Read the big trick, then the small note tells you what it unlocks. Say them out loud — silly is memorable.

Rhetorical Situation

Purpose is a verb, not a noun
Never write "the purpose is technology" — write "to warn readers about..." If it's not phrased as "to ___," it isn't purpose yet.
Subject ≠ Purpose
Subject is WHAT it's about. Purpose is what the writer wants to happen because of it. Two totally different questions, always answer both.

Appeals & Fallacies

E-P-L: Ethics, Passion, Logic
Ethos=credibility (think "ethics"). Pathos=emotion (think "passion" or "sympathy"). Logos=logic (think "logical").
Name it, then explain it
"This is pathos" earns nothing alone. Always finish the sentence: "...which makes the audience feel ___, moving them to ___."
Attack the argument, not the arguer
If the criticism is about the PERSON instead of their actual claim, it's probably ad hominem, not real logos.

Devices

Anaphora starts, epistrophe ends
Anaphora repeats at the BEGINNING of clauses. Epistrophe repeats at the END. Both start with vowels near the front of the alphabet — 'a' comes before 'e,' just like 'anaphora' comes at the start.
Simile has the 'like/as' sibling
'Simile' sounds like 'similar' — it's a comparison, and it always keeps the word 'like' or 'as' as a visible sibling.

Style

Short = sharp, long = layered
Short sentences hit hard and fast. Long sentences build, accumulate, and layer ideas on top of each other.
Ban vague tone words
If your tone word could describe a hundred different passages ('good,' 'bad,' 'interesting'), it's too vague — get specific.

Argument Building

"So what?" after every quote
Every time you cite evidence, silently ask yourself "so what?" — the answer to that question IS your commentary.
Concede, then pivot
"Sure, X has a point, BUT..." is the whole shape of a concession-rebuttal — acknowledge fairly, then turn back to your claim.

The Three Essays

Synthesis = your argument + their sources
Never summarize sources in order. Build YOUR claims first, then drop sources in as support — like citations in a research paper, not a book report.
Rhetorical analysis = HOW, not IF
You are never arguing whether the writer is right. You are only explaining how they built their case and why it works.
Argument = your evidence, no packet
No sources are given — dig into history, current events, or your own experience for real, specific proof.

Grammar

A comma alone can't join two sentences
Two complete sentences need a period, a semicolon, or a comma PLUS a conjunction (and/but/so) — a lone comma creates a splice.
Match the list's grammar
If one item in a series ends in '-ing,' they all should. Mismatched forms in a list is a parallel structure error.
